Page Seven
and irreversible environmental impact would not result. With respect to the parks, national monuments and national historic sites, we note that the encouragement of enjoyment by recreational users is a congressionally established goal which should be actively pursued wherever compatible with the steward-ship or environmental preservation functions of the NPS with respect to such lands.
B. Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife (BSFW) -
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BSFW is responsible for the management of some 30 million acres of public land and is charged with the primary responsibility of the protection and perpetuation of wildlife resources. Historically, BSFW has followed a fairly restrictive use policy similar to that of the National Park Service described above. The Association is in agreement as to the applicability of the "prohibited except where specifically permitted" regulatory approach when applied to BSFW lands. However, it is again emphasized that the Secretary does have a responsibility for promoting recreational use of this land to the extent that such use will not adversely affect environmental values. Accordingly, BSFW should be encouraged to actively review its land areas with a view towards designation of ORRV areas and trails wherever possible under the aforesaid criterion.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eight
C. Bureau of Land Management
As pointed out in the Draft Statement, BLM is responsible for the management of approximately 452 million acres of public land. In general, the BLM lands do not possess the unique scenic, natural, historic or archeological characteristics present in the NPS lands nor do they generally function as important wildlife conservation centers as is the case with the BSFW lands. Public use of BLM lands is generally low density in nature and BLM has limited personnel available for the purpose of enforcing any regulation of ORRV use. Based on these factors. the historical BLM policy with respect to ORRV use has been to permit such use in all areas except those which are closed to such use for a specific reason. The Department's proposed implementation of the Executive Order would apparently reverse this policy and would provide for the confining of ORRV use to areas and trails designated as open to such use. Even in such open areas, ORRV use would be subject to certain controls.
while the Association does not disagree with the goal of imposing reasonable restrictions on ORRV use in any area of the BLM lands, it does strongly disagree with the Department's apparent intention to reverse BLM's historical approach with respect to the classification of lands. For the reasons set forth below, such reversal is not only unwise from an environmental

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Nine
point of view but is also in direct contravention of the Secretary's responsibilities under the 1963 Outdoor Recreation Act. In our opinion, such reversal of policy would have the following aspects:
Indefinite and Unjustified Limitation of Available Outdoor Recreation Resources Pending Completion of Classification - BLM, as noted above, is responsible for the management of over 452 million acres of public land which land is widely dispersed and of highly diverse characteristics. Given existing staff resources, it would be expected that the envisaged classification of all BLM lands into that which is open for use and that which is closed to use will be a project of at least several years in duration. Since no significant amount of public lands has yet been classified as opened to ORRV use, the effect of the proposed sudden reversal in policy will be to close all BLM lands to ORRV use until the above-referenced classification scheme is completed. Thus, the proposed scheme of regulation would presume that ORRV use - a beneficial recreational activity - is environmentally objectionable until the contrary is proven. It is submitted that such policy is not reasonably calculated to promote and develop recreational resources for the American people. To the contrary, it seems more reasonably calculated to have the opposite result. The appropriateness

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Ten
of such a policy is clearly questionable in light of the manifest Congressional intention set forth in the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963. There is no justification for this contravention of Congressional policy either by reference to the characteristics of BLM lands or by any demonstration of environmental damages which have resulted from the historical implementation of the present open use policy.
2. Concentration of ORRV Use Within the

Specifically Defined Areas  As noted above, ORRV use
on BLM lands is now widely dispersed and it is clear that
such low density use tends to have a less significant\nenvironmental impact than high density use in designated
areas. The effect of the reversal in policy referenced
above would be, especially in the earlier years of the
policy's implementation, to concentrate ORRV use in such
areas as have been specifically classified as open. Thus,
with respect to BLM lands, the proposed reversal in policy
would not protect the environment but, by concentration of
ORRV use in certain areas, would tend to heighten any impact
which such use might have.
3. Placing of Impossible Burdens Upon BLM

Enforcement Personnel  As indicated above, BLM has limited staff resources and, even assuming that such staff is adequate to evaluate and classify all of the 452 million

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Eleven
acres of public domain land under BLM jurisdiction, it is ludicrous to expect that staff to post and deny public access to all of such lands except those that are specifically classified as open. If, on the other hand, BLM is permitted to follow its existing policy of focusing on the specific areas where adverse environmental impact is likely to occur and devoting its resources towards the exclusion of ORRV users from those specified areas, there is at least some hope of achieving an effective scheme of regulation which will be adhered to by the users.
Compared to these apparent and significant adverse impacts of reversal of existing BLM policy, the only advantage of such reversal of which we are aware is that of achieving uniform policy for all lands under Interior jurisdiction. Such uniformity is a mere matter of administrative convenience. It is not dictated either by the Executive Order or by any other Interior enabling statute. Elimination of the positive environmental and recreational benefits of the existing regulatory approach as a mere matter of administrative convenience is clearly inappropriate and we would therefore suggest that the Department reconsider its apparent intention to deviate from ELM's existing land management policy with respect to ORRV use.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Twelve
D. Bureau of Reclamation Lands - The Bureau of Reclamation Lands are similar in characteristic to those under the management of BLM. Historically, the Bureau of Reclamation has followed an "open except where prohibited" policy similar to that of BLM. For the reasons discussed above with respect to the BLM lands we believe that the existing regulatory approach of the Bureau of Reclamation should be preserved and that departure from this historic approach would have adverse impacts both from the environmental point of view and the point of view of available outdoor recreational resources.
Based on the foregoing, it is our opinion that the Draft Environmental Impact Statement and the proposed regulations discussed therein give inadequate attention to the varying characteristics of the lands administered by the several Bureaus. This approach appears to be in direct contravention of the Task Force Study's recommendations that, in developing the new regulations consideration be given to existing regulations and specific land classifications. It is our opinion that the significantly divergent characteristics of the several land categories require significant variations in regulatory approach. These factors should be taken into account in finalizing the regulations in implementation of the Executive Order.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Thirteen
III. Safety and Operating Requirements -
While we are somewhat doubtful as to whether the National Environmental Policy Act gives the President and the Department legal authority to promulgate safety related requirements for ORRV use, the Association is not opposed to the imposition of reasonable regulations in this area. However, perhaps because of the absence of clear authority, the proposed safely related regulations are inequitable in that they impose the entire burden of compliance on the consumer although, in fairness, at least a portion of the compliance responsibility should rest on the vehicle manufacturer.
Moreover, a review of the proposed safety criteria indicates that they are not based on a careful consideration of the precise characteristics of the types of vehicles to be covered. As an example, consider the proposed requirement that persons operating ORRVs have valid permits to operate a motor vehicle. In the case of snowmobiles there is no demonstrated correlation between the ability to pass an automobile or motor-cycle drivers test and the ability to safely operate a snowmobile. In the absence of such a demonstrated correlation the proposed regulation is clearly improper in that it excludes many persons from the recreational opportunities of snowmobile operation without any showing of a safety related basis for such exclusion and thus the major snowmobiling states have seen fit to

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Fourteen
specifically eliminate any connection between snowmobile operation and motor vehicle licensing. The Association does support programs designed to educate snowmobile operators and to require youthful snowmobile operators to obtain safety certificates. A further indication of the failure to consider the specific nature of the types of vehicles regulated is the requirement for "spark arrestors" on snowmobiles. In virtually all states where snowmobile equipment requirements have been adopted, it has been recognized that, because of the environment in which snowmobiles operate, the spark arrestor requirement is inapplicable to snowmobiles.
Department's proposed regulations insofar as they pertain to safety, together with the generally rudimentary and superficial character of such regulations in their presently proposed form, point up the need for additional legislative action granting the Department authority to regulate the safety characteristics of ORRVs used on public lands. The Association would support responsible legislation of this type.
IV. The Department's Responsibilities Vis-a-Vis
Other Land Responsible Federal Agencies -
Executive Order 1164 stresses the need for "a unified Federal policy toward the use of [ORRVs] on public lands" and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963 directs the Secretary to "promote coordination of Federal plans and activities generally relating to Outdoor Recreation." Pursuant to these directives,

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Fifteen
the Draft Statement and the proposed regulations discussed therein do direct the Assistant Secretary -- Program Policy to provide "liaison" and "technical assistance" to other land responsible Federal agencies in an effort to coordinate ORRV regulation. Such "liaison" and "technical assistance", however, would appear likely to fall considerably short of the kind of close interagency cooperative effort which is necessary to obtain the joint regulatory approach which is necessary if agency actions are to be truly coordinated. We would suggest that the Executive Order can best be implemented by carrying forward the interagency task force approach followed in development of the Task Force Study in an effort to develop joint regulations implementing the Executive Order. We would, of course, anticipate that Interior would be the lead agency in this task force. If legislation is necessary to implement this approach, we would support such legislation.
V. The Department's Responsibilities Vis-a-Vis
State, Local Governments and Private Lands -
We note with approval the indication in the Draft
Statement that the Department intends to devote some effort
towards assisting states, local governments and private organizations and individuals in developing areas and facilities for
ORRV use. It should be emphasized, however, that, to a very
major extent, the real effectiveness of any national program

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Sixteen
7
to reconcile ORRV use with the need for environmental protection will depend on the program's effectiveness with respect to the state, local and private lands where a very significant portion of the ORRV use occurs. In this connection, we question whether "technical assistance" is enough. We see a definite need for the Department to take an active role in the development of a nationwide federal-state program for the proper regulation of ORRV use on all lands. As a necessary adjunct to this program, we believe that some consideration might be given to the development and nationwide enforcement of minimum safety and environment related performance standards for the vehicles themselves. It may well be that a basis for at least a portion. of this program is provided by the Outdoor Recreation and Land and Water Conservation Acts when considered in light of NEPA's directive that federal agencies must use "all practicable means" to improve and coordinate their policies in order to achieve environmental goals. In light of this directive, we believe that the Department should carefully consider the question of whether it might not do more to promote a unified national policy applicable to lands other than those for which the Department is directly and primarily responsible. To the extent that such a program cannot be based on existing legislative authority, we would support reasonable enabling legislation.

Department of Interior June 28, 1972
Page Seventeen
7
25
VI. Conclusion -
In closing, we should like to state that the foregoing comments should not in any way be construed as a criticism of the Department's efforts to date. In view of the magnitude of the task with which the Department was faced and the time constraints under which it has operated, we believe that the Task Force Study, the Draft Statement and the proposed regulations are an excellent work product. Even excellence can be improved upon, however, and the foregoing comments are presented to that end.
Yours very truly,
J. Gordon Arbuckle
Patton, Boggs, Blow, Verrill, Brand & May
111
Counsel for International Snowmobile Industry Association

entries.summary: Governor O'Callaghan expressed concern that local and state government needs would be ignored in implementing Executive Order 11644, noting that Nevada is 87% federally owned and its residents have historically enjoyed open public lands. He urged the Secretary of the Interior to consult local entities—specifically county commissioners and elected city officials in all 17 Nevada counties—before closing or restricting any areas to off-road vehicles. He also called for public hearings in each county seat prior to implementation, warning that failure to consider local needs could prompt Congressional intervention.
entries.statement_text:
MIKE O'CALLAGHAN GOVERNOR
THE STATE OF NEVADA

EXECUTIVE CHAMBER

CARSON CITY, NEVADA 89701
July 3, 1972
Action Office...................................
The Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
I have recently had the opportunity to review your letter of May 5, 1972, instructing your assistant secretaries of Public Land Management, Fish and Wild Life and Parks, and Water and Power of departmental policy on off-road vehicle use on federal lands.
I have great concern that in implementing the President's Executive Order 11644, dated February 8, 1972, that consideration of local and state government needs will be ignored by your administrators. As you well know, Nevada is 87 percent federally owned and the people of Nevada have historically enjoyed the great open spaces. I urge you to seek advice and council of local entities prior to closing or restricting any areas to offroad vehicles.
In Nevada, I believe that the County Commissioners of the 17 counties plus the elected city officials in these counties should all receive copies of the Draft Environmental Statement immediately so they may make written comments to you. Furthermore, hearings by the Department of Interior should be held in each county seat prior to the implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
I feel that unless the needs and desires of the local people are given proper consideration, that eventually Congress will step in and prescribe off-road management practices for all federal land managing agencies.
I look forward to you advising your staff of this important need.
Sincerely,
12
Governor of Neva

entries.summary_quote: We wish to commend the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation for its fair and well-developed impact statement dealing with the Off Road Vehicles (ORV) problem. With a few exceptions the statement reflects the concerns we as conservationists share toward the use of the ORV.
entries.summary: The Oregon Environmental Council generally commends the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation's impact statement on ORV use, praising its fairness and the restrictions placed on National Parks. However, they raise two main objections: the statement lacks enforceable noise standards (recommending a maximum of 73 decibels at 50 feet), and they oppose the 'monitor after the fact' approach to determining ORV compatibility with land resources, insisting that studies be conducted before ORV use is permitted in any area.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
We wish to commend the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation for its fair and well-developed impact statement dealing with the Off Road Vehicles (ORV) problem. With a few exceptions the statement reflects the concerns we as conservationists share toward the use of the ORV.
We are particularly pleased with the policy established for ORV use in the National Parks. We are impressed by the restrictions and would encourage the BOR to place this type of control on all lands. However, we realize the ORV is here to stay and no matter how strongly we object, the ORV users have a right to use the public lands. They have a right to use them, but not destroy them. We hope the Department of the Interior controls can prevent any destruction.
There are two areas, however, that we must object to and encourage revisions in the policy. The first is the treatment of noise. The statement recognizes that there is a real problem, but makes no effort to minimize the levels. The most stringent statement concerning noise is found on page 5. "An ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The problem here is that there is no indication as to what is considered excessive so enforcement would be extremely difficult.
The problem of noisy ORVs, particularly snowmobiles, is regarded as one of the greatest problems with the vehicles. The Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission says, in its publication "Snowmobiling in Washington State" that "Probably the greatest concern relating to snowmobiles is noise encroachment in a naturally quiet environment." Here is where ORV users encroach upon the rights of other recreation users. How noisy are these machines? The level of the snowmobile is about 112 decibels at the operator's ear. That is over standards set up under Walsh-Healy

Letter to Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. July 6, 1972 Page 2
18
for a 30-minute per day period. At 50 feet the noise level is about 86 decibels, which is just below the maximum for an eight hour period. Not too many non-users will suffer hearing loss from these machines but the noise levels at which they operate certainly indicates they could do a rather thorough job of destroying the peace and quiet of an outdoor area.
Why are these machines not quieter? A Conservation Foundation publication by Malcolm F. Baldwin entitled "The Off-Road Vehicle and Environmental Quality" attributes the reason to what the American buyer wants. Industry representatives say they could be made half as noisy but they would not sell. The Oregon Environmental Council recommends that BOR establish stringent noise restrictions in order to force the ORV industry into using a quieter machine. We suggest a maximum level of 73 decibels at 50 feet. This will not alleviate the problem by any means but it will help control it and possibly cut down the antagonism between ORV users and other more traditional recreation users.
Our second main objection to the statement is found on pp. 12-13. Reference is made to the negative environmental impact on the areas. Mention is made of the difficulty of determining the levels of use compatible with the resource. The method of determination is to monitor effects of ORV use on the lands to discover this data. We find this unacceptable. Extensive studies should be made of the areas before ORV use is allowed. If the monitor method is implemented, once it is found that the ORV is non-compatible with the resource, it will be too late. This determination must be made before ORV use is allowed.
Page 7 of the report discusses public review of the area policies before implementation. This would be a good time to conduct these studies to determine if use is compatible with the area. We commend the BOR for allowing public review and we encourage them to follow through with this proposal.
The Oregon Environmental Council is very concerned with the ORV problem and the potential damage they can cause to the environment. Generally we approve of the impact statement but encourage that there be:
. More stringent noise restrictions on the vehicles; and
. Better review before allowing the vehicles into an area.
Sincerely,
(Larry Williams
Executive Director

entries.summary: McNiff, writing on behalf of the Wyoming Recreation Commission, argues that national ORV regulations must be flexible enough to accommodate state and local conditions, warning that Wyoming does not face the same problems as heavily populated areas and that imposing uniform rules could create problems where none currently exist. He recommends an 'open until closed' policy rather than a 'closed until open' approach, and stresses that Wyoming's agencies actively encourage ORV use. He also raises concerns about inconsistent federal guidance, the need to address non-recreational ORVs (e.g., mineral exploration), and the importance of a clear definition of 'road.'
entries.statement_text:
INTER-OFFICE MEMO
DATE
 June 29, 1972
Paul H. Westedt - Director
FROM. Peter J. McNiff - Chief, Planning Division
SUBJECT DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT, PROPOSED
EXECUTIVE ORDER 11644 PERTAINING TO USE OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES ON THE
PUBLIC LANDS
COPIES TO: Dr. Clynn Phillips; P. J. McNiff; RF.
The first recommendation we would like to make in connection with the above mentioned draft is that procedures be established to insure that any rules and regulations adopted in connection with this subject have sufficient built-in flexibility to allow for administration on the state and local level, thus enabling their adjustment to the existing situations.
The theme that must be stressed by Wyoming in connection with this type of topic dealing with standardized land use and administration is that problems and potentials in Wyoming cannot be dealt with the same as problems and potentials found east of the Mississippi or on the West coast. (On page 9 of the Department of the Interior Task Force Study of Off-Road Recreation Vehicles, it states that Task Force Staff members selected thirteen (13) states for personal visits to gather much needed information for the report. All 13 of these states were east of the Mississippi River.)
There is a tendency in all national observations of this type to lump the United States into one category and administer all areas in accordance with rules and regulations adopted to solve problems found in heavily populated areas. If this is done, Wyoming, not having the problems to be treated by this type of administrative procedure, may see the creation of a bad situation where none previously existed.
When viewing and analyzing a standardizing administrative proposal, we first look to see if a problem exists in Wyoming which would be serviced by the proposal. We find Wyoming is not experiencing a great off-road vehicle problem, on the contrary, the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission, the Wyoming Recreation Commission, the Department of Economic Planning and Development, the Wyoming Agriculture Department, and many of the federal agencies encourage off-road vehicle use in connection with their various interests and activities. In the few cases where problems have been spotted, they have been solved by existing authority on both the
The second recommendation relates to the above but more specifically to the Wyoming situation. If rules and regulations on this subject are to be successful in Wyoming, they must be based on the principle that all the areasunder administration are open to use with only those areas already closed or where problems develop, closed to use. Both the open and the closed areas must be continually studied with respect to use and non-use and a review process established whereby their respective status can be changed if merited.

We were very disturbed when we learned at the recent Governor Hathaway Recreation Action Team meeting that the National Forest Service had apparently received instructions from Washington that the open until closed philosophy was fine, but that the Bureau of Land Management had been told by Washington to work for a closed until open policy. This dichotomy of federal guidance is strange in itself, but frightening when the Bureau of Land Management and presumably the National Park Service is contemplating a course of action on the Washington level contrary to the suggestions of their local representatives, the Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan, and of sister federal agencies.
The following are general overall observations of the draft, etc., and hopefully will serve as a review of areas of concern with respect to the final product of this proposal.
There appears to be a difference in the titles between the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement which might be of some significance, i.e., the Task Force Study is entitled off-road Recreational vehicles and the Draft Environmental Statement indicates that all off-road vehicles, i.e., those used for agriculture and accdemic purposes, terrain mapping, administrative inspection, mineral prospecting, etc., are represented and included within the statement but not within the Task Force Study. In any case, there should be an addendum to the Statement concerning the effect of the proposal on these important non-recreation off-road vehicles. In connection with this, a study of the various conflict in laws involving the proposal and the established prospecting and mineral exploration laws, etc., should be carefully analyzed and effectively dealt with.
The definition of a road will also be of primary importance to the success of this proposal. With over 50 percent of Wyoming in federal ownership and potential roads involving everything from the dimmest game trail to Interstate Highways, it takes little imagination to think up problems of administration if the definition of a road is left nebulous.
Attached hereto please find a copy of the Draft upon which comments, suggested wordings, etc., have been made. .

entries.summary: Blackmore expresses concern that the environmental impacts of ORVs are not fully understood, and criticizes the draft statement for making vague or undocumented claims about impacts. He recommends that impact statements be made for each type of vehicle in its most common use environment, and urges that ORV use not be permitted where impacts are unclear or where local land managers have concerns, citing the example of over-snow vehicles in Acadia National Park potentially harassing wildlife.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Watt:
We have been giving serious consideration to the many public land management problems which must be solved because of the growing popularity of recreational use of off-road vehicles. • believe the impact of these vehicles on the environment is not fully understood at this time. The draft environmental statement enclosed with Mr. Hofe's letter of June 1, 1972, reinforces our feelings, particularly in those sections that outline the damages which may be done.
In commenting on the statement we would suggest that it repeatedly points out possible impacts without stating that one thing or another will happen. For example, to say "there is reason to believe that family relationships are strengthened by these activities," is hardly a documented statement of favorable impact upon the environment. Another we note for your consideration is that, "use of over-snow vehicles for fishing purposes may result in some water pollution from the litter and waste left on the ice." We have every reason to believe pollution will occur.
A fatal weakness of the statement is that it pertains to all types of off-road vehicles, even those at this time not invented. We would suggest an impact statement should be made regarding each type vehicle in its most common use environment.

In closing, we suggest that great care should be taken not to allow use where the impact is not fully understood or where the local land manager believes no harm will be done. An example of the type of permitted use that concerns us is the opening of selected roads in Acadia National Park to over the snow vehicles. While it is probably true that little or no damage will be done to the roads so used, we would be concerned about the harrassment of wildlife of the park. During the winter months land animals are under great stress in finding food and shelter and great rafts of migratory waterfowl numbering in the thousands of birds nest and feed off shore if not disturbed.
Thank you for asking for our comments.
Sincerely,
Rob R. Blackmore
Director

mentions.stance_basis: Recommends caution and per-vehicle-type impact statements; concerned about wildlife harassment

entries.summary_quote: To summarize, our position, all ORRV's cannot and must not be grouped together as a class. To do so would be to contravene the intent and the words of Executive Order 11644 and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963.
entries.summary: Roger P. Worth, as Legal Counsel for Arctic Enterprises, Inc., argues that different types of ORRVs must be classified and regulated individually rather than as a single class, because their environmental impacts differ significantly — snowmobiles, for instance, travel over frozen ground in winter and leave no permanent damage, unlike other ORRVs used in warmer seasons. He supports the ISIA's broader comments and emphasizes that snowmobiles should have access to more areas in winter given minimal competition for land use. He also calls for the development of uniform, meaningful safety performance standards for snowmobiles in cooperation with the Department of Interior.
entries.statement_text:
June 28, 1972
Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
Re: Notice of Availability of Draft
Environmental Statement (Int Des 72-58)
Gentlemen:
The following comments are submitted on behalf of Arctic Enterprises, Inc., (Arctic) in response to the Notice of Availability of Draft Environmental Statement (Int Des 72-58) published in the Federal Register, Volume 37, No. 107 on June 2, 1972.
Arctic is the largest manufacturer of snowmobiles in the United States and second worldwide only to Bombardier, Ltd., the Canadian manufacturer of the Ski Doo and Motor Ski snowmobiles. Arctic also produces a line of mini-bikes, another type of off-road recreational vehicle (ORRV). Arctic produced over 110,000 snowmobiles during the 1972-73 snowmobile season.
Arctic firmly supports the position of the International Snowmobile Industry Association (ISIA) as set forth in the comments submitted on behalf of the ISIA by Patton, Boggs, Blow, Berill, Brand & May, as counsel for the ISIA. There are however, a few points that we believe need to be stressed.
Arctic believes that the various types of ORRV's <u>must</u> be classified and considered on an individual basis due to their differences in use, effects on other users of a particular area and the effects on the environment itself. A snowmobile travels over the temporary medium of snow. Underlying the snow is the <u>frozen</u>, dorment vegetation and ground. In contrast, other ORRV's travel over and can easily adversely affect the soft spongy ground, as in the Spring, and the growing plant life. In addition, during the winter months the areas are free of migratory birds and the hibernating animals.

Department of the Interior Page #2
June 28, 1972
Some ORRV's greatly damage the vegetation over which they travel and this damage is readily apparent to the eye while in most instances one cannot spot in summer the paths snowmobiles took the previous winter. While snowmobiles change the appearance of the landscape by leaving tracks in the snow, there is not sound evidence that there is any permanent adverse affects on the underlying vegetation. Snowmobilers have damaged seedlings and small shrubs, but we believe this is a matter that can be handled through education and restricting snowmobiles from those areas that are susceptible to such damage.
Arctic does not advocate the summer use of snowmobiles, since the vehicle is not designed for such use. If snowmobiles are fitted with wheels or otherwise modified for use on mediums other than on ice or snow, it is our position that they <u>must</u> be classified during those months of use with the other ORRV's that are similarly used and have similar effects.
Additionally, snowmobiles are used in the winter months when the competition for the use of any land area is at a minimum. Consequently, more areas should be open for snowmobiling in the winter than for an ORRV use during the other season.
Snowmobiles are not alone in the need for classification of ORRV's. Campers, for instance, should be allowed in certain areas where motorcycles and dunebuggies are prohibited for obvious reasons.
In order to insure safe use of snowmobiles on public lands, uniform safety performance standards must be developed and enforced. The current state standards are underdeveloped and inconsistent one with the other. The Department of Interior is the logical agency to work with the industry to develop meaningful standards since it will understand the vehicle, the conditions of its use and will be charged with the responsibility of controlling the enforcement of the snowmobile use and required safety equipment. The safety and machine operating requirements in the Draft Environmental Statement, are rudimentary and must be greatly expanded upon to insure safe operation on public lands.
8

To summarize, our position, all ORRV's cannot and must not be grouped together as a class. To do so would be to contravene the intent and the words of Executive Order 11644 and the Outdoor Recreation Act of 1963.
Very truly yours,
ARCTIC ENTERPRISES, INC.
Roger P. Worth Legal Counsel

mentions.stance_basis: Objects to treating all ORRVs as one class; supports individual classification

entries.summary_quote: I strongly urge that you amend your instructions to the Assistant Secretaries to except geological and geophysical survey equipment, while being used exclusively for their designed purposes, from the general category of off-road vehicle to which the proposed regulations will apply.
entries.summary: The Society of Exploration Geophysicists, through its President Carl H. Savit, argues that geological and geophysical survey vehicles should be exempted from the proposed ORV regulations, just as farm tractors, construction equipment, and forestry vehicles are exempted. The Society contends that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground impact and serve vital national interests related to energy and mineral resource discovery. They urge the Secretary of the Interior to amend his instructions to exclude such survey equipment from the recreational ORV regulatory framework.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Sir:
Members of the Society of Exploration Geophysicists have called to my attention Executive Order 11644 and your consequent memorandum of May 5, 1972 to the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish and Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources.
Our members are deeply concerned by the text of that memorandum which fails to take account of the special nature of off-road vehicles used in geological and geophysical surveys throughout the public lands of the United States. In particular, they feel that recognition of the exceptional nature of such vehicles should be included among the exceptions listed in the third paragraph of the subject memorandum. Vehicles for geophysical or geological surveying, when used exclusively for their designed purposes, should logically fall into the same broad category as farm tractors, self-propelled agricultural equipment, equipment for harvesting and transporting forest products, and earth moving and construction equipment when such vehicles are used for their designed purposes. It should be noted that survey vehicles are designed for minimal ground loading consistent with their survey purposes and are therefore inherently far less likely to leave permanent imprints on the ground than are self-mobile construction and excavation devices or forest product transporters, vehicles which carry heavy loads and, of necessity, create large local ground loading.
Geological and geophysical surveys of the public lands are undertaken, in conformity with statutory requirements, for the purposes of discovering or assessing mineral, fuel, or thermal resources of the United States or for scientific and educational purposes. As such, the continuation of such surveys is of vital interest to the people of the United States in view of the present energy crisis and of the critical shortages of many of our mineral resources. To impose upon such surveys the requirement to conform to regulations designed for the control of recreational vehicles rather than to
11
* . · · · · · · ·

The Honorable the Secretary of the Interior June 30, 1972
Page 2
include such surveys along with agricultural, forestry, and construction operations would appear unjustified on any reasonable basis.
Our nearly 8000 members would be adversely and vitally affected in their activities on the public lands of the United States by being required to adhere to regulations designed for recreational activities. On behalf of our membership, I strongly urge that you amend your instructions to the Assistant Secretaries to except geological and geophysical survey equipment, while being used exclusively for their designed purposes, from the general category of off-road vehicle to which the proposed regulations will apply.
Sincerely,
Carl H. Savit
President

entries.summary_quote: I urge you to seek advice and council of local entities prior to closing or restricting any areas to offroad vehicles.
entries.summary: Nevada Governor Mike O'Callaghan expressed concern that implementation of Executive Order 11644 would ignore the needs of state and local governments, noting that Nevada is 87% federally owned and its residents have historically enjoyed open public lands. He urged the Secretary of the Interior to consult local entities before closing or restricting areas to off-road vehicles, and called for copies of the Draft Environmental Statement to be distributed to all 17 county commissioners and city officials, with hearings held in each county seat. He warned that failure to consider local needs could prompt Congressional intervention in federal land management practices.
entries.statement_text:
MIKE O'CALLAGHAN GOVERNOR
THE STATE OF NEVADA

EXECUTIVE CHAMBER

CARSON CITY, NEVADA 89701
July 3, 1972
Action Office...................................
The Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
I have recently had the opportunity to review your letter of May 5, 1972, instructing your assistant secretaries of Public Land Management, Fish and Wild Life and Parks, and Water and Power of departmental policy on off-road vehicle use on federal lands.
I have great concern that in implementing the President's Executive Order 11644, dated February 8, 1972, that consideration of local and state government needs will be ignored by your administrators. As you well know, Nevada is 87 percent federally owned and the people of Nevada have historically enjoyed the great open spaces. I urge you to seek advice and council of local entities prior to closing or restricting any areas to offroad vehicles.
In Nevada, I believe that the County Commissioners of the 17 counties plus the elected city officials in these counties should all receive copies of the Draft Environmental Statement immediately so they may make written comments to you. Furthermore, hearings by the Department of Interior should be held in each county seat prior to the implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
I feel that unless the needs and desires of the local people are given proper consideration, that eventually Congress will step in and prescribe off-road management practices for all federal land managing agencies.
I look forward to you advising your staff of this important need.
Sincerely,
12
Governor of Neva

entries.summary: The Alaska Conservation Society conditionally supports Executive Order 11644 and its implementation, expressing particular concern about the unique vulnerabilities of Alaska's tundra and boreal forest ecosystems to ORV damage. They criticize the draft EIS as poorly written and fragmentary, and argue that regulations must cover non-recreational ORV uses (such as mineral exploration and government surveys) in addition to recreational ones. They urge that strong, clear regulations be promulgated, with specific attention to Alaska's permafrost conditions and the need for better-defined criteria for BLM land classifications.
entries.statement_text:
Alaska Conservation Society
Box 80192 College, Alaska 99701
July 6, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
US Department of the Interior
C Street Between 18th and 19th
Washington, D. C. 20240
Subject: Comments on Interior DES 72-62 RE: Draft Environmental Impact Statement: "Proposed Departmental Implementation of E. O. 11644 Pertaining to Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands".
Dear Sir:
The Alaska Conservation Society appreciates the spirit and philosophy behind E. O. 11644 establishing the basis for departmental control of off-road vehicle use on all of our public lands. Because of the vast proportion of Alaska's lands within the public domain, and because of the present and potential damage to the tundra and boreal forest ecosystems, and their wildlife resources, we are anxious to see that strong regulations are promulgated.
The Draft Environmental Impact Statement prepared by your Bureau applies to all Interior Agencies, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, National Park Service and the Bureau of Reclamation. Because of the importance of these agencies in the management of Alaska's public lands, we offer the following comments for your review and consideration.

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Two
1. The draft environmental impact statement appears to be generally poorly written and fragmentary. The mention of various "impacts", both environmental and economic, and both positive and negative, is poorly developed and little or no attempt is made to relate these impacts to one another quantitatively. The discussion of the economic impacts of ORV is useless, as well as fragmentary throughout the entire document. The concept that ORV use could aid in strengthening family relationships, mentioned several times in the statement, is undocumented and, in truth, use of ORV by young people may contribute to the destruction of the American family that has paralleled the evolution of the automobile.
2. The Preamble to E.O. 11644 refers specifically to "recreational" vehicles. The subsequent statements refer to off-road vehicles without the qualifier "recreational". The regualtions should apply to all vehicles, including official use by governmental agencies, etc. Throughout Alaska, much of the damage done by ORV is the direct result of mineral and petroleum exploration, government-sponsored surveys, forestry activities and construction equipment. It is essential that these uses be adequately regulated, in addition to recreational uses. We recognize that the use of ORV for emergency fire or law enforcement and other such purposes may be needed, however, the increasing use of aircraft in these cases may soon preclude much of the ORV use.
3. Since the issuance of E.O. 11644, considerable confusion has arisen concerning whether lands will be classified as "open unless otherwise designated" or "closed unless otherwise designated". The statement partially clarifies this problem by stating that Wilderness and Primitive Areas are closed, and that trails and areas will be established in National Parks, Monuments, Natural Areas, and National Wildlife Refuges and Ranges only if the Bureau head so decides.
However, the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Reclamation lands appear open to access unless closed (except for Bureau of Land Management Primitive Areas). The

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Three
The statement is made in Memorandum K-14 that "Areas and trails shall not be located in areas possessing unique natural, wildlife, historic or recreational values unless the Bureau head determines that these unique values will not be adversely affected". This statement is not referred to in the outlining of the Bureau of Land Management's responsibilities in DES 72-62, thus leaving the criteria for Bureau of Land Management classification vague.
4. Although various criteria are mentioned by which Bureaus will establish open and closed areas, no mention is made of the unique Alaskan tundra and Boreal forest permafrost regime. In summer, ORV travel on permafrost-underlain areas can be severely destructive, as permafrost, once thawed, may never reform. Travel over a deep winter snowbed is less destructive, although compression of the snow layer and thin vegetative mat may result in damage to the plant covering. Although research into this possible damage is still continuing, it may be possible to open some areas in winter, and close them the remainder of the year. This technique has proven somewhat effective on the North Slope of Alaska.
I realize that the above comments are, by no means, a comprehensive criticism of DES 72-62. However, I hope our suggestions will result in an improved, stronger statement and policy for use of ORV on our public lands.
Sincerely,
ALASKA CONSERVATION SOCIETY
Ernst Mueller President

entries.summary: AMAX Exploration, Inc. supports mineral exploration activity on public lands and expresses concern that the four-month advance permit requirement for ORV events would cause costly delays to legitimate mineral exploration operations. They suggest that a country-wide general permit be issued to those engaged in legitimate mineral exploration, covering both corporate exploration groups and individual prospectors, to eliminate the need for a separate permit for each ORV event.

AMAX EXPLORATION, INC.
A SUBSIDIARY OF AMERICAN METAL CLIMAX, INC.
12620 WEST CEDAR DRIVE. P.O. BOX C LAKEWOOD. COLORADO 80226 (303) 985-8701

Re: Executive Order 11644
Dear Sir:
We have read Executive Order 11644 and the Draft Environmental Statement, (Int Des 72-62) dated May 26, 1972, and make the following comments for your consideration.
As you are aware, much mineral exploration activity in the western U. S. is focused on public lands and, in many cases, such activity is carried out through use of four-wheel drive vehicles on old logging and/or mining roads which give access to hinterland areas. Additionally, in the normal course of events in minerals exploration, it is usually not possible to determine far in advance what specific areas are to be considered.
The requirement that permits for ORV events "...shall be submitted no less than four months, or a lesser time as each Bureau may determine, in advance..." will cause innumerable, expensive delays to those engaged in legitimate minerals exploration on public lands if the logging and mining roads are considered to be "off established roadways" (U.S. Dept. of Interior Memorandum K14 dated May 5, 1972).
We suggest, therefore, that provision be made for issuance of a country-wide general permit to those engaged in legitimate mineral exploration to eliminate the need for a permit for each ORV event; legitimate mineral exploration (activity) being defined to include both members of corporate

exploration groups and such individuals as are known to make a significant portion of their livelihood from prospecting activity.

AMAX EXPLORATION, INC.

entries.entity: American Petroleum Institute, Committee on Exploration
entries.summary_quote: it is strongly urged that geological, geophysical, and other vehicular equipment necessary to mineral development be exempted in a revised memorandum and impact statement and in the regulations being prepared to implement Executive Order 11644
entries.summary: The American Petroleum Institute's Committee on Exploration argues that the draft environmental statement and implementing memorandum focus almost exclusively on recreational ORV use while failing to adequately consider legitimate mineral and energy resource development on public lands. They contend that geological, geophysical, and other vehicles essential to oil, gas, and mineral exploration are vital to the nation's energy needs and should not be restricted by Executive Order 11644. They strongly urge that such vehicular equipment be explicitly exempted in any revised memorandum, impact statement, and implementing regulations.
entries.statement_text:
AMERICAN PETROLEUM
1801 K STREET, NORTHWEST
(202) 833-5722
WILSON M. LAIRD, Director Committee on Exploration
July 10, 1972
Hon. Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
The attention of the Committee on Exploration of the American Petroleum Institute has been called to Executive Order 11644, "Use of Off-road Vehicles on Public Lands." Your May 5 memorandum directing the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources in implementing this Order and the Draft Environmental Statement prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation on May 26, 1972, have been reviewed, and the following comments are offered:
Neither the memorandum nor the impact statement suggest that the entire spectrum of public land use has been considered. Emphasis is almost entirely on recreational use. Other uses, such as oil, natural gas, mineral and geothermal development, forestry and grazing, are not given adequate consideration, indeed, it appears that the mineral resources area of your own department has been bypassed.
Exploration and development of oil and natural gas resources require the use of wheeled and tracked vehicles, and the statement should reflect legitimate uses of such vehicles. An example of primary importance to exploration is the use of off-road vehicles for geological and geophysical work. Should substantial quantities of oil or gas be discovered as a result of exploratory work, other vehicles, such as trucks, drilling rigs and other auxiliary vehicles, would be needed to develop the deposits and make them available for use.
That the development of such resources is vitally needed for the nation's welfare is beyond question in view of the energy crises expected in the near future. Inasmuch as public lands account for approximately one-third of the land surface of the United States, it is obvious that these areas are likely to contain much of the country's oil and gas potential.

In view of the danger that undue and unnecessary restrictions on legitimate exploration and development of oil and gas, as well as other minerals, on public lands may ensue under the definitions and terms of this order, it is strongly urged that geological, geophysical, and other vehicular equipment necessary to mineral development be exempted in a revised memorandum and impact statement and in the regulations being prepared to implement Executive Order 11644 in order to assure that there can be no misunderstanding and that such vehicular equipment is not intended to be included in the terms of the order.

entries.summary: Charles S. Watson, Jr., representing the Nevada Outdoor Recreation Association, strongly opposes uncontrolled ORV use on public lands, citing severe ecological damage to the fragile Great Basin desert environment, including toxic plant infestations and lasting soil disturbance. He criticizes the draft EIS for failing to address BLM range conversion projects as a related environmental issue, and proposes a system of designated 'Adventure Roads' to channel ORV use while protecting roadless areas. He also objects strenuously to what he views as politically motivated, environmentally insensitive commentary from officials like Governor O'Callaghan, urging that public land policy prioritize genuine environmental stewardship over narrow utilitarian interests.
entries.statement_text:
TESTIMONY STATEMENT
Subject: Draft Environmental Impact Statement by USDI affecting Off-Road Vehicular uses on the public lands
On February 8, 1972, President Richard M. Nixon issued Executive Order #11644, which directed the U.S. Department of Interior to develop a unified interagency policy for the purpose of alleviating the growing use of off-road vehicles(ORV) on essentially defacto roadless public lands. In his executive order, the president apparently recognizes the massive debilitating effects of ORV use and that such use has become a major threat to our desert environment.
The Nevada Outdoor Recreation Association, Inc. has long expressed its grave concern over ORV activities on the public lands, and has attempted to develop meaningful solutions which would allow for reasonable ORV use on the public lands while restricting such use where there are fragile flora, wildlife, unique-natural, wilderness, archeological, historic, recreational and open space values.
In 1967, this organization began consulting the St.Louisbased Committee For Environmental Information(CEI), one of
the nation's foremost and widely respected environmental\ninstitutions, which includes amongst its trustees the noted\necologist, Dr. Barry Commoner. Our consultations with CEI
were mainly co-ordinated through its science director, Dr.

Kevin P. Shea. Basically, recent investigations by CEI has developed information which tends to conclude that our Great Basin desert and steppe environment is one of the most fragile and most threatened in North America. The threat posed takes many forms and one of the most serious is toxic, poisonous, exotic and nonpalatable plant infestations due to man-made disturbance of both the soil and plant communities. Since 1942, when the notorious poisonous Ukrainian plant halogeton was first detected near Wells, Nevada, this and several other strains of toxic and poisonous exotic plants have taken over an estimated 20,000,000 acres of western rangelends. Almost all of this biological destructionknown to ecologists as an "eco-catastrophe"—can be directly traced to man-made effects, such as roads, railroad beds, pipelines, transmission lines and worst of all—Bureau of Land Management range conversion projects. The latter has been described by these reputable ecologists at CEI, and other respected organizations, as the most destructive program ever fostered by the Federal government on our western rangelands. Make no mistake about it, the chief objection this organization has with this MEPA impact statement is its failure to recognize range conversion as a lagitimate issue in these proceedings.
As we see it, there is little to choose between the debilitating effects of programs that call for massive removal of native plants and plantings of notoriously undependable enotic grasses—the sole objective of which is to convert huge acreages of public lands over to one <u>dominant use</u> for the livestock industry—and these which fail to control the enormous harm now being wrought by indiscriminate ORV use on the public lands. Recently, the National Wildlife Federation—the nation's largest conservation organisation—cited ORV use as the chief cause of massive destructive effects

in the Mojave Desert and along the Colorado River. To paraphrase National Wildlife, ORV use in the Mojave Desert is rapidly converting that once magnificent desert region into one vast slum.
One source of vivid, irrefutable evidence of vehicular use destruction can still be seen in many of the early pioneer emigrant trails which crisscrossed the Creat Basin during the early and mid-1800's. The Oregon Trail, for instance, has not seen use since its abandonment in 1872—yet, in many areas the trail ruts are still there, with their complement of exotic infesting plants, a century after vehicular use(in this instance, by covered wagons) ceased. The same destructive effects can be directly attributed to ORV use on defacto roadless public lands. One far-reaching form of remedial action proposed by NORA has been the selective designation of existing remote and back country primitive, jeep and macadam roads and trails (excluding, in the latter case, those lands deemed suitable for wilderness and natural area preservation) as part of a system of Adventure Roads. Since 1958, when NORA began its pioneer effort to seek out and identify scenic, unique-natural, wilderness, and recreational sites and arcss (which now numbers mearly 450 in Nevada alone), we have included in our program a comprehensive inventory of roads and trails which would be cuitable for this Adventure Roads program on our public lands. Where we observed such roads and trails in exceptional open space conditions, we included—and are presently still developing—a district by district plan for open space receives. The latter would include a system of 24 Adventure Roads, while restricting use of ORV's over defecto roadless
24 Adventure Roads, while restricting use of ORV's over defacto roadless areas, and recommending development of a management framework plan under true multiple use principles. As such, Open Space Reserves would be subject

out indianous prairiests, take roat
1.6
to a continuing inventory and analysis to determine the existence of fragile scenic, unique-hatural and wilderness conditions as well as attempts to identify endangered species habitats and valuable forage areas needing further ORV restrictions.
Lastly, may we further inject our strenuous objections to those who would use these proceedings to promote purely transient utilitarian criteria while demonstrating almost total insensitivity to paramount environmental considerations. What these proceedings need the least are gratuitous, self-serving political rhetoric on the part of certain politicians-whose sole concerns are for the predatory vested interests who are the root cause of this malignant public land environmental crisis. Specifically, we object-most strenuously—to the naive, irrelevant remarks attributed to Governor Mike O'Callaghan in the Nevada press last July 3 and 4. We are sorely distressed over what appears to be a complete changeover from the environmental concern he registered during the governor's early days in office. We consider it appropriate to advise the governor—as it pertains to the issues in these proceedings—to spend more time doing his "homework" on them. In short, the mark that distinguishes a politician from a statesman might be described as the ability to put brain in gear before accelerating one's mouth. We sincerely hope that Hevada political leaders, in addressing this gravely serious problem, will focus their concern on what constitutes the public interest. Indeed, there must be an over-riding awareness that our public lands constitute a priceless 21 stional treasure and heritage—which must be protected and managed in the best interests of all Americans.
Respectfully submitted.
Charles S. Watson.Jr.
Director

Carson City, Nevada 89701

entries.summary_quote: EDF supports the controlled use of off-road vehicles (ORV) on public lands in order to protect its resources.
entries.summary: The Environmental Defense Fund conditionally supports controlled ORV use on public lands, emphasizing that public recreational use must be secondary to protecting wildlife resources and ecological integrity. EDF calls for careful determination of use levels, including regulation of ORV events and rallies, as well as attention to noise, traffic, and litter impacts. They also urge continued bureau supervision of open lands and meaningful public participation before designating areas as open or closed to ORVs.
entries.statement_text:
ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND
1712 -1910 N STREET, N.W., WASHINGTON, D.C. 20036/202 833-1485
July 6, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Sir:
The Department of the Interior has circulated for comment a draft impact statement on proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands. As a national membership organization of scientists, lawyers and concerned citizens, the Environmental Defense Fund takes this opportunity to submit our remarks.
EDF supports the controlled use of off-road vehicles (ORV) on public lands in order to protect its resources. We recognize the Department's responsibility in managing the use so as not to create an adverse environmental impact or cause irreparable damage to existing ecology. We feel, however, that public use is secondary to protecting and perpetuating wildlife resources. Although the growth of public interest in ORV makes its own controversial impact, primary concern should still be the environment.
EDF feels that the determination of use levels, including recreational benefits, is crucial to the environmental impact of the proposed action. Specifically, the determination of where and how often, if at all, ORV events and rallies should be conducted. It seems that the adverse effects of such events would be damaging to the public as well as to the land itself, unless properly regulated. In order for ORV recreational use to be "safe" for the environment, responsible determination should be made as to the physical impact on susceptible land forms. Also, noise control and the problem of increased traffic and litter are primary areas of our concern.
In implementing Executive Order 11644, those ORV activities and uses which may cause irreparable harm to ecological balances must be fully evaluated. The Department's draft impact statement carefully delineates the situations it anticipates facing with respect to ORV control and use. However, if public lands are to be "open" to off-

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Page Two July 6, 1972
road vehicles, then continued supervision of these lands by the various bureaus is essential. We also hope that public participation is encouraged and solicited before declaring a land "open" or "closed" to the public.
The Environmental Defense Fund appreciates this opportunity to submit our comments for your consideration.
Respectfully submitted,
23
Roberta Danzansky
Administrative Assistant

entries.summary: Ernst Mueller, as President of the Alaska Conservation Society, conditionally supports the spirit of Executive Order 11644 but criticizes the draft EIS as poorly written, fragmentary, and inadequate in addressing Alaska's unique permafrost and tundra ecosystems. He raises specific concerns about the lack of regulation for non-recreational ORV uses (such as mineral and petroleum exploration), vague criteria for BLM land classifications, and the absence of any discussion of permafrost damage. He hopes his suggestions will lead to an improved, stronger statement and policy for ORV use on public lands.
entries.statement_text:
Alaska Conservation Society
Box 80192 College, Alaska 99701
July 6, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
US Department of the Interior
C Street Between 18th and 19th
Washington, D. C. 20240
Subject: Comments on Interior DES 72-62 RE: Draft Environmental Impact Statement: "Proposed Departmental Implementation of E. O. 11644 Pertaining to Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands".
Dear Sir:
The Alaska Conservation Society appreciates the spirit and philosophy behind E. O. 11644 establishing the basis for departmental control of off-road vehicle use on all of our public lands. Because of the vast proportion of Alaska's lands within the public domain, and because of the present and potential damage to the tundra and boreal forest ecosystems, and their wildlife resources, we are anxious to see that strong regulations are promulgated.
The Draft Environmental Impact Statement prepared by your Bureau applies to all Interior Agencies, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, National Park Service and the Bureau of Reclamation. Because of the importance of these agencies in the management of Alaska's public lands, we offer the following comments for your review and consideration.

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Two
1. The draft environmental impact statement appears to be generally poorly written and fragmentary. The mention of various "impacts", both environmental and economic, and both positive and negative, is poorly developed and little or no attempt is made to relate these impacts to one another quantitatively. The discussion of the economic impacts of ORV is useless, as well as fragmentary throughout the entire document. The concept that ORV use could aid in strengthening family relationships, mentioned several times in the statement, is undocumented and, in truth, use of ORV by young people may contribute to the destruction of the American family that has paralleled the evolution of the automobile.
2. The Preamble to E.O. 11644 refers specifically to "recreational" vehicles. The subsequent statements refer to off-road vehicles without the qualifier "recreational". The regualtions should apply to all vehicles, including official use by governmental agencies, etc. Throughout Alaska, much of the damage done by ORV is the direct result of mineral and petroleum exploration, government-sponsored surveys, forestry activities and construction equipment. It is essential that these uses be adequately regulated, in addition to recreational uses. We recognize that the use of ORV for emergency fire or law enforcement and other such purposes may be needed, however, the increasing use of aircraft in these cases may soon preclude much of the ORV use.
3. Since the issuance of E.O. 11644, considerable confusion has arisen concerning whether lands will be classified as "open unless otherwise designated" or "closed unless otherwise designated". The statement partially clarifies this problem by stating that Wilderness and Primitive Areas are closed, and that trails and areas will be established in National Parks, Monuments, Natural Areas, and National Wildlife Refuges and Ranges only if the Bureau head so decides.
However, the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Reclamation lands appear open to access unless closed (except for Bureau of Land Management Primitive Areas). The

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Three
The statement is made in Memorandum K-14 that "Areas and trails shall not be located in areas possessing unique natural, wildlife, historic or recreational values unless the Bureau head determines that these unique values will not be adversely affected". This statement is not referred to in the outlining of the Bureau of Land Management's responsibilities in DES 72-62, thus leaving the criteria for Bureau of Land Management classification vague.
4. Although various criteria are mentioned by which Bureaus will establish open and closed areas, no mention is made of the unique Alaskan tundra and Boreal forest permafrost regime. In summer, ORV travel on permafrost-underlain areas can be severely destructive, as permafrost, once thawed, may never reform. Travel over a deep winter snowbed is less destructive, although compression of the snow layer and thin vegetative mat may result in damage to the plant covering. Although research into this possible damage is still continuing, it may be possible to open some areas in winter, and close them the remainder of the year. This technique has proven somewhat effective on the North Slope of Alaska.
I realize that the above comments are, by no means, a comprehensive criticism of DES 72-62. However, I hope our suggestions will result in an improved, stronger statement and policy for use of ORV on our public lands.
Sincerely,
ALASKA CONSERVATION SOCIETY
Ernst Mueller President

mentions.quote: I hope our suggestions will result in an improved, stronger statement and policy for use of ORV on our public lands.
mentions.stance_basis: supports stronger ORV regulations but finds the draft inadequate and calls for revisions

entries.summary_quote: these non-recreational uses must be addressed to provide strict control if E011644 is to have any meaning in Alaska
entries.summary: The Fairbanks Environmental Center argues that the draft EIS is too vague regarding BLM land management responsibilities and fails to adequately address non-recreational ORV uses (such as military, commercial, and government activities) that are particularly damaging to Alaska's fragile tundra and permafrost ecosystems. They call for strict controls on all ORV uses—recreational and non-recreational alike—and insist that no ORV use should be allowed in existing or future Alaskan national parks and monuments. They also request that the revised statement more accurately reflect Alaska's unique ecological conditions and clarify the 'open until closed' versus 'closed until opened' question for BLM lands.

I wish to be brief and helpful in these remarks. I feel that the draft statement omits too many problems which are peculiar to the vast Public Domain lands in Alaska which are particularly subject to ecological and other damages by both recreational and non-recreational uses of ORVs.
It is not possible from your draft to determine whether public lands—especailly those within BLM management—are open to uprestricted CRV use until administratively closed, or the reverse situation. The Center wishes to ask you to revise your statement to reflect this lack of clarity in EOl1644. We also wish to call your attention to the time necessary for public input prior to the actual promulgation of regulations governing the use of ORVs in certain areas of BLM lands.
In Alaska we also have considerable use and/or potential use of ORVs by military personnel for non-military use. We have large tracts of lands under U.S. Forest Service management for commercial timber. We have learned that our interior forests are of interest to the U.S.F.S., and that they will be opened to lumbering. U.S.F.S. use of ORVs could be intensive

in our interior. We fail to see by your draft how E0116 will be interpreted to control this non-recreational use. Our fragile tundra and its associated eco-systems on these public lands are very easily damaged.

We find your statements suggesting ORV use may strengthen family relationships to be absurd in the extreme and without any evidence. In this part of Alaska the very opposite effect in the use of ORVs--particularly the snowmobile--is likely to be closer to the truth.

My name is John W. Grandy, IV. I am Administrative Assistant for Wildlife at the National Parks and Conservation Association.

I appreciate the invitation of this Committee to submit the views of the NPCA on this important matter.
The National Parks and Conservation Association is the leading conservation organization concerned primarily with the protection of the National Park System, but also with other major environmental and conservation subjects such as wildlife and forestry.
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the draft environmental impact statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
while the statement seems adequate in most places, alternatives to the proposed actions are insufficiently discussed.

The Secretary's memorandum (Page 3, paragraphs (a)(4) and (a)(5))
gives criteria for use of vehicles by area classifications such
as wilderness. The impact statement, however, considers all
areas as a group when considering alternatives.
27 Costs and benefits of the vehicle use pattern assigned, and alternative patterns, should be considered with reference to each area for which regulations (guidelines) are considered in (a)(4)

and (a)(5).
By adequately evaluating areas such as National Parks in relation to their legal status, their primary purposes, and all alternative sets of vehicle regulations, we believe that you will satisfy the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act. In addition, analyses will likely bring clearly to focus the extent of prohibitive regulations necessary on recreation areas, natural areas, or historic areas of the National Parks; wildlife refuges; and Bureau of Land Management lands.
The concept of multiple-use, cited as the major rationale for not closing all Interior lands to ORV use (Page 29 of draft, statement), has never been applied to national park areas either by the Congress or the adminstering agencies. Many of the recreational pursuits provided on other public lands are thus excluded from the parks. Hence, we at NPCA are certain that analyses such as we suggested will indicate that off-road vehicles should be prohibited on natural areas of the National Park System.
Again, we thank you for this opportunity to present our views and we look forward to effective regulations for individual areas published in the Federal Register.
27
Respectfully submitted,
John W. Grandy, IV, Ph.D.

entries.summary: A group of mineral exploration geologists from Tucson, Arizona conditionally supports ORV regulations, but protests any implementation that fails to distinguish between recreational use and working use for mineral exploration. They argue that modern mineral exploration requires sophisticated geophysical equipment that cannot be transported by burro or backpack, making off-road vehicles essential. They support controlling recreational ORV use but insist that mineral exploration must be recognized as a vitally necessary exception on all public lands open for mineral entry, consistent with the economic and technical considerations required by the Environmental Policy Act of 1969.

6520 East 22nd Street Tucson, Arizona 85710
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
"C" Street between 18th & 19th Sts. N.W.
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Sir:
We, as a group of mineral exploration geologists, wish to go on record as protesting the "Review of Departmental Implementation Proposals" made by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation.
This review mentioned various uses for off road vehicles: recreation, fire fighting and tending domestic grazing animals, but there was not a single notation of their value and necessity for minerals exploration. Such a use is also important, along with fire control and care of livestock.
To quote from the Environmental Policy Act of 1969, all agencies of the Federal Government are directed to:
"identify and develop methods and procedures which will insure that presently unquantified environmental amenities and values are given appropriate consideration in decision making along with economic and technical consideration."
The required economic and technical consideration must certainly be given to mineral exploration on the public lands available for that purpose.
Spending, as we do, a great part of our working time in the mountains and deserts of the Western U. S., we realize the necessity for some type of control on the use of off road recreational vehicles in certain areas. However, a definite and clear cut distinction should be made between recreational use which can be carried out in almost any area, and the productive economic values of such vehicles. The firefighters must be allowed to go to the site of the blaze, the rancher must be able to reach his stock, and the exploration geologist must investigate mineralized zones, which are fixed, immovable, limited in individual area, and rare.

57
San Bernardino County, California, recently passed an ordinance relating to off road vehicles (County ordinance No. 1590, Sec. 2, Title 2, Division 8, Chapter 4, of San Bernardino County Code, dated 8 September, 1970). We requested an opinion on the effect of this ordinance as related to mineral prospecting and exploration from a highly regarded legal firm. To quote from the reply:
"The general mining laws provide that the public domain is open to entry for the purpose of prospecting, developing and mining, and thus those engaged in these activities may cross the surface. As a consequence, a motor vehicle engaged in prospecting, etc., may cross the surface.
"However, such permitted surface use, without the benefit of a permit from the Bureau of Land Management should not and would not include the operation of recreational vehicles such as dune buggies, motor cycles and the like."
Any restriction on ORV that does not allow for the working use of such vehicles would effectively prevent mineral exploration over large areas of the public domain, despite the fact that such areas may be legally open to mineral entry. The days when a grizzled prospector, leading a burro can discover valuable surface outcrops are long since gone. To explore for minerals today requires the use of sophisticated geophysical equipment that cannot be transported by burro or backpack. In some cases, a general area of possible geologic interest can be outlined by the use of such equipment mounted in aircraft, but more thorough investigation can only be done on the ground.
We do not question, and in fact support, regulations that will control the unrestricted use of amusement vehicles, but we strongly protest any implementation that does not allow for the economic and technical considerations required by the Act of 1969, and feel that mineral exploration should be considered as a vitally necessary exception on all public lands open for mineral entry.
Respectfully submitted,
