They propose a system of designated 'Adventure Roads' using existing remote roads and trails to channel ORV use while protecting roadless areas, and they criticize the draft EIS for failing to address BLM range conversion projects as a related environmental threat. They also object to what they characterize as politically motivated, environmentally insensitive remarks by Nevada Governor O'Callaghan regarding ORV regulation.

entries.summary: Shelley M. Mark found the draft environmental statement to be quite thorough overall, but raised a concern about the minimum operator age of 21, suggesting it might be lowered to 18 or 20 given that Hawaii's age of majority is 18. He also noted the importance of preparing and publicly circulating maps designating ORV-permitted and prohibited areas within national parks, and acknowledged limited information about ORV problems on Hawaii's federal public lands.
entries.statement_text:
DEPARTMENT OF PLANNING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
P. O. BOX 2359 . HONOLULU, HAWAII 96804
JOHN A. BURNS Governor
SHELLEY M. MARK
Director
EDWARD J. GREANEY, JR. Deputy Director
STATE OF HAWAII
July 7, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
28
Your Reference: K14
Dear Mr. Watt:
This is in response to your letter dated June 1, 1972, which we did not receive until July 3, 1972, transmitting a draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
We have studied the draft statement and find it to be quite thorough in its discussion of the subject matter. On page 5, under Operating Criteria, we note that 21 years is the minimum age limit set for operators unless they have a learner's permit or they are accompanied by a person 21 years of age or older if they are under licensing age for their state of residence. The licensing age in most states is under 21; likewise they can now vote at the age of 18; and in Hawaii they reach the age of majority at 18. You may want to give this age limit matter some more thought to decide if it should be lowered to 20 or 18 years. Otherwise, the operating criteria seem reasonable.
Our other area of concern was to visualize how control of CRV's would actually be implemented. We would assume that each national park would have to prepare some maps indicating areas in the park which would permit CRV's and other areas where ORV's would be prohibited. Such maps should be prepared in draft form and be circulated and made available to the public before they are finally adopted. There could be a variety of arguments about the boundaries of such area designations.
Actually, we do not have any information about the ORV problem on public lands in Hawaii. Most of the Federal public lands in Hawaii are either military lands or the two National parks. I am sure the military commands can keep the problem under control on their bases. We have not heard of complaints of this nature in the two National parks. However, this is not to say they do not exist, or that ORV's are not causing damage; it is probable that such complaints would not be directed to our office.

We are forwarding one copy of your draft environmental statement to the Governor's Office of Environmental Quality Control. It is the agency in our State which reviews and processes all required Federal and State environmental statements. It also makes the statements available to other governmental agencies and the general public. Should further comments be forthcoming, we have asked that office to forward them to you. Our copy of the statement shall also be made available for public review. Thank you for the opportunity of reviewing your statement.
Sincerely,
Shellev M. Mark

entries.summary_quote: We agree that the opening or closing of all Interior Department lands to off-road vehicle use would be an undesirable solution to the current problem. We support the program policy whereby the Assistant Secretary of the Department of the Interior would be responsible for reviewing and coordinating off-road vehicle use activities on Interior lands.
entries.summary: The Wisconsin DNR finds the draft EIS a reasonable appraisal of ORV impacts but calls for more detailed use and operating criteria, better documentation of adverse effects, and greater attention to the private sector in ORV planning. The agency conditionally supports the proposed program, agreeing that neither opening nor closing all Interior lands to ORVs is desirable, and endorsing the Assistant Secretary's coordinating role, while urging caution in originally permitting vehicles on various public land types.
entries.statement_text:
State of Wisconsin \ DEPARTMENT. OF NATURAL RESOURCES
L. P. Voigt Secretary
July 10, 1972
BOX 450 MADISON, WISCONSIN 53701
IN REPLY REFER TO: 1600
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation US Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Re: Draft Environmental Impact Statement (Int. DES 72-62)
We have completed reviewing the draft environmental impact statement for the proposed "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to the Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands" -- Int. DES 72-62.
This statement appears to represent a reasonable appraisal of off-road vehicles and their potential impact on public (federal) lands. However, we submit the following comments for your consideration.
The use criteria and the operating criteria are desirable but they are general and more detailed standards should be developed to permit effective enforcement. Comments on adverse effects of off-road vehicles should also contain some documentation as to source of reference. Because of the broad scope of the proposed program and the diverse public lands involved the actual environmental impact of the proposed action on Executive Order 11644 will be difficult to determine. As pointed cut in the draft environmental impact statement, the most difficult ranamment assessment will be the determination of use levels which will be compatible with the resource base and which will still provide the type of recreation sought by the user group. While the monitoring of effects is desirable entreme caution should be used in the original decision to permit vehicles on the various types of public lands.
The physical and biological impacts are well presented in the proposal. The human impacts have been fairly well presented. However, our Eureau of Correctal Recreation believes that the snowmobile in Wisconsin is carrying a greater share of the off-road vehicle impact at the present time. In the area of human impacts there will continue to be tremendous conflict between motorized and non-motorized interests.
Some of the problems identified in the draft statement will apply to both motorized and non-motorized users of public land (i.e. littering, signing for public information, erosion, etc.)

2.
Point 2 of the Assistant Secretary's program policy states that technical assistance will be provided to all Interior bureaus, other federal agencies, states and their local governments, and the private sector in coordinating planning and programming for the development of areas and facilities for the use of off-road vehicles. This is the only place in the program proposal where the private sector is mentioned. We feel that more attention must be given to the private sector in planning for these vehicles. Off-road vehicle programs on private lands can have a significant impact (both beneficial and adverse) on public lands. Perhaps a companion program can be developed to assist the private sector in coping with off-road vehicles.
Point 3 discusses public information. This section should be broadened to include commercial facilities.
The draft statement does not include a discussion on inventory and demand. This is an important part of the broad program policy and should be considered in the final statement. The proposal indicates that each bureau of the Department of the Interior will be charged with locating areas that can stand the development of off-road vehicle facilities and then conceivably these bureaus could proceed with independent development. Executive Order 11644 requires development of a well-coordinated and planned program at the Assistant Secretary's office to get away from a piece-meal approach to public land development.
A statement is made on page 21 that additional resources will be needed to designate areas, develop facilities, post signs and conduct enforcement. This is an important part of program planning but the impact statement does not contain information on how these critical needs will be met.
Because of the growing interest and concern relating to off-road vehicle use public agencies will be required to concentrate more effort on the private sector for satisfying the demand of the more environmentally damaging recreational activities. The multiple use concept of land use has certain advantages where there is a tremendous amount of public land available and where various activities can be segregated for optimum use. In areas where public land is at a premium, the private sector may be the logical place for certain recreational activities.
The off-road vehicles is undoubtedly a permanent addition to the recreational industry. We agree that the opening or closing of all Interior Department lands to off-road vehicle use would be an undesirable solution to the current problem. We support the program policy whereby the Assistant Secretary of the Department of the Interior would be responsible for reviewing and coordinating off-road vehicle use activities on Interior lands.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this draft environmental impact statement.
Very truly yours,
Bureau of Environmental Impact

entries.role: Director, Committee on Exploration, American Petroleum Institute
entries.summary_quote: it is strongly urged that geological, geophysical, and other vehicular equipment necessary to mineral development be exempted in a revised memorandum and impact statement and in the regulations being prepared to implement Executive Order 11644
entries.summary: Wilson M. Laird, writing on behalf of the American Petroleum Institute's Committee on Exploration, argues that the Draft Environmental Statement and implementing memorandum fail to adequately consider non-recreational uses of public lands, particularly oil, gas, and mineral exploration. He contends that geological and geophysical vehicles are essential to energy development on public lands, which constitute roughly one-third of U.S. land area. He urges that such vehicular equipment necessary for mineral development be explicitly exempted from the terms of Executive Order 11644 and its implementing regulations.
entries.statement_text:
AMERICAN PETROLEUM
1801 K STREET, NORTHWEST
(202) 833-5722
WILSON M. LAIRD, Director Committee on Exploration
July 10, 1972
Hon. Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
The attention of the Committee on Exploration of the American Petroleum Institute has been called to Executive Order 11644, "Use of Off-road Vehicles on Public Lands." Your May 5 memorandum directing the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, Fish Wildlife and Parks, and Water and Power Resources in implementing this Order and the Draft Environmental Statement prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation on May 26, 1972, have been reviewed, and the following comments are offered:
Neither the memorandum nor the impact statement suggest that the entire spectrum of public land use has been considered. Emphasis is almost entirely on recreational use. Other uses, such as oil, natural gas, mineral and geothermal development, forestry and grazing, are not given adequate consideration, indeed, it appears that the mineral resources area of your own department has been bypassed.
Exploration and development of oil and natural gas resources require the use of wheeled and tracked vehicles, and the statement should reflect legitimate uses of such vehicles. An example of primary importance to exploration is the use of off-road vehicles for geological and geophysical work. Should substantial quantities of oil or gas be discovered as a result of exploratory work, other vehicles, such as trucks, drilling rigs and other auxiliary vehicles, would be needed to develop the deposits and make them available for use.
That the development of such resources is vitally needed for the nation's welfare is beyond question in view of the energy crises expected in the near future. Inasmuch as public lands account for approximately one-third of the land surface of the United States, it is obvious that these areas are likely to contain much of the country's oil and gas potential.

In view of the danger that undue and unnecessary restrictions on legitimate exploration and development of oil and gas, as well as other minerals, on public lands may ensue under the definitions and terms of this order, it is strongly urged that geological, geophysical, and other vehicular equipment necessary to mineral development be exempted in a revised memorandum and impact statement and in the regulations being prepared to implement Executive Order 11644 in order to assure that there can be no misunderstanding and that such vehicular equipment is not intended to be included in the terms of the order.
Sincerely,
Stilson m. Land
33
Wilson M. Laird Director
Committee on Exploration American Petroleum Institute

entries.summary: Corson, as Director of New Hampshire Fish and Game, notes that a state committee is already using the Interior Department's memorandum and Executive Order 11644 as a guide for developing ATV/ORV regulations on state lands. He expresses a preference for a policy that keeps lands open to ORVs by default unless there is a specific reason to restrict them, rather than imposing blanket restrictions. He also supports adaptive management, where areas with light use remain open but can be restricted if traffic becomes too heavy.

entries.statement_text:
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION WASHINGTON, D.C: 20554
IN REPLY REFER TO:
9400
Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton Secretary, United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
This concerns the draft environmental statement prepared by the Department of the Interior's Bureau of Outdoor Recreation and dated May 26, 1972. The statement proposes regulations for use of motorized off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The Commission wishes to avail itself of the opportunity extended on June 2, 1972 (37 F.R. 11078) to comment on the draft environmental statement. We are in general agreement with the objectives of the statement which would restrict the use of off-road vehicles on lands administered by the Department to ensure that such use, where permitted, would be compatible with other uses, and would not result in significant adverse environmental impact or cause irreversible damage to existing ecological balances.
The proposed regulations would implement Executive Order 11644 which appears to have been prompted primarily because of the rapidly increasing use of off-road vehicles such as minibikes and snowmobiles for recreational purposes. However, the restrictions appear broad enough to be applicable as well to motorized vehicles used for business or other non-recreational purposes. Accordingly, we are concerned that provision be made so that common carriers and others who have wire, cable or radio communications facilities on public lands pursuant to land-use permits may have reasonable access to such facilities, to whatever extent may be necessary or desirable, in connection with the construction, operation and maintenance of such communications facilities. In this connection, we note that any vehicle whose use was expressly authorized by an agency head of the Department under a permit, lease, license, or contract would be exempt from the proposed use restrictions on off-road vehicles. However, it is not apparent whether existing or future authorizations for use of Department lands for

communication requirements by common carriers and Commission licensees would include authority for use of off-road vehicles necessarily incidental to construction, operation, and maintenance of the necessary communication facilities.
As you are aware, communication facilities on or traversing public lands often provide vital public and national defense communication circuits. Continuity of such service is dependent upon immediate access to the lines and other facilities at all times. Further, spurious emissions from radio transmitters could cause destructive electrical interference to communication requirements of others, including harm to common carrier circuits which the Commission is charged with protecting from such interference. It is also possible that such interference could pose risks to safety of life and property.
The foregoing public interest considerations are merely illustrative of those with which the Commission may be concerned and are not intended to encompass all such considerations which we may properly consider in discharging our statutory responsibilities.
Such responsibilities are discharged, in part, via inspections and investigations by Commission employees and other governmental agents in the field, often involving the off-road use of motorized vehicles. It would appear that such operations would be exempt from the proposed restrictions in light of the provision excepting law enforcement vehicles. We believe it imperative that it be made clear that such governmental inspection and investigatory operations will be exempted.
In short, the Commission wishes to stress the necessity for ensuring that whatever regulations are finally promulgated restricting off-road uses of vehicles, adequate provision be made to ensure that vital communication requirements are capable of being duly satisfied at all times.
This letter was adopted by the Commission on July 6, 1972. Commissioner Nicholas Johnson concurring in results; Commissioner Benjamin Hooks absent.
BY DIRECTION OF THE COMMISSION
11.1
Chairman

entries.summary: Continental Oil Company's Minerals Department protests Executive Order 11644 for severely limiting off-road vehicle use on public lands without adequate provision for productive uses such as mineral and fossil fuel exploration. Minerals Department 
Continental Oil Company 1024 South Plumer Avenue Tucson, Arizona 85719
July 12, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Gentlemen:
This letter is in protest of Executive Order 11644 which would severly limit the use of off-the-road vehicles on public lands. Although I believe that some restrictions should be placed on off-the-road vehicles to prevent people from indiscriminately tearing up the countryside, little provision has been made for the productive use of such vehicles, such as in the exploration for and development of our mineral and fossil fuel resources.
The proposal that permits be readily available for those people having legitimate reasons for using off-the-road vehicles on public lands is a good one. Thus, constructive use of such vehicles would be encouraged, while at the same time those people obtaining said permits would be more responsible for their actions while using off-the-road vehicles.
Sincerely yours,
R. C. Mebres II Geolopies

OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES
The need for an environmental statement involving off-road vehicular use has been essential with the widespread use and evident interest across the country. An established policy to protect natural resources and users of public lands will help eliminate further problems that could have had early solutions.
The proposal as described in the environmental statement of off-road vehicles (ORV) appears to indicate positive direction for this type of mechanized use on public lands. Coordination of involved land use agencies toward implementing consistent and comprehensive ORV policies is a key factor in establishing a compatible program. Highest priorities must be given to minimize abuse of natural resources and conflicts with other public land users. Policies should allow use only with the enforcement of rules and regulations.
If we are to accept ORVs on public lands, we must face the responsibilities of protection and safety of all public land users. An effective policing procedure must be implemented. Control must be organized and established to eliminate conflicts and avoid abuse. The "Operating Criteria" are excellent; however, these regulations will need enforcement to penalize violators of designated ORV lands. We endorse stringent penalties of ORV abusers—these abusers only jeopardize ORV use for nonviolators.
In order to achieve the stated purpose of Executive Order 11644, several components must be implemented. A review of existing restrictions and rules regulating ORV use on public lands would be highly feasible.

Additionally, lands compatible to ORV use could be easily identified

through this type of inventory. All lands should be designated as CLOSED TO ORVs or OPEN MITH RESTRICTIONS ON ORVs. Some lands may not be suitable and others may be opened for limited ORV use. No lands should be open without restrictions. Future research may indicate revision in our present conception of a particular land use. To designate an area without restriction would open the land to unlimited ORV abuse. Lands open to ORVs with restrictions would allow an area to be closed when use impairs environmental values.
In reference to the "adverse effects which cannot be avoided should the proposal be implemented", we believe that some of the stated adverse effects can be avoided. For example, most non-ORV user groups would not resent concentration of ORVs in certain areas if the areas were located in places where conflicts would not occur. The proposed inventory of existing potential ORV lands could supply information of lands that are separated from non-ORV user groups. Most objection to ORV land use lies in the indiscriminate vehicle noise levels and abuse to land. Secondly, noise levels do not necessarily have to be discomforting to users of public lands. Noise levels coupled with land damage by ORVs need drastic and immediate action to retain any semblance of a quality daily existence for living plants and animals. A noise level allowable could be specified by the establishment of an acceptable decibel reading. Violators should be fined or penalized. Continued violations would cause loss of license to operate an ORV. Lastly, historical and archeological structures need not be destroyed by ORV use. These sites could be inventoried and designated as areas "off-limits" to ORVs. Further study of additional adverse effects may be necessary prior to opening lands to ORVs with controls.
1/5 In summary, we are not opposed to ORV land use; however, some

restrictions must be established to avoid indiscriminate abuse of public lands. Certain areas must be identified and maintained for ORV use without conflict to other public land users. The need of these types of areas cannot be overlooked. If demand and interest indicates the need for an ORV area, the site should be provided where feasible. Prior to designation of such an area, thorough examination of all related factors and conflicts must be completed. With this type of planning, land use provisions of off-road recreational vehicles can be established to the satisfaction of the majority of public land users.

entries.summary: The Department of Commerce reviewed the draft EIS and offered two specific editorial suggestions: correcting 'directive' to 'memorandum' in the summary paragraph, and recommending that the statement more clearly delineate which resources are affected and to what degree. The Department also flagged that restrictions on ORVs to designated areas could not apply to prospecting access protected under 16 USC 478, though it noted that environmental, health, and safety information should still be made available to prospectors.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
The draft environmental impact statement for "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands" which accompanied your letter of June 1, 1972, has been received by the Department of Commerce for review and comment.
The Department of Commerce has reviewed the draft environmental statement and has the following comments to offer for your consideration.
Summary Paragraph 2 line 4 - We suggest that you amend the sentence that begins "The directive establishes policies..." to read "The memorandum . . ."
Page 12 line 3 and 4 - In stating "Further, many resource interests will be affected" the implication derived is one of wide ranging affects. We suggest that you delineate those resources affected and to what degree of affectation this directive will have. We would call your attention to 16 USC 478 which provides for access to public lands for the purpose of prospecting. The restriction of ORV's to designated areas could not apply in this case. However, environmental, health and safety concerns should be made available to the prospector.
We hope these comments will be helpful to you in the preparation of the final statement.
Sincerely,
Sidney P. Galler
Deputy Assistant Secretary for Environmental Affairs

entries.summary: Harmston, writing on behalf of the Utah Department of Natural Resources, agrees with the EIS's identification of ORV impacts but argues that most public lands should be designated 'open' and then managed according to resource capability and improved management practices rather than defaulted to closure. He acknowledges that intensified management will require additional resources but warns that failing to do so would underutilize public lands and neglect a legitimate public need. He also recommends that states be required to play a role in ORV regulation on public lands, citing Utah's own comprehensive ORV Act as a model.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Watt:
This is in response to a request from your office, which we received on June 19, 1972, for comments on a draft environmental statement concerning use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
We duplicated the information sent us and distributed it to agencies representing a variety of resource and user interests. A meeting with representatives from each of these agencies was held July 11, 1972 to discuss the statement and their respective comments. Some agencies unable to attend the meeting are sending us their comments. We hope to summarize this information and send it to you by the last week in July. We will have many specific comments to make at that time; but would like to give you our general impression of the environmental statement now.
We agree with the E.I.S. in terms of the existing and potential impacts identified in relation to use of ORV's on public lands. We note, however, that many existing and traditional uses of these lands do similar, if not worse damage, if not properly managed. Our plea, therefore, is for designating most areas "open," then managing the use based on resource capability and on increased capacity resulting from proper design, maintenance, and other management practices.
We recognize that intensified management will require additional manpower, training, and funding. To do less, however, will be to under utilize our resources and to fail to meet a justifiable public need.
The State of Utah has recently passed a comprehensive Off-Road Vehicle Act which addresses itself to many of the problems mentioned in the Executive Order and in the environmental impact statement. Our experience to date leads us to recommend that you require state involvement in ORV regulation on public lands. Copies of our regulations will be sent with our more detailed comments.

entries.summary_quote: We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
entries.summary: Hancock concurs that the proposed ORV management policy—closing some public lands and opening others with controls—is consistent with responsible stewardship of natural resources and recreation interests. However, she raises several concerns: the noise criterion is too vague, issuing permits for ORV races and events is unwise (better left to the private sector), and monitoring must be built into any designation system. She also notes that New Hampshire cannot fully endorse the policy until the Department of Agriculture issues its own statement covering the White Mountain National Forest, and that any specific designation plans for federal lands within New Hampshire must be open to state evaluation.
entries.statement_text:
INTER-DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION
JUL 6 572
FROM Mary Louise Hancock, Director
DATE June 29, 1972
AT (DAFICE) State Planning
SUBJECT Draft Environmental Statement, Department of Interior, regarding the Use of Qff - Road Vehicles
To Alexander M. Taft, Director Comprehensive Planning
Members of my staff have reviewed the draft environmental statement, prepared by the Department of Interior, entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11544 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands."
We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
The designation of areas closed to ORV use based on physical and biological impacts makes a great deal of sense. Predictions of impacts are not in themselves sufficient. Monitoring of designated use areas must be provided for, and management must be sufficiently flexible to allow changes based on the results of monitoring.
We question the wisdom of issuing permits for the use of public lands as sites for ORV races, rallies, meets, etc. Such intensive use can be better provided by the private sector.
The issue of excessive noise poses some difficult problems. First, there is the definitional problem. No attempt is made to specify what decibel level is considered to be acceptable. Second, the Operating Criteria include a clause that "...an ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The environmental impact of that management policy states in part that "...most motorized ORV are noisy in excess of acceptable levels." Logic demands, therefore, that most motorized ORV shall not be permitted on Interior lands. Obviously, the criterion of "excessive noise" is too vague to be of any use.
Since the State of New Hampshire will be affected greatly by policies yet to be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture through its large White Mountain Muticaul Forest, we cannot at this time be certain that we fully endorse the policy and projected impact set forth by Interior. This can better be ascertained after we have had an opportunity to review Agriculture's 102 Statement.
We wish to emphasize that New Hampshire feels a need to evaluate any specific plans for designating use and non-use areas on Federal lands within the State. The evaluation of a national policy involving lands of great diversity is necessary but not sufficient for an adequate environmental assessment.
MLH: Imd

entries.summary_quote: Enclosed herewith are the comments of the Sierra Club on the draft environmental impact statement for the Department of the Interior's implementation of Executive Order 11644 concerning the use of off road vehicles on public lands.
entries.summary: Michael McCloskey, on behalf of the Sierra Club, submitted detailed comments arguing that ORV use should be presumed harmful and all public lands should be closed to ORVs by default, with areas opened only after studies confirm acceptable impact levels. The Sierra Club called for stronger protections including licensing of operators, carrying capacity limits, rationing of use through permits, and strict restrictions near wilderness, wildlife, and desert areas. While accepting that some controlled ORV use may be permitted under Executive Order 11644, the Club insisted that resource protection and the interests of all the public must take priority over ORV user groups.

entries.summary: Stewart R. Wallace, president of Mine Finders, Inc., expresses alarm that proposed ORV restrictions—particularly a four-month advance notice requirement for permits—would severely hamper mineral exploration activities that depend on flexible, unplanned off-road vehicle use. He argues there is a meaningful distinction between recreational 'joy-riding' and professional use of ORVs for making a living, and urges the Bureau to develop a licensing arrangement that allows exploration geologists to work without undue restriction. While he shares concern about environmental degradation from indiscriminate ORV use, he contends that the proposed regulations as written would jeopardize mineral discovery efforts critical to the nation's raw material supply.
entries.statement_text:
MINE FINDERS, INC.
8700 WEST 14TH AVENUE LAKEWOOD, COLORADO 80215 (303) 233-0585
July 12, 1972
44
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Sir:
I am writing to express my concern for legislation or regulation which may come about as a result of executive order 11644 regarding the use of off-road vehicles — Draft Environmental Statement, Int DES 72 - 62, May 26, 1972, notice of which I understand appeared in the Federal Register June 2.
I am a professional geologist with two graduate degrees and have worked in the field for about 24 years. I was employed by the U.S. Geological Survey on both full-time and part-time bases from 1948 to 1955 and worked in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. For the last 17 years I have been a mining and exploration geologist and was fortunate enough, while in the employee of the Climax Molybdenum Company, to participate in two major mineral discoveries. For the last two and one-half years I have been working for a small company, of which I am the president, engaged in contract exploration in western North America for a major raw material company. We now have a staff of seven full-time geologists plus supporting personnel, and hope to add one or two more people during the next eighteen months.
As a geologist and one who enjoys and appreciates nature, I share your concern for the degradation of our remaining "wild lands" by the indiscriminate use or over use by off-road vehicles. On the other hand I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business. I am not familiar with all of the proposed regulations but understand that a four month advance notice would be required for the application of a permit for an off-road vehicle event. It is literally impossible for us to predict four months in advance a specific or, in many cases, even a general off-road vehicle usage. Thus, I am fearful that such restrictions rigidly enforced would greatly reduce our chances of success in making a mineral discovery and in properly locating it according to existing laws governing the location of mineral claims. I might add that mineral exploration is a particularly hazardous business at best and that the odds are great against making a significant find.

lfl
Since the end of World War II, the American mining companies (and others, too) have spent a great deal of time, effort and money here and abroad in the exploration for, and development of, new material resources. Now, for the first time in the last thirty years, the world has finally caught up with itself in that the supply of basic earth materials is sufficient to meet the immediate demand. This situation, however, will not long continue. If the U.S. is to maintain a competitive position (in any field) among the community of nations, it must have access to an assured supply of raw materials at reasonable prices. I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
I do not know what ethical or moral problems there may be in denying use to some while allowing others freedom from such restrictions. I do contend, however, that there is a real difference between simple "joy-riding" and travel for the purpose of making a living. I also maintain that the exploration geologist does perform useful and necessary work, not only for himself and his company, but for the country.
Sincerely yours,
Stewart R. Wallace

entries.summary: The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission conditionally supports the ORV implementation framework but raises several concerns, including the need for clearer, more accessible language in the statement and stronger safeguards to prevent ORV users from gaining unfair advantages over non-users in hunting and fishing areas. Most notably, they recommend that noise levels for ORVs be established in specific decibel measurements on the 'A' scale, suggest restricting ORV use to hours between 7:00 A.M. and sunset, and propose concrete wording for noise criteria rather than the vague 'unusual or excessive noise' standard in the draft.
entries.statement_text:
Nebraska Game and Parks Commission
2200 North 33rd Street / P.O. Box 30370 / Lincoln, Nebraska 68503
July 11, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240
RE: K14
Dear Mr. Hofe:
We have reviewed the draft Environmental Statement for implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to off-road vehicles on the public lands. Following are our comments:
1. Our first concern relates to the need for an impact statement for this action. In the Secretary of the Interior's memorandum dated May 5, 1972, it is stated "The Department will manage its lands so as to control the use of off-road vehicles on Interior lands and ensure that such use, where permitted,... will not result in significant adverse enrivonmental impact or cause irreversible damage..." We would suggest the action is being taken to correct the causes of serious environmental degradation and intrusion that is now taking place. Is the controversy related to the subject the basis for issuing a Statement vs. a less lengthy negative declaration? Surely, both sides represented in the issue can accept the necessity for management of ORV use. Furthermore, the controversial aspects could better be provided for in the statements as needed for individual management plans.
2. It would be most disconcerting to receive an Environmental statement as loaded with technical terms related to other disciplines. We therefore can appreciate the possible apprehension of the typical ORV user who in this instance may already view the action as discriminatory against him. We suggest a review of the entire statement with consideration given to the use of more easily understood terms.
3. Under point 3 of the Summary page, it is incorrectly stated to the effect that the action would have an environmental impact on ORV users and non-users. The action will of course be of concern to these users.
4. We believe there should be an additional point under <u>Use Criteria</u> on page 4. We realize that it is legitimate and desirable in some instances to make it possible to use ORV's to gain access to certain areas for hunting and fishing purposes. However, we also believe that safeguards are needed in some instances to prevent ORV Users from having unfair advantage over non-users of such contrivances in gaining access to certain areas.

Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Washington, D. C. 20240
July 11, 1972
Page Two
5. The statement under 5(b)(1) to the effect that a licensed operator over 21 years of age may not supervise more persons under age at any time than the conditions warrant will need to be more specific in the developed regulations. Otherwise, interpretation may frustrate enforcement efforts.
6. For enforcement purposes we suggest that the allowable noise levels of ORV's operated both singly and in groups of 2 or more be established in allowable decibles as measured on the "A" scale. There is also a possible need for providing considerable flexibility for the different areas according to the type, time of day and/or season of conflicting uses. Examples of the types of recreation experiences that could be seriously degraded by sound intrusion would be stream fishing and cross country skiing. The combination of the safety of the users of ORV and the comfort of campers would appear to justify regulation of ORV use to only those hours from 7:00 A.M. to sunset.

Director

P.S. Also, under (b)(iii), page 5, relative to noise criteria it states that such vehicles shall not produce "unusual or excessive noise." Again, in whose opinion and how does one enforce it?
We suggest the following wording, "Any ORV that produces sound levels in excess of _____ decibels measured on the "A" scale shall be deemed to produce unusual or excessive noise and shall not be permitted on Interior lands."
At the moment we are not well enough "up" on the state of the art to suggest a figure, but it should probably be somewhere around 80 decibels and subject to revision when the industry further sophisticates their technology.

entries.summary: New Hampshire State Planning concurs with the proposed management policy of closing some public lands to ORVs and opening others with controls, while emphasizing the need for monitoring and flexible management. They question the wisdom of issuing permits for ORV races, rallies, and meets on public lands, suggesting such intensive use is better handled by the private sector. They also raise concerns about the vagueness of noise criteria and note they cannot fully endorse Interior's policy until they have reviewed the Department of Agriculture's statement covering the White Mountain National Forest.
entries.statement_text:
Members of my staff have reviewed the draft environmental statement, prepared by the Department of Interior, entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11544 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands."
We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
The designation of areas closed to ORV use based on physical and biological impacts makes a great deal of sense. Predictions of impacts are not in themselves sufficient. Monitoring of designated use areas must be provided for, and management must be sufficiently flexible to allow changes based on the results of monitoring.
We question the wisdom of issuing permits for the use of public lands as sites for ORV races, rallies, meets, etc. Such intensive use can be better provided by the private sector.
The issue of excessive noise poses some difficult problems. First, there is the definitional problem. No attempt is made to specify what decibel level is considered to be acceptable. Second, the Operating Criteria include a clause that "...an ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The environmental impact of that management policy states in part that "...most motorized ORV are noisy in excess of acceptable levels." Logic demands, therefore, that most motorized ORV shall not be permitted on Interior lands. Obviously, the criterion of "excessive noise" is too vague to be of any use.
Since the State of New Hampshire will be affected greatly by policies yet to be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture through its large White Mountain Muticaul Forest, we cannot at this time be certain that we fully endorse the policy and projected impact set forth by Interior. This can better be ascertained after we have had an opportunity to review Agriculture's 102 Statement.
We wish to emphasize that New Hampshire feels a need to evaluate any specific plans for designating use and non-use areas on Federal lands within the State. The evaluation of a national policy involving lands of great diversity is necessary but not sufficient for an adequate environmental assessment.

1. 45

OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES
The need for an environmental statement involving off-road vehicular use has been essential with the widespread use and evident interest across the country. An established policy to protect natural resources and users of public lands will help eliminate further problems that could have had early solutions.
The proposal as described in the environmental statement of off-road vehicles (ORV) appears to indicate positive direction for this type of mechanized use on public lands. Coordination of involved land use agencies toward implementing consistent and comprehensive ORV policies is a key factor in establishing a compatible program. Highest priorities must be given to minimize abuse of natural resources and conflicts with other public land users. Policies should allow use only with the enforcement of rules and regulations.
If we are to accept ORVs on public lands, we must face the responsibilities of protection and safety of all public land users. An effective policing procedure must be implemented. Control must be organized and established to eliminate conflicts and avoid abuse. The "Operating Criteria" are excellent; however, these regulations will need enforcement to penalize violators of designated ORV lands. We endorse stringent penalties of ORV abusers—these abusers only jeopardize ORV use for nonviolators.
In order to achieve the stated purpose of Executive Order 11644, several components must be implemented. A review of existing restrictions and rules regulating ORV use on public lands would be highly feasible.

Additionally, lands compatible to ORV use could be easily identified

through this type of inventory. All lands should be designated as CLOSED TO ORVs or OPEN MITH RESTRICTIONS ON ORVs. Some lands may not be suitable and others may be opened for limited ORV use. No lands should be open without restrictions. Future research may indicate revision in our present conception of a particular land use. To designate an area without restriction would open the land to unlimited ORV abuse. Lands open to ORVs with restrictions would allow an area to be closed when use impairs environmental values.
In reference to the "adverse effects which cannot be avoided should the proposal be implemented", we believe that some of the stated adverse effects can be avoided. For example, most non-ORV user groups would not resent concentration of ORVs in certain areas if the areas were located in places where conflicts would not occur. The proposed inventory of existing potential ORV lands could supply information of lands that are separated from non-ORV user groups. Most objection to ORV land use lies in the indiscriminate vehicle noise levels and abuse to land. Secondly, noise levels do not necessarily have to be discomforting to users of public lands. Noise levels coupled with land damage by ORVs need drastic and immediate action to retain any semblance of a quality daily existence for living plants and animals. A noise level allowable could be specified by the establishment of an acceptable decibel reading. Violators should be fined or penalized. Continued violations would cause loss of license to operate an ORV. Lastly, historical and archeological structures need not be destroyed by ORV use. These sites could be inventoried and designated as areas "off-limits" to ORVs. Further study of additional adverse effects may be necessary prior to opening lands to ORVs with controls.
1/5 In summary, we are not opposed to ORV land use; however, some

restrictions must be established to avoid indiscriminate abuse of public lands. Certain areas must be identified and maintained for ORV use without conflict to other public land users. The need of these types of areas cannot be overlooked. If demand and interest indicates the need for an ORV area, the site should be provided where feasible. Prior to designation of such an area, thorough examination of all related factors and conflicts must be completed. With this type of planning, land use provisions of off-road recreational vehicles can be established to the satisfaction of the majority of public land users.
45

Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U. S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Re: Draft Environmental Statement for the Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to the Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands - File No. 80-72
We have completed our review of the subject draft environmental statement, which was transmitted by your letter of June 1, 1972.
On the basis of our review and the comments of other State agency representatives who have reviewed the statement, we have no comments relative to the assessment of environmental effects of the proposed action, and consider the statement adequate.
The North Carolina Recreation Task Force, an inter-agency committee which provides policy direction for recreation planning and establishes priorities for the allocation of Land and Water Conservation Fund grants, has adopted the following goal as stated in "Goals of North Carolina Outdoor Recreation Planning," published May 5, 1970: "In order that public funds be used efficiently, it is the goal of the State that all levels of government work cooperatively and without duplication to meet North Carolina outdoor recreation needs identified in the Plan (State Comprehensive Cutdoor Recreation Plan). To this end, this Plan, and its subsequent ammendments, will be used as a basis for evaluating, assigning priorities, and endorsing projects of Federal, State and local Government."

In keeping with this goal, we submit for your consideration the following recommendations for implementation of Executive Order 11644:
1. Heads of the various land managing bureaus and agencies within the Department of the Interior should contact and coordinate with the applicable regional office of the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation in developing regulations regarding ORV use.
2. Heads of these bureaus and agencies, in developing regulations governing the use of ORV on lands within their jurisdictions, should coordinate with the applicable Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP) for the purpose of: 
a. Assuring that such regulations are in compliance with the SCORP.
b. Providing input data (location, size, etc.) concerning "open" areas for inclusion in the SCORP inventory and information system.
c. Affording SCORP planners the opportunity to help formulate regulations and establish criteria for the use of ORV. It is felt that this would mutually improve the "state of the art" at Federal, State and local levels regarding the techniques and methods for determining and understanding the impact of ORV.
d. Maximizing the satisfaction of recreation needs identified in the SCORP.
Sincerely yours,
- Bhalliers
RANDOLPH HENDRICKS
Planning Coordinator

Gentlemen:
This letter is in protest of Executive Order 11644 which would severly limit the use of off-the-road vehicles on public lands. Although I believe that some restrictions should be placed on off-the-road vehicles to prevent people from indiscriminately tearing up the countryside, little provision has been made for the productive use of such vehicles, such as in the exploration for and development of our mineral and fossil fuel resources.

Sincerely yours,
R. C. Mebres II Geolopies

Mills Tower, San Francisco 94104

Dear Director Hofe:
Enclosed herewith are the comments of the Sierra Club on the draft environmental impact statement for the Department of the Interior's implementation of Executive Order 11644 concerning the use of off road vehicles on public lands.
We appreciate having had this opportunity to submit comments on this important environmental matter.

Executive Director
Enclosure. MM:1kn

Sierra Club Comments on the
Draft Environmental Impact Statement
For Department of Interior Implementation Of
Presidential Order 11644
Concerning the Use of Off Road Vehicles on Public Lands
General Comments
(1) ORV areas should be located near urban areas where possible and not allowed in more remote lands of a wilderness or semi-wilderness character. Most ORV users are interested in testing their machines and not in access to scenic areas. These areas, however, should not be immediately adjacent to homes where a citizen's right to privacy, peace, and quiet would be threatened. ORV areas distant from urban areas would create traffic congestion with accompanying air pollution. Control would be easier to maintain closer to urban centers.
(2) No mention is made of the amount of land that will be closed to ORV vs. that which will be open. This will probably turn out to be the most critical issue when the program is implemented. The statement should recognize this problem and state that the interests of all of the people will be placed above those of the ORV operators when those interests are in conflict. The primary charge of public land administrators is to protect resources first and to accommodate various users of the land second.
(3) Since our public lands are not limitless, regulation beyond the zoning emphasized in the statement will be needed. If ORV areas are over-used and are receiving unacceptable damage, the solution should not be to open up more areas to their use. Consideration must be given to rationing their use. This could be done by issuing permits to individual ORV operators and restricting the frequency of their use. This is being considered for wilderness areas now and there is no reason why other users of public lands should not be similarly restricted. Before any ORV area is opened up an attempt to determine its carrying capacity should be made in order to limit damage. The carrying capacity should not be

exceeded under any circumstance.
Specific Comments
<u>Page 5, b-i.</u> The Sierra Club strongly supports the statement requiring operators of ORVs to be licensed. Since a lot of ORV damage to the environment is caused by unsupervised, under age operators, strong regulations regarding under age operators must be made and enforced. The adult supervisor should be held legally responsible for any damage caused by under age operators under his supervision.
<u>b-i (d)</u>. <u>Excessive</u> damage should be changed to something like <u>permanent</u> and noticeable damage. Damage by ORV should be controlled far short of being excessive.
<u>b-iii</u>. The Sierra Club strongly supports this good provision requiring proper muffler and spark arrestor equipment on all vehicles and that this equipment be in good working order and in constant operation.
<u>Page 6 (iv)</u>. Organized off road vehicle events must not be allowed <u>under any</u> <u>circumstance</u> in any areas normally closed to ORVs. Bonds must be put up by people conducting such events. Provision must also be made to rehabilitate and restore areas impacted by these events.
Page 10, lines 10-11. This states that lands will remain open to public use unless closed for a specific reason. This should not apply to ORVs because of their unquestioned damage. All BLM lands should be closed to ORV and then opened up on a parcel by parcel basis after a study has been shown that the leval of ORV damage will be acceptable. This should be true of all federally owned land, not just BLM land.
Page 11, lines 1-5. The terms used to identify ORV areas are qualitative.

Objective criteria are needed or at least a system for arriving at objective criteria. If the decision to open or close an area becomes merely subjective, then we can expect decisions to be made only on the basis of pressure and not on what is best to protect the resources. Furthermore, determination of ORV carrying capacity must be made for all areas open for their use and limited to such levels as the environment can handle without significant environmental damage.

Page 12, lines 8-11. ORVs do cause damage in most areas with substantial use. Repeated use by large numbers (in excess of the carrying capacity) causes excessive damage in nearly all types of terrain and vegetation.
Furthermore, ORVs are not primarily used for access to remote areas when all use is considered collectively. Very few ORV operators are interested in access as much as they are in testing out their machine. ORVs are used for sport and not for an appreciation of the aesthetic and cultural qualities of the public lands. If ORVs were used merely for access we would have minimal conflict with them.
Page 13, line 1. Emphasis is placed upon the benefits to user groups. This statement should acknowledge that the public lands belong to everyone, not just user groups. The public lands of the nation need to be managed so that the resources are managed in the best interests of all the people -- present and future generations -- and not just for the user groups who happen to be on the scene at this point in time.
<u>Page 13</u>. The discussion of soil erosion in the last paragraph should include wind erosion of desert soils. Under normal conditions much of the desert surface is covered by desert pavement — a covering of pebble to boulder size rocks, the smaller material having been carried away by wind erosion. ORV wheels break up this thin crust exposing the finer soil beneath to further wind erosion. The problem is especially severe where cross country races are held in the desert. Participants take off in waves, sometimes one-mile-across lines, axle to axle, cutting a huge swath of destruction across the desert.
Page 14, paragraph 2. Snowmobiles do more than create a litter problem.

Studies are increasingly demonstrating significant environmental impact on vegetation from snowmobiles as the result of twig breakage and snow compaction. Also, the snowmobile is used as a vehicle to chase a number of species of wildlife, which all too frequently causes severe exhaustion and sometimes death. Harassment

129
of wildlife of any sort must not be allowed.
Page 14, last paragraph. The dust problem is especially bad in the desert and should be mentioned in this statement.
Page 15, last paragraph. The California Department of Fish and Game has set up quali guzzlers in many areas of the California desert and some game birds are entirely dependent on this source of water. Cross country motorcycle races have been routed right by some of these. Vandalism in areas accessible only by ORVs has also been a critical problem with quali guzzlers.
The Desert Bighorn Sheep is known to disappear in areas of heavy human use.

This species should receive a higher priority in management decisions than ORVs.
Page 16, paragraph 2. It should be emphasized here that ORV use should be considered harmful to wildlife until proven otherwise. All areas should be considered closed until it is shown that ORVs would have an acceptable impact upon wildlife.
Page 16, paragraph 3. The only ORV users who might need access to game management purposes are the game and land managers themselves. If it is determined that an area should be closed to ORVs, then hunters should walk or ride horses. It should be very clear that an area normally closed to ORVs will not be opened to hunters on ORVs merely because of a surplus of game.
Page 17, line 11. This mentions revenues from sales of motorcycles. It should be recognized that not all motorcycles are used as ORVs. Only those that are used as ORVs should be included in the statement.
Page 17, lines 15-16. Winter access to small towns via snowmobiles can be on snow covered roads and need not be cross country.
Page 18, line 11. The case for strengthened family relationships caused by ORV use should be proven. Saying there is reason to believe this is true is not enough. The reasons should be spelled out.

Page 19, last paragraph. The signs of ORV use are very offensive to non-users. This remark should remain in the statement and receive more emphasis.
Page 21, paragraph 2. It is true implementation will be costly. The statement should place more emphasis upon this fact and groups like the Sierra Club can help in acquiring the necessary funds to effectively control ORVs.
Page 22, line 6. This recognizes a land ethic itself. This is very important and should be greatly emphasized by the use of a separate heading and a greatly expanded text.
This same paragraph again only refers to users of public lands and does not mention that all of the people own the public lands. Their best interests need to be considered.
Page 24, line 10. Urban dwellers will be especially resentful if ORV areas are established within hearing range of homes.
Page 26, lines 6-8. This sentence implies that decisions will be semi-permanent. If ORV areas are shown to suffer unacceptable damage they should be closed. It should not be implied that any ORV area will not be closed at a future date if necessary.
Page 26, lines 9-12. The problems mentioned in this paragraph would be minimized if all areas were considered closed and then opened to ORVs only after a careful study shows damage would be acceptable.
Page 29, line 4. "Inspiration" is hardly the word to use when discussing the benefits of ORV benefits. It should be deleted.

entries.summary_quote: Our plea, therefore, is for designating most areas "open," then managing the use based on resource capability and on increased capacity resulting from proper design, maintenance, and other management practices.
entries.summary: The Utah Department of Natural Resources agrees with the EIS's identification of existing and potential impacts from ORV use, but argues that many traditional land uses cause similar or worse damage if unmanaged. Their primary position is that most areas should be designated 'open' and then managed based on resource capability, proper design, and maintenance, rather than defaulting to closure. They also recommend requiring state involvement in ORV regulation on public lands, citing Utah's own comprehensive Off-Road Vehicle Act as a model.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Watt:
This is in response to a request from your office, which we received on June 19, 1972, for comments on a draft environmental statement concerning use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
We duplicated the information sent us and distributed it to agencies representing a variety of resource and user interests. A meeting with representatives from each of these agencies was held July 11, 1972 to discuss the statement and their respective comments. Some agencies unable to attend the meeting are sending us their comments. We hope to summarize this information and send it to you by the last week in July. We will have many specific comments to make at that time; but would like to give you our general impression of the environmental statement now.
We agree with the E.I.S. in terms of the existing and potential impacts identified in relation to use of ORV's on public lands. We note, however, that many existing and traditional uses of these lands do similar, if not worse damage, if not properly managed. Our plea, therefore, is for designating most areas "open," then managing the use based on resource capability and on increased capacity resulting from proper design, maintenance, and other management practices.
We recognize that intensified management will require additional manpower, training, and funding. To do less, however, will be to under utilize our resources and to fail to meet a justifiable public need.
The State of Utah has recently passed a comprehensive Off-Road Vehicle Act which addresses itself to many of the problems mentioned in the Executive Order and in the environmental impact statement. Our experience to date leads us to recommend that you require state involvement in ORV regulation on public lands. Copies of our regulations will be sent with our more detailed comments.

entries.role: President, Mine Finders, Inc.; professional geologist
entries.summary_quote: I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
entries.summary: Stewart R. Wallace, a professional geologist and president of Mine Finders, Inc., supports environmental protection but is alarmed by proposed ORV restrictions that would severely hamper mineral exploration activities. He argues that requiring four months advance notice for permits is impractical for exploration work, which cannot be planned that far in advance. He urges the Bureau to develop a licensing arrangement that allows exploration geologists to conduct their work without undue restriction, distinguishing between recreational 'joy-riding' and professional use necessary for making a living and serving the national interest in raw materials.
entries.statement_text:
MINE FINDERS, INC.
8700 WEST 14TH AVENUE LAKEWOOD, COLORADO 80215 (303) 233-0585
July 12, 1972
44
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Room 4410
Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Sir:
I am writing to express my concern for legislation or regulation which may come about as a result of executive order 11644 regarding the use of off-road vehicles — Draft Environmental Statement, Int DES 72 - 62, May 26, 1972, notice of which I understand appeared in the Federal Register June 2.
I am a professional geologist with two graduate degrees and have worked in the field for about 24 years. I was employed by the U.S. Geological Survey on both full-time and part-time bases from 1948 to 1955 and worked in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. For the last 17 years I have been a mining and exploration geologist and was fortunate enough, while in the employee of the Climax Molybdenum Company, to participate in two major mineral discoveries. For the last two and one-half years I have been working for a small company, of which I am the president, engaged in contract exploration in western North America for a major raw material company. We now have a staff of seven full-time geologists plus supporting personnel, and hope to add one or two more people during the next eighteen months.
As a geologist and one who enjoys and appreciates nature, I share your concern for the degradation of our remaining "wild lands" by the indiscriminate use or over use by off-road vehicles. On the other hand I am very much alarmed about some of the proposed restrictions on the use of such vehicles viewed from the position of one who finds them essential for the efficient conduct of his business. I am not familiar with all of the proposed regulations but understand that a four month advance notice would be required for the application of a permit for an off-road vehicle event. It is literally impossible for us to predict four months in advance a specific or, in many cases, even a general off-road vehicle usage. Thus, I am fearful that such restrictions rigidly enforced would greatly reduce our chances of success in making a mineral discovery and in properly locating it according to existing laws governing the location of mineral claims. I might add that mineral exploration is a particularly hazardous business at best and that the odds are great against making a significant find.

lfl
Since the end of World War II, the American mining companies (and others, too) have spent a great deal of time, effort and money here and abroad in the exploration for, and development of, new material resources. Now, for the first time in the last thirty years, the world has finally caught up with itself in that the supply of basic earth materials is sufficient to meet the immediate demand. This situation, however, will not long continue. If the U.S. is to maintain a competitive position (in any field) among the community of nations, it must have access to an assured supply of raw materials at reasonable prices. I urge you, therefore, to work out some licensing arrangement that would permit the exploration geologist to conduct his studies without undue restriction.
I do not know what ethical or moral problems there may be in denying use to some while allowing others freedom from such restrictions. I do contend, however, that there is a real difference between simple "joy-riding" and travel for the purpose of making a living. I also maintain that the exploration geologist does perform useful and necessary work, not only for himself and his company, but for the country.
Sincerely yours,
Stewart R. Wallace

entries.role: Director, Nebraska Game and Parks Commission
entries.summary_quote: We suggest that the allowable noise levels of ORV's operated both singly and in groups of 2 or more be established in allowable decibles as measured on the "A" scale.
entries.summary: Barbee supports ORV management on public lands but offers several conditional recommendations for improving the draft statement, including clearer language, better enforcement provisions, and access safeguards for hunters and fishers. He specifically urges that noise levels for ORVs be established in measurable decibel limits on the 'A' scale rather than vague terms like 'unusual or excessive noise,' and suggests ORV use be restricted to hours between 7:00 A.M. and sunset. He also recommends flexibility in noise standards based on area type, time of day, and season to protect sensitive recreational experiences such as stream fishing and cross-country skiing.
entries.statement_text:
Nebraska Game and Parks Commission
2200 North 33rd Street / P.O. Box 30370 / Lincoln, Nebraska 68503
July 11, 1972
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240
RE: K14
Dear Mr. Hofe:
We have reviewed the draft Environmental Statement for implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to off-road vehicles on the public lands. Following are our comments:
1. Our first concern relates to the need for an impact statement for this action. In the Secretary of the Interior's memorandum dated May 5, 1972, it is stated "The Department will manage its lands so as to control the use of off-road vehicles on Interior lands and ensure that such use, where permitted,... will not result in significant adverse enrivonmental impact or cause irreversible damage..." We would suggest the action is being taken to correct the causes of serious environmental degradation and intrusion that is now taking place. Is the controversy related to the subject the basis for issuing a Statement vs. a less lengthy negative declaration? Surely, both sides represented in the issue can accept the necessity for management of ORV use. Furthermore, the controversial aspects could better be provided for in the statements as needed for individual management plans.
2. It would be most disconcerting to receive an Environmental statement as loaded with technical terms related to other disciplines. We therefore can appreciate the possible apprehension of the typical ORV user who in this instance may already view the action as discriminatory against him. We suggest a review of the entire statement with consideration given to the use of more easily understood terms.
3. Under point 3 of the Summary page, it is incorrectly stated to the effect that the action would have an environmental impact on ORV users and non-users. The action will of course be of concern to these users.
4. We believe there should be an additional point under <u>Use Criteria</u> on page 4. We realize that it is legitimate and desirable in some instances to make it possible to use ORV's to gain access to certain areas for hunting and fishing purposes. However, we also believe that safeguards are needed in some instances to prevent ORV Users from having unfair advantage over non-users of such contrivances in gaining access to certain areas.

Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director Washington, D. C. 20240
July 11, 1972
Page Two
5. The statement under 5(b)(1) to the effect that a licensed operator over 21 years of age may not supervise more persons under age at any time than the conditions warrant will need to be more specific in the developed regulations. Otherwise, interpretation may frustrate enforcement efforts.
6. For enforcement purposes we suggest that the allowable noise levels of ORV's operated both singly and in groups of 2 or more be established in allowable decibles as measured on the "A" scale. There is also a possible need for providing considerable flexibility for the different areas according to the type, time of day and/or season of conflicting uses. Examples of the types of recreation experiences that could be seriously degraded by sound intrusion would be stream fishing and cross country skiing. The combination of the safety of the users of ORV and the comfort of campers would appear to justify regulation of ORV use to only those hours from 7:00 A.M. to sunset.
Very truly yours,
NEBRASKA GAME AND PARKS COMMISSION
Willard R. Barbee
Director
WRB/GRC/1w
P.S. Also, under (b)(iii), page 5, relative to noise criteria it states that such vehicles shall not produce "unusual or excessive noise." Again, in whose opinion and how does one enforce it?
We suggest the following wording, "Any ORV that produces sound levels in excess of _____ decibels measured on the "A" scale shall be deemed to produce unusual or excessive noise and shall not be permitted on Interior lands."
At the moment we are not well enough "up" on the state of the art to suggest a figure, but it should probably be somewhere around 80 decibels and subject to revision when the industry further sophisticates their technology.

entries.role: commenter, Allan Hancock College area resident
entries.summary_quote: ORV's should be severely restricted and prohibited in wildlife refuges.
entries.summary: William Denneen, writing from the Allan Hancock College area, draws on 12 years of personal ORV ownership and local observation to argue that ORVs have been very destructive to natural habitats. He cites noise disturbance to wildlife and people, vegetation damage from tires, and littering as specific harms. He calls for severe restrictions on ORV use and an outright prohibition in wildlife refuges.
entries.statement_text:
Allan Hancock College 500 South College Drive Sinta Maria, California 93454
July 13, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Director,
Re: INT-DES-72-62
I wish to add my observations to your consideration of offroad-vehicle plans on public lands. We have a considerable number of such vehicles in our area and I have owned one for 12 years.
My observation has been that ORV's have been very destructive to the natural habitat in all areas where they are permitted. The noise disturbs wildlife and people, the tires tear up vegetation and the drivers often leave prodigious quantities of litter. ORV's should be severely restricted and prohibited in wildlife refuges.
Sincerely yours,
Villiam Denneen
