entries.role: Director, National Campground Owners Association; Member, Executive Committee, Ski Touring Council
entries.summary_quote: Healthful recreation activities should be promoted, motorized activities should be discouraged.
entries.summary: C. R. Agnew Jr. argues that healthful, non-motorized outdoor recreation activities such as hiking, ski touring, backpacking, and camping should be promoted on public lands, while motorized activities should be discouraged because they do not foster physical, mental, or spiritual health. He contends that ORV users should be accommodated on private lands rather than vast public lands, as the government has no obligation to subsidize vehicle owners. He urges stringent controls on ORVs, warning that opening public lands to them will cause environmental damage, noise and air pollution, and irreversible harm to wilderness recreation opportunities.
entries.statement_text:
C. R. AGNEW JR. 357 ROUND HILL ROAD BREENWICH, CONN. 06830
203 869-1368
July 19, 1972
Honorable Rogers C. B. Morton, Secretary Department of the Interior Washington, D. C.
Dear Mr. Morton:
70
My affiliations are: Director, National Campground Owners Association; Member, Executive Committee, Ski Touring Council. I comment on your letter of May 5th, 1972 and the Draft Environmental Statement.
1. Healthful recreation activities should be promoted, motorized activities should be discouraged. The President issued Order 11644 by virtue of authority vested in him by the Constitution. He is empowered to promote regulations for the benefit of the American people.
It is submitted that the healthful outdoor sports and recreation activities of benefit to the minds, bodies and spirits of the American people are the non-motorized sports of: hiking, ski touring, backpacking and camping, fishing, canoeing, sailing, horseback riding.
These activities contribute to the healthful growth and development of Americans. By the opposite token motorized activities do not essentially foster and promote body, mental and spiritual health. Indeed in some instances motorized activities are counter productive to healthful recreation activities and detract from healthful recreation of others.
2. Motorized recreation activities should be undertaken on private lands and by arrangement with private landowners.
Owners of off-road vehicles are not poverty stricken. Government has no obligation to subsidize these vehicle owners, nor to allow them to use vast areas of our public lands.
The experience of the compground industry in the past 15 years can be cited. Formerly, government provided the bulk of campsites. In the past 15 years a longe private or reproved industry has risen. Today the great bulk of American convers - 705 - are accomplated at private campgrounds. Government arenaies have greatly reduced expenditures for construction of campgrounds.
It has been demonstrated that family campers and toruists are not basically interested in the wilderness and nature. They wish to vacation amid conventional man-made surroundings. They wish to bring the commercial comforts of home to the wilderness. If given the chance they would commefcially exploit our wilderness treasures.

There is no need to turn over vast areas of public lands for the use of off-road vehicles. Users can be accommodated by arrangement with private landowners.
3. Stringent Controls Urged for Off-road Vehicles.
a. The use of ORVs is to be discouraged for health reasons. The throwing open of large areas of public lands to them will encourage the growth and development of the industry. Strict controls will hold back industry expansion. 
b. If areas are now thrown open to ORVs the following will ensue: 
i. Environmental damage from operation of machines.
ii. Noise and air pollution will occur.
iii. The pollution will seriously detract from healthful ourdoor recreation pursuits of persons who enjoy the peace and serenity of wilderness type areas.
iv. Once a pattern is set for ORVs it will be difficult or impossible to reverse it later if we find that we are overwhelmed with motor driven vehicles.
Ray Cigner.

C. R. Agnew Jr.

entries.summary_quote: The increasing use of off-road vehicles is presenting problems that must be recognized and dealt with by land management agencies. The time to consider and solve the problems is before they become uncontrollable.
entries.summary: Carl J. Hocevar, a director of the Idaho Environmental Council, presented a statement arguing that off-road vehicle use on public lands causes serious problems including soil erosion, wildlife harassment, and noise pollution, and that these problems must be addressed before they become uncontrollable. He surveyed regulatory efforts in other states and proposed specific local measures including immediate trail closures where erosion or user conflicts exist, restrictions on snowmobiles in wildlife wintering areas, and mandatory noise level limits of 70-75 decibels for ORVs.
entries.statement_text:
Idaho Environmental Council
P. O. Box 3371 - University Station Moscove, Idaha 83843
February 18, 1971
Presented to Panel -- "Off-Hoad Vehicle Use of Public Lands"
Upper Snake River Chapter of the Federal Executive Association
by Carl J. Hocevar
The increasing use of off-road vehicles is presenting problems that must be recognized and dealt with by land management agencies. The time to consider and solve the problems is before they become uncontrollable.
Before one can attack a problem he must identify it. In the first part of my presentation I will present the problem areas associated with the use of off-road vehicles as seen by conservationists. Having identified the problems I will then describe some efforts designed to regulate the use of off-road vehicles in other parts of the country. Finally, I will propose steps that should be taken locally to regulate off-road vehicle use.
I. What are the problems?
In general the problems created by the use of off-road vehicles may be classified in three categories: (1) damage to soil and vegetation. (2) impact on wildlife, and (3) esthetic considerations.
Trailbikes and four wheel drive vehicles are the cause of soil erosion in many areas. This is especially true where the vehicles are used indiscriminantly in granitic soils and in high alpine areas. Wet meadou areas are quite susceptible to damage by motorized vehicles. Long deep ruts are cut into these areas resulting in erosion paths. Even if used on trails these vehicles may cause severe erosion, especially if the trails are on steep slopes.
At this time I would like to show a few slides depicting soil damage caused by trailbikes in the Caribou National Forest.

Soil erosion problems may be compounded by the introduction of several new vehicles. A two-wheel drive trailcycle is now on the market. Even more frightening is the all terrain vehicle. These vehicles may be appropriately referred to as miniature tanks and they will do just about as much damage to the terrain as their big brothers.
Large areas of land are no longer safe from damage after the snow falls; the propositing season is then just beginning. In some areas enoughbles are used on thin layers of snow. Grasses and undergrowth may be torn up in these areas and small shrubs may be exushed if the snow is not deep enough to cover them. In many instances the damage is done inadvertently and the snowhobilers may not even be aware of the damage they are doing.
The impact of off-road vehicles on wildlife is becoming more of a problem, especially with the advent of the snow-mobile. Besides using snowmobiles to get into the backcountry some indiscrete hunters also use them to chase animals and may actually run deer to exhaustion.
Wildlife harassment does not end with the close of the hunting season since, unfortunately, some of the most accessible snowmobiling areas are also some of the best big game wintering areas. During the midwinter and early spring months the anommobiling activities are at their peak. This period also coincides with the time when the animals are also the least mobile and the most vulnerable from a physical standpoint. The wildlife in their winter ranges have a tough time just surviving without having to contend with harassment from snowmobilers. It does not take much exertion to cause animals to contract pneumonia once they are in their weakened condition. Any form of harassment is particularly hard on pregnant females.
Not all harassment of wildlife is done maliciously, but much is done by thoughtless individuals who are only trying to get close enough to photograph or observe the anitals. Neverthôless, the game is still frightened by the noise and the mobility of the snowpobiles. Shew whilers any inadvertently scare wildlife just by being in the same vicinity. The transmendous racket made by these machines carries long distances and disturbs the anitals.
I do not know whether there has been a problem in Ideho of people chasing courans or predators such as coyates, but this practice has been a problem in other parts of the country. This type of problem could easily occur if it does not already exist.
Smaller forms of wildlife may also be adversely affected by snowmebiles. A noted Canadian wildlife expert. Philip Corbet, has noted that show is an excellent insulator and a natural protection for sice and other small animals. When the snow is packed down by snowmobiles it loses its insulating qualities thereby reducing protection for the such each animals.

The use of off-road vehicles increases hunting pressures in many areas which were formerly inaccessible to most hunters. These refuges are lost then retorized vehicles are used to bring in larger numbers of heaters.
Index is being compromised by the use of motorized vehicles. The principal value of these lands lies in their ability to provide primitive type experience for an increasing number of people. Here people are beginning to look to our public lands as a means of escape from the procesures of medern living. They are looking for colitude or at least a minimum of disturbance. However, even in the backcountry silence is becoming much more difficult to find as recreational motorized vehicles are increasing in numbers. People are continually being affronted by noisy trailbikes and snow obiles. Even a small number of these vehicles can reduce the enjoyment others may derive from the use of our public lands.
Is noise a real problem? Very definitely. It is recognized as one of our major forms of pollution. Loud noises are not only annoying and disturbing but can also cause damage to hearing. To give us an idea of what noise levels we are talking about I will first list some thresholds and then list the noise levels generated by a number of familiar situations. The unit of measurement is the decibel.

one additional potential problem areas I would like to mention one additional potential problem area that I can foresce. This is not an immediate problem but is included to provide an example of things to come. I am referring to the one-men flying platform. This vehicle is jet powered and is capable of transporting people at up to 60 mph. This vehicle will be a real noise polluter and could possibly be used to but form. I think we may be seeing these vehicles on the market within the next ten years.

II. What is being done around the country to regulate the use of off-road vehicles?
We have heard this morning from the Park Service and the Forest Service concerning the edministration of off-road vehicles in Yelloustone Park and in the Tarthee National Porest. I would now like to present additional information concerning attempts to regulate the use of off-road vehicles in other parts of the country.
The control of snowmebiles is attracting attention throughout the snowbelt regions of the United States. There are over 1000 miles of snowmobile trails in the national forests in the eastern part of the United States. By designating appropriate trails the Forest Service is controlling the areas in which snowmobilers go thus avoiding conflicts with wildlife.
Several of the national forests in Washington have closed trails to snowmobiles.
In January, 1971, an area around Sun Valley was closed to snowmobile use due to damage done to ski areas, vegetation, and watersheds.
Some state and local governments are using registration fees to lay out trails in parks and in state forests. As of January, 1969 Michigan had built 500 miles of trails and had plans for an additional 1300 miles by 1973.
The state of New York currently has legislation pending that would limit muffler noise from snowmobiles to 73 db.
On February 8. 1971 President Nixon presented a package of environmental bills to Congress. Included was a noise pollution regulation pertaining to snowmobiles.
Although trailbikes are a problem in all the western states the coastal states have taken the load in trailbike regulation. In California 6 of the 18 national forests have off-road vehicle restrictions. In late 1969 sinteen percent of the trails in non-wilderness areas had been closed to vehicles. The principal reason given was soil erosion but conflicts with non-vehicle users also was a factor.
Colorado has closed about 85 of the trails in non-wilderness areas to four-wheel drive vehicles due to resource damage and to conflicts with foot and horse travellers and compers.
In June, 1970, the Menatchee National Forest in Washington had closed 89 trails to all motorized vehicles. Ten trails were closed to four-wheel drive vehicles. In addition, certain areas were also closed to cross-country use of vehicles.

In March, 1969, the Snequalmic National Forest, also in Washington, had closed 11 trails and has considering the closure of 25 additional trails.
In Oregon, the Deschutes National Forest closed 42 trails and in addition closed the entire Broken Top area to trailbikes. These restrictions want into effect on April 15, 1970.
In Idaho the only closure to trailbikes in a non-wilderness area that I know of is in the Mallard-Larkins Pieneer Area in the St. Joe National Porest.
In the western slopes of the Tetons the trail to Alaska Basin has also been closed to trailbikes.
III. What should be done to regulate the use of off-road vehicles. 
1. Trails should be closed to trailbikes immediately where soil erosion is currently a problem.
2. Trails should be closed to trailbites immediately where there are conflicts with non-vehicle users.
3. Where it appears that persistent use of trailbikes will damage fragile soils then trails should be closed.
4. Trail closures should be effected if potential conflicts with increasing numbers of hikers and horses seems inevitable.
5. In general, off-trail use of trailbikes should be eliminated. It is particularly important that trail cycles not be allowed on high alpine meadous. Certain areas may be designated for cross country use if soil damage is not deemed to be a problem and if conflicts with other groups will not be a problem.
6. Four-wheel drive vehicles should be restricted to well established roads or four-wheel drive trails where there is no drager of soil erosion.
7. Snowmobiles should not be allowed in areas that are prime wintering grounds for wildlife.
8. Trails should be established for snowmobile use. This practice will insure that snowmobiles are not used in wintering areas and will minimize conflicts with other groups.
9. Certain high country areas should be established where snowmobiles are not allowed. In these areas other groups such as ski tourers may enjoy quiet surroundings. Zoning 73 areas for snowmobile use will insure that more than one recreational user group will be satisfied.

July 23, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Pepartment of the Interior
Washington, D.C. 20515
Re.: Int DES 72-62
Dear Sir:
Indiana Sassafras Audubon opposes the establishment of motorized vehicle trails in national forests. We feel there is no reason that national forests have to consider ORVs as an important recreational asset in the forest land.
Our opinions are based on close observation of the controversy in our own National Hoosier Forest, participation at a hike conducted by the Forest Service on July 15, 1972 (see enclosed newspaper clipping) in the Hickory Ridge Area near Monroe Reservoir, and the Draft Environmental Analysis, proposed Off Road Vehicle Policy, Hoosier National Forest (2350) of July 14, 1972 as supplied to this society by U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service.
Out of app. 160,000 acres of land in National Hoosier Forest the Forest Service proposes to open app. 99,000 acres to ORV trail use, while only 62,000 acres would remain closed. The initial cost for these trails would be anywhere between 0500,000.00 to 01,000,000.00 with the maintenance cost 050,000.00 per year and administrative cost 025,000.00 to 050,000.00 per year. This would benefit with the exception of a few independent users, almost exclusively the app. 1000 nembers of the Indiana Motorcycle Association. entries.summary: Indiana Sassafras Audubon strongly opposes establishing motorized vehicle trails in national forests, arguing there is no justification for treating ORVs as an important recreational asset on public lands. The organization raises concerns about the disproportionate cost to taxpayers, damage to wildlife and ecosystems, noise pollution, adverse effects on non-motorized users, and the fact that the primary beneficiaries would be motorcycle manufacturers and a small number of riders rather than the general public. They contend that ORV use is fundamentally incompatible with sound land management and the long-term enjoyment of public lands by future generations.

entries.summary: The Natural Resources Defense Council found the draft Environmental Impact Statement totally inadequate, arguing it failed to comply with NEPA, Executive Order 11644, and other laws governing Interior Department responsibilities for public lands. They contended that the draft statement accommodated ORV use rather than protecting environmental values, and demanded that both the draft statement and the Secretary's May 16 memorandum be withdrawn so that implementation of E.O. 11644 could begin anew. Their attached detailed comments further argued that ORVs should be banned from national parks and wildlife refuges, and that environmental values must be given the highest priority in any revised policy.

Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
1600 TWENTIETH STREET, N.W. WASHINGTON, D.C. 20009
147
202 387-2855
July 17, 1972
New York Office 36 WEST 44TH STREET NEW YORK, N.Y. 10036 212 986-8310
Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Hofe:
Enclosed are the comments of the Natural Resources Defense Council on the Draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on public lands.
We find the draft statement to be totally inadequate. It does not comply with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, Executive Order 11644, or other laws which define Interior Department responsibilities in managing the public lands. Instead, it militates against the clear duty imposed by these directives to identify and protect environmental values. It indicates that the policy of the Department is not to insure that the use of off-road vehicles is "controlled and directed so as to protect resources on [the public] lands," as required by E.O. 11644, but rather to accommodate all demands for ORV use. For these reasons we believe that the draft statement must be withdrawn.
Furthermore, the Secretary's memorandum of May 16 is an inadequate attempt to implement E.O. 11644. It fails to take account of Interior's legal responsibilities to identify environmental values, and fails to propose concrete policies for the regulation of ORV use. It is useful neither as a proposal for action, nor as a guide to substantive policy. Therefore, we believe that the memorandum must be withdrawn along with the draft statement, and the entire process of implementation of E.O. 11644 must begin again.

We are shocked that Interior, as the agency charged with the protection of natural resources on over 60% of Federal lands, should reject the opportunity to declare its commitment to the protection of environmental values and choose instead to accommodate an environmentally-destructive activity. The effect of this choice is to seriously weaken and misdirect the implementation of laws which are intended to promote environmental quality. In its revised implementation of E.O. 11644, Interior must change its policy on ORV use to give environmental values the highest priority. Only in this way can the Department properly fulfill its responsibilities.
Sincerely yours,
Thomas B. Stad, Jr.
Thomas B. Stoel, Jr.
Grey & Studen
Greg E. Studen

Dear Sir:
Thank you for giving the State of South Dakota the opportunity to respond to your draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 which pertains to the use of off-road vehicles on public lancs.
In general, we agree that unregulated off-road vehicle traffic on public and private lands creates a nuisance and that ignoring the popularity of such vehicles is not an approach which should be taken. Also, we believe that recreation participants desiring such an experience should be allowed to fulfill that need. However, a fulfillment of their desires should not take place at the expense of other recreationists who feel a need for a quieter, more isolated type of experience without interruption by noise, etc. In addition, we are cognizant of the fact that harmful effects on grazing, wildlife preceding and vegetation can be intensified by disruption due to OPV traffic. Therefore, special controlled areas should be designated for OPV use in order to make OPV use compatible with other uses of public lands.
The following are brief references to specific statements found in your draft with comments directed toward clarifying problem areas and delineating points implied but not necessarily spelled out:

Therefore, the document should delete the word "special" in line 4.

As you know, past decisions have been made with a bias toward project development or utilization of space even though consequences were unknown.

9. Page 23  In many cases, land reclamation in terms of Lines 14 returning the landscape to its original and 15 appearance and the capability of the land to its original use is not very workable. The major problem appears to be that reclamation often seriously lags behind use-over-use mis-use and scarring of the landscape.
10. Page 22 - We agree with the statement that operating Last four criteria and registration requirements for lines ORV should conform to State Laws.
Thank you for the opportunity of responding to your draft statement.
Jun P. indurus Physical Planner
Sincerely yours,

entries.summary: Governor Hathaway expresses Wyoming's strong concern about the proposed ORV regulations, emphasizing that the key to success is an 'open until closed' philosophy where all areas are presumed open to ORV use unless specific conditions warrant closure. He argues this approach has worked well in Wyoming and provides the flexibility needed for successful administration across diverse regions. Given that nearly 50% of Wyoming's land is federally owned, he stresses the state's substantial interest in ensuring the proposal supports major economic activities like mineral exploration, agriculture, hunting, and fishing.

GOVERNOR

The Honorable Rogers C.B. Morton Secretary of the Interior U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Mr. Secretary:
The State of Wyoming is quite concerned regarding the proposed rules and regulations to be established by the Department of the Interior concerning the use of off-road vehicles.
Federal consideration and thinking on this proposal was first officially brought to our attention at a recent Wyoming and federal Recreation Action Team meeting and subsequently when the State was given the opportunity to review the Draft Environmental Statement on the subject.
The one aspect of the proposal which both the State and Wyoming based federal administrators point to as the key to success is that the proposal must be based on the philosophy that all areas will be considered open to use until circumstances and conditions develop which would merit specific action to the contrary. This open until closed philosophy has successfully been used in Wyoming for pears and by its continuance we feel that enough flexibility will be built into the proposal to allow for successful administration in Wyoming as well as the highly populated areas east of the Mississippi and on the west coast.
As you know, almost 50 per cent of the surface land of this state is owned by the federal government, and this land will obviously be directly affected by this proposal. Major activities such as mineral exploration, agriculture, hunting and fishing and all general outdoor recreational activities directly and substantially

July 20, 1972
affect Wyoming's economy and our way of life. Thus, we feel we have a substantial interest in the initiation and success of this proposal.
Thank you for your consideration of this matter.
With best wishes, I am
Sincerely yours,
MISYL

entries.summary: Walter L. Criley, writing on behalf of the Tennessee Department of Conservation's Division of Planning & Development, offers conditional support for ORV regulation, raising specific concerns about environmental disturbances from designated ORV areas, the difficulty of controlling underage vehicle operators, and the risk that opening some areas will lead users to assume all public lands are open. He concludes by welcoming the Department of the Interior's recognition of the problems ORVs create, but insists that the resulting regulations must be carefully analyzed and strictly enforced to protect the integrity of public lands.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Wellborn:
We have reviewed the above captioned statement and offer the following comments:
a. (Page 6) Under the operating criteria subsection, permits may be issued for the operation of Off-Road Vehicles on areas designated for their use for organized races. Criteria for the selection of these areas should carefully weigh the resulting environmental disturbances to the area. Also relating to this subsection, the operation of motorized vehicles (especially motorcycles and minibikes) by persons under legal licensing age will be difficult to control.
b. (Page 12) The second paragraph on this page states that ORV's provide safe and convenient transportation to portions of the public lands not otherwise accessible to the benefit of society. The inaccessibility of many public lands is the very factor that attracts many people to these areas. Cheapening the quality of a person's visit by making all areas easily accessible (along with the resultant environmental disturbances inherent to ORV's) will accelerate the already rapidly diminishing areas suitable for a quality natural experience.
c. (Page 14) ORV use in camping and picnicking areas will tend to push wildlife in these areas into more remote sections. The loss of these animals will detract from the quality of a recreational visit.
d. (Page 16) In the long run, ORV use will result in more forest fires being started than it will aid in the prevention of these fires.

e. (Page 19) Care should be taken to insure that, with the opening of certain areas to ORV use, the user does not come to think that all areas of the public lands are open to the use of his vehicle.
146
f. (Page 26) On this page a paragraph states: "Within designated ORV areas some irreversible or irretrievable impacts upon land forms, wildlife and their habitat, and historical and archeological sites may occur despite the utmost of precautions." Again careful attention should be focused upon the criteria of areas zoned for ORV use to hold their cultural and environmental impact to a minimum.
It seems that any recreational form that becomes popular and economical will be welcomed to the public lands. Accepting this fact leads one to wonder, should the average citizen find himself capable of purchasing bulldozers and army surplus tanks, will he be allowed access with these vehicles to the public lands?
It is good to see that the Department of the Interior recognizes the problem that ORV's create and is trying to regulate their use. These regulations should be carefully analyzed and strictly enforced to insure the perpetuation and undiminished integrity of our public lands.
Sincerely,
Walter L. Criley

entries.summary: The Bureau of Land Management reviewed the draft environmental impact statement and offered detailed comments requesting additional clarification and information on several fronts. BLM noted that the statement focused too narrowly on recreational ORV use, called for clearer criteria and definitions, and requested more accurate description of BLM's own proposed planning-based approach to ORV management. The agency also provided numerous specific editorial and substantive suggestions to improve the accuracy and completeness of the document's environmental analysis sections.
entries.statement_text:
We have reviewed the subject draft statement. Enclosed are our comments which indicate areas in which additional clarification or information would aid in assessing the impacts of the proposed action on the environment.
he laye
Enclosure

General Comments
The statement generally focuses in the impacts of recreational use of ORVs on the public lands. The statement should recognize that ORVs have an impact whether they are associated with the recreational or other authorized uses. The impacts of failing to administer ORV uses uniformly should be discussed.
There is a diverse variety of environmental impacts which can occur as a result of the various types of ORV (dune buggy vs. snomobile), and the terrain (desert vs. tundra). Additional discussion of the impacts of the various types of ORV and their impact on different type of terrains would be helpful.
The "use" and "operating criteria" identified in the statement appear to be a reiteration of the criteria identified in Secretary's memo to implement Executive Order 11644. They are very general in nature. The statement is not clear whether these are the only criteria Interior agencies will use to identify use and operation of ORV or whether the various agencies will develop more specific criteria to implement the Executive Order. If this section is meant merely to quote the Secretary's memo, that should be clarified.
The statement should clarify the interim status of all Interior lands prior to designation of ORV use areas. Will they be open or closed to ORV use? What effect will this have on the human environment?

Specific Comments
I. Description of the Proposal.
If the .criteria for "use" and "operation" provide a guide for more specific criteria to be developed by each Interior agency the following is suggested:
Page 4. a). The heading indicates criteria for official use may by different from that of the public. Establishment of "double standard" can raise questions as to its appropriateness. Search and rescue, firefighting, or other types of administrative duties may require exceptions. Official use should generally comform with the constraints placed on the public.
(iv). "Areas and trails shall not be located on officially designated Wilderness Areas or Primitive Areas." Should the exclusive language of this section be modified to provide for administrative determination with full public input?
Page 6. (iv). Should running lights, etc., be allowed as an alternative to taillights? Dune buggies, for instance, do not use taillights since they cannot be seen by other vehicles. At night they are marked by a light carried atop a fiberglass staff.
"All applications for permits for such ORV events shall be submitted no less than four months, or a lesser amount of time ..." The four months acts as a constraint on advance notice. In many cases, six months or more prior to an event, may be desirable.
If the criteria for "use" and "operation" are the only criteria to be used by Interior agencies to regulate ORV use a more definite description of terms such as, "minimize", "excessive", "unique", etc., should be provided.
11. Description of the Environment.
The discussion of the implementation of EO.11644 seems out of place. It's the BLM alternative in approaching management of ORVs. The statement is not an accurate description of the proposed BLM regulations as now drafted.
Addiscussion of the BLM proposal should include the following information: "BLM through its planning system will identify areas for ORY use and the stipulations which will guide such use. Through the planning system all resource values will be identified. Areas which present an opportunity for ORV use as well as those in need of protection from ORV will be identified.

The public will be presented this information. They will be requested to provide additional information on resources or environmental values requiring protection as well as the needs and opportunities for ORV use. BLM will then analyze the information provided by the public, information it has previously identified, and conflicts which exist between resource uses and identify areas to be closed and stipulations governing ORV use which will insure maintenance of environmental quality.
In the case of commercial use of ORVs, the statement should indicate:
"Commercial use e.g., races, rallies, etc., of the public land will
be allowed only on those areas designated as suitable for ORV use
by the planning system and an environmental analysis which indicates
there will be no serious degradation of the environment. The\nenvironmental analysis will be used to indicate the need for
stipulations to protect both the public and environmental values
during the event".
Page 11, first sentence. "Low vegetative production potential" should not be a controlling factor in ORV trail selection. Properly laid-out and managed trails can be successful in timber or other vegetated areas. In fact, heavy vegetation often helps confine the vehicles to the trails and good vegetative potentials can help heal environmental wounds.
III. Environmental Impacts of the Proposed Action.
Page 12, last sentence, paragraph 2, appears to conflict with first sentence, paragraph 5. In one sentence, it is stated that properly operated ORVs do limited damage; in the other sentence, it states that even when properly operated, impacts may be great and, in many instances, irretrievable. The last sentence of the paragraph could be re-worded as follows: "In most areas, ever where properly operated and managed, ORVs are capable of serious damage..." The third paragraph should also be re-worded to read: "In all areas ..." rather than "In some areas ...".
Paragraph 4. Would this paragraph be more appropriate in Section VII?
The following sentences describe mitigating measures which would appear to be more appropriate in Section IV.
Page 13. Paragraph 3  last two sentences.
Page 15. Paragraph 2  last two sentences.
Page 16. Paragraph 2  last sentence.
Page 18. Paragraph 3  last sentence.
Page 19. Paragraph 2  last sentence.

Page 20. All of paragraph 2 and paragraph 3, last sentence.
Page 21. Paragraph 1  last sentence.
Page 13 A) Physical Impacts. The discussion provided appears to contradict the last sentence in paragraph 1 on page 12. The following re-wording would eliminate this contradiction: First paragraph, third sentence "Prohibition ... would prevent further impact...". Paragraph 2, fourth line, change "impaction" to "compaction".
Page 14. Line 3 from the bottom. Change "increase" to "vary". 
Page 15. Paragraph three, third and fourth sentences suggest the following: "A few animals will be killed by ORV use. Some will be temporarily driven from their natural habitat and others will adjust to the presence of the vehicles".
Page 16. Line 3. Change "accomodate" to "tolerate".
Third paragraph, last sentence. Discusses the advantages of increased fire-spotters and fire fighters as a result of ORV use. It should be noted that increased incidence of fire caused by the ORV users may be much more hazardous and costly than the benefits provided by the increased number of fires detected and extinguished.
Page 18. Line 2. Change "negative" to "adverse".
Page 20. Line 5. Could be re-worded as follows: "Increased ORV accidents, litter, and sanitation...".
Paragraph 2, the discussion of designation and signing techniques identifies a multitude of problems. Notifications of restrictions of use requires authority for enforcement. Signs, a basic tool of notification, create a visual impact which cannot be minimized. Guidance is needed. Standardization of signs, with a readily identifiable format, will help the user making it possible to use smaller individual signs.
Page 21. Third line from the bottom, change "of" to "to".
V. Any Adverse Effects Which Cannot be Avoided should the Proposal be Implemented.
The adverse effects of the BLM's lack of authority or manpower to efficiently and effectively implement the Executive Order should be identified and discussed.

VIII. Alternatives to the Proposed Action.
The effects the various alternatives will have on the incidence of fire could be discussed. For example, no action can be expected to result in an increase in fires from campfires and sparks from overtaxed exhaust systems, requiring increased fire protection; closing all Interior lands will result in a reduced incidence of fire; and opening all Interior lands could be expected to result in a corresponding increase, similar to no action, in the incidence of fires.
Page 30, paragraph 4, first sentence. Will fewer trespass problems result from opening lands to ORV? Less ORV trespass may result, but there will probably be an increase of related activities such as illegal occupancy, antiquity trespass, etc.

entries.entity: Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
entries.summary_quote: The document represents a comprehensive statement setting forth criteria for protection of natural resources on Federal lands. If the criteria are conscientiously followed and agencies carry out their mission responsibilities, adverse environmental effects should be minimized.
entries.summary: The Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife conditionally supports the draft environmental statement, finding it a comprehensive document that, if conscientiously followed, should minimize adverse environmental effects. However, the Bureau raises specific concerns, including the inconsistency of permitting ORV racing on public lands with its wildlife protection mission, requesting explicit exclusion of National Wildlife Refuges from such activities, and calling for clearer noise standards, better enforcement mechanisms, and more consistent open/closed policies across bureaus. The Bureau also requests rewording of the section describing its mission to better reflect its primary responsibility for fish and wildlife protection.
entries.statement_text:
United States Department of the Interior
FISH AND WILDLIFE SERVICE BUREAU OF SPORT FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE WASHINGTON; D.C. 20240
AUG 1 1 1972
Memorand m
To:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Acting Deputy
From:
Director, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
Subject: Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order
11644, pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the
Public Lands (DES 72-62)
This Bureau appreciates the opportunity to review and comment on the subject draft statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on public lands. The document represents a comprehensive statement setting forth criteria for protection of natural resources on Federal lands. If the criteria are conscientiously followed and agencies carry out their mission responsibilities, adverse environmental effects should be minimized.
Our specific comments are as follows:
1. The proposal description should include all of the definitions as given in Section 2 of Executive Order 11644, unless a copy of the document is to be attached to the environmental statement. Of particular interest to the public would be the definitions of "off-road vehicles" and "public lands." Additionally, the statement does not mention ORV use on public lands which are open to mineral and mining entry and to established mining claims. The Executive order is not clear on this point; it is recommended that it be clarified in the statement.
2. The proposal to permit ORV racing, rallies, endurance contests, etc., on public lands is inconsistent with existing land management policies of this Bureau. It is recognized that the multiple-use concept is promoted when consistent with wise resource management. The broad authorization given to this proposal which will admittedly adversely affect the natural resources of this Bureau, in particular the National Wildlife Refuge System, is not responsible

management. Concessions such as this should be beyond the expectations of any user group. It is recommended that this Bureau be specifically excluded from participation in this activity by means of the draft environmental statement.
3. It is suggested that the paragraph concerning this Bureau (page 9) be reworded to read as follows: "The mission of the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife is to assure maximum opportunity for the American people to benefit from fish and wildlife resources as part of their natural environment. The Bureau is responsible for the management and operation of a nationwide system of national wildlife refuges and waterfowl production areas comprising 30 million acres of land, including wilderness areas, 90 national fish hatcheries and 6 research stations along with associated lands. A significant portion of Bureau lands have been specifically designated as protected habitat for rare and endangered species of wildlife. Travel in or use of any motorized vehicle, including land, water, ice, snow, and aircraft types, is prohibited on areas administered by the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, except on specific routes of travel or in designated areas posted for public use. In accordance with paragraph 3(a)(4) of Executive Order 11644, areas and trails will be established only if the Bureau head determines that ORV use on Bureau lands will not adversely affect the natural, aesthetic, or scenic values. Because of the Bureau's primary responsibility for the protection and perpetuation of fish and wildlife resources, with wildlifeoriented public use as a secondary objective, administration of the ORV program must necessarily be more restrictive than other bureaus or agencies."
4. On page 17 it is stated that the Upper Great Lakes Regional Commission reported snowmobiling was worth $212,180,000 to the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan in 1970-71. The Bureau feels it inappropriate to use this gross, or net figure without some follow-up discussion of associated impacts in terms of environmental degradation or possible human benefits received. Use of such an isolated figure as a beneficial impact only is misleading to the reader. Nuch of the description of economic impacts is inappropriate and unnecessary.
5. The last paragraph of page 17 is suggested for rewording as follows: "Controlled use, adequately administered, would have a minor alverse impact on the economic effects of ORVs. An enhancement of vacation land and home values is a possibility, but as yet is unproven. Environmental degradation could detract from previously established vacation land uses during the same or other seasons, and real estate values could actually decrease because of ORV intrusions and disturbances: Past off-season tourist periods could be eliminated or reduced. In individual areas where ORV use is prohibited, a negative impact would result."

6. While the Executive order and introductory statement of the draft refer to visually designating only those trails and areas open to ORV use, it should be readily recognized that posting only the open areas would pose enforcement problems. This is acknowledged in the environmental statement on page 20, line 13, which reads "...adequate posting must be improved to permit enforcement of any restrictions." In essence, this means areas not open should be posted. This may not be possible to do in some areas, and will require an expanded effort in communication, designation of areas, and enforcement.
7. We believe that completed studies on noise pollution contain enough information for definite acceptable noise levels to be spelled out (in decibels) for the different types of ORVs and outdoor public use areas. Included in the acceptable levels of noise must be the cumulative effect of several ORVs even though they are operating at their individual acceptable level. This determination must be made before adequate administrative controls can be developed—spice zoning, time zoning, restricted areas, etc. A general statement referring to "unusual or excessive" noise will not suffice because interpretation by individual land managers will vary and this will ultimately mean problems in administration.
8. Although we are aware of the problems that exist we feel there will be many problems regarding the open or closed policies of each of the Bureaus. They should be consistent.
It is hoped that the above will be helpful in preparation of the final document.

entries.summary: Claude E. Hastings, on behalf of Georgia's Game and Fish Division, found the draft environmental statement adequate in describing the problems of off-road vehicle use on public lands. He conditionally supported the proposed regulations but insisted that any ORV rules promulgated by federal secretaries should require concurrence from Georgia's Director of the Division of Game and Fish, since wildlife resources belong to the state. He also recommended specific protections for streams, trout habitats, and wildlife areas where ORV use would cause significant adverse effects.
entries.statement_text:
Date: July 19, 1972
Georgia State Clearinghouse
Bureau of State Planning and
Community Affairs
270 Washington Street, S. W.
Atlanta, Georgia 30334
FROM:
Name:
Claude E. Hastings
Title:
Environmental Protection Coordinator
Agency:
Project:
Department of Natural Resources
Game and Fish Division
SUBJECT:
PROJECT SUMMARY NOTIFICATION REVIEW
Applicant: Department of the Interior
Implementation of Executive Order 11644
State Clearinghouse Control Number: 72-06-22-18
This agency does not have an interest in the above project. ____
This agency has further interest in and/or questions concerning the above project and wishes to confer with the applicant.
This agency is interested in the above application and wishes to make the following comments:
The Department of Natural Resources, Division of Game and Fish for the State of Georgia would like to make the following comments relative to this environmental statement.
This agency believes that the statement is adequate in describing the nultiplicity of problems inherent with off-road vehicular use on our public lands. We recognize the conflicts of interest which can occur due to these vehicles. Since the fish and wildlife resources on all public lands belong to the State and the State is charged with the responsibility of the protection, management and perpetuation of the fisheries and wildlife resources, it is our judgement that off-road vehicle regulations promulgated by the Secretary of the Interior or the Secretary of Agriculture should have the concurrence of the Director of the Division of Game and Fish, Department of Natural Resources.

218
Department of the Interior Implementation of Executive Order 11644 72-06-22-18
It is recommended that extreme caution be used to preserve public lands for beauty, solitude, remote values and wildlife habitat. These are what are presently making these lands valuable.
On Page 4 of the Environmental Impact Statement under "a) Use Criteria (except for official use): " "(i) Areas and trails shall be located to minimize damage to soil, water, vegetation or other resources of the public lands." should be changed to include streams and their tributaries. This is especially important on trout streams to control silt pollution and all soil disturbances that would result in disruptions to the stream bottom habitats.
We are certainly in agreement with (ii) which states, "Areas and trails shall be located to minimize harrassment of wildlife or significant disruption of wildlife habitats."
On Page 14, the sentence, "Use of machines in stream beds can affect the spawning, migrating, and feeding habits of fish and other aquatic life" is true and we would not wish to see the use of off-road vehicles permitted in stream beds. Where certain off-road vehicle trails cross streams, the vehicles should cross the streams on bridges rather than disrupting the stream beds, which causes silt pollution with its adverse effects on fisheries habitat.
On Page 16, the statement, "Certain animals will not be able to accommodate the opening of their habitat to off-road vehicle traffic and accompanying human activities" is quite true. In those instances where it is recognized that the use of off-road vehicles will have a significantly adverse effect upon certain wildlife resources, such use should be prohibited.

entries.summary: Continental Telephone Corporation, as a utility company with installations on public lands requiring off-road access, expressed concern that neither the Executive Order nor the draft environmental statement explicitly permitted utility vehicles to access authorized facilities without a permit. The company hoped the regulations were intended to target recreational ORV use rather than impede utility maintenance operations, and suggested language be added to exempt utility company vehicles performing maintenance on public lands from permit requirements. They also requested that any permit system clearly specify the procedure and the responsible federal land management agency.
entries.statement_text:
1800 K Street, N.W. Washington, D. C. 20006 (202) 466-2895
William Friedman
Vice President — Governmental Relations
August 3, 1972
, 31
Mr. James Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Re: Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644, Use of Off Road Vehicles (ORV) on Public Lands
Dear Mr. Watt:
Continental Telephone Corporation is the third largest independent telephone company in the United States. In our operations we have a number of installations which are located on public lands and require off road access.
We have followed with interest the subject Executive Order and the Draft Environmental Statement prepared by your office and published on May 26, 1972. We are obviously affected by any instructions which may be published on this matter. We are advised by your Mr. Stuart Davey and Mr. William Honore that an implementing order is soon to be published, but prior to its publication, they suggested we send you any comments that we may have.
As we can interpret, neither the Executive Order nor your draft memorandum specifically consider the problem of expressly permitting the use of vehicles off established roadways for the purpose of maintaining authorized communication (and other utilities) facilities without first requiring that a permit be obtained. We would hope that the intent of the Executive Order and Environmental Statement is to regulate pleasure off-road vehicles, and not to impede the servicing of communications equipment. Accordingly, you might wish to consider including a statement such as: "Vehicles belonging to utility companies performing maintenance of authorized facilities on public lands may transit those lands without permit."
Further, may we suggest that any regulation which does require permits establish the procedure of obtaining its permits and the mechanism for determining what federal land management agency will be exercising transit authority over a particular piece of federal land on which we may have to operate.
We trust that these comments may be of use to you. We would be pleased to discuss this further with you if you desire.
Very truly yours,
William Friedman

entries.summary_quote: I ask that ATV, snowmobiles, and off the road vehicles in general be banned from use on all public lands.
entries.summary: Er. Jon Polisle strongly opposes ORV use on public lands, calling for a complete ban on ATVs, snowmobiles, and all off-road vehicles from all public lands. He argues that their trail use causes erosion and unnecessary noise, and that private enterprise—not public lands—should provide areas for such recreation. He uses the analogy of a recreational caterpillar tractor to underscore the absurdity of allowing ORVs in natural settings.
entries.statement_text:
2040 Wilson, Apt. 28 St. Paul, Minn. 55119 July 14, 1972
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Department of the Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Subject: Statement Number INT - DES - 72 - 62
Dear Sir:
Concerning your Draft Environmental Statement, I ask that ATV, snowmobiles, and off the road vehicles in general be banned from use on all public lands. Their trail use, causing erosion and unnecessary noise should not be permitted.
If I bought a caterpillar tractor for recreation and asked to use it in a national forest I would be laughed at, so why should someone (and others will quickly follow) trail ride through the serene setting nature can provide.
Private enterprise supplies the equipment and private enterprise can supply the riding area for off the road vehicle; They should not be permitted on public lands.
Sincerely,
Er. Jon Polisle

entries.summary: Gary J. White, along with numerous co-signers, opposes more restrictive federal regulations on off-road vehicles on federally owned land in Nevada. They argue that the rugged terrain of northern and northeastern Nevada makes four-wheel drive vehicles virtually essential for hunting and fishing, and that they cause no harm to the terrain in the remote areas they frequent.
entries.statement_text:
July 7, 1972
Bureau of Land Management Elko, Nevada
Gentlemen:
We wish to add our voice of protest to more restrictive regulations by the Federal Government of off road vehicles on federally owned land in the state of Nevada.
We have chosen to live in this large and sparsely populated area for the expressed purpose of being near free and open land areas and as you know we have less than one person per square mile in Nevada.
The terrain in northern and north eastern Nevada is so rugged it is almost an abstract to negotiate most of this area without four wheel drive vehicles.
The lakes and reserviors are in very remote areas, mostly without roads. Hunting and fishing is our most popular out door sport in Nevada. Deer and chuckar partridge country is located in the most rugged and remote sections of our state. Four wheel drive vehicles are virtually a must in the pursuit of this sport.
Flease consider these sports and our feelings that these are our sacred rights. We feel we do no harm to the terrain hunting in these rugged areas where we go for weeks without seeing another person.

entries.summary_quote: This agency believes that the statement is adequate in describing the nultiplicity of problems inherent with off-road vehicular use on our public lands.
entries.summary: The Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Game and Fish Division found the draft environmental statement adequate in describing the problems of off-road vehicular use on public lands. The agency argued that ORV regulations issued by federal secretaries should require concurrence from the state's Game and Fish Division, since fish and wildlife resources on public lands belong to the state. They also recommended specific protections for streams, trout habitat, and wildlife areas where ORV use would have significantly adverse effects.
entries.statement_text:
Date: July 19, 1972
Georgia State Clearinghouse
Bureau of State Planning and
Community Affairs
270 Washington Street, S. W.
Atlanta, Georgia 30334
FROM:
Name:
Claude E. Hastings
Title:
Environmental Protection Coordinator
Agency:
Project:
Department of Natural Resources
Game and Fish Division
SUBJECT:
PROJECT SUMMARY NOTIFICATION REVIEW
Applicant: Department of the Interior
Implementation of Executive Order 11644
State Clearinghouse Control Number: 72-06-22-18
This agency does not have an interest in the above project. ____
This agency has further interest in and/or questions concerning the above project and wishes to confer with the applicant.
This agency is interested in the above application and wishes to make the following comments:
The Department of Natural Resources, Division of Game and Fish for the State of Georgia would like to make the following comments relative to this environmental statement.
This agency believes that the statement is adequate in describing the nultiplicity of problems inherent with off-road vehicular use on our public lands. We recognize the conflicts of interest which can occur due to these vehicles. Since the fish and wildlife resources on all public lands belong to the State and the State is charged with the responsibility of the protection, management and perpetuation of the fisheries and wildlife resources, it is our judgement that off-road vehicle regulations promulgated by the Secretary of the Interior or the Secretary of Agriculture should have the concurrence of the Director of the Division of Game and Fish, Department of Natural Resources.

218
Department of the Interior Implementation of Executive Order 11644 72-06-22-18
It is recommended that extreme caution be used to preserve public lands for beauty, solitude, remote values and wildlife habitat. These are what are presently making these lands valuable.
On Page 4 of the Environmental Impact Statement under "a) Use Criteria (except for official use): " "(i) Areas and trails shall be located to minimize damage to soil, water, vegetation or other resources of the public lands." should be changed to include streams and their tributaries. This is especially important on trout streams to control silt pollution and all soil disturbances that would result in disruptions to the stream bottom habitats.
We are certainly in agreement with (ii) which states, "Areas and trails shall be located to minimize harrassment of wildlife or significant disruption of wildlife habitats."
On Page 14, the sentence, "Use of machines in stream beds can affect the spawning, migrating, and feeding habits of fish and other aquatic life" is true and we would not wish to see the use of off-road vehicles permitted in stream beds. Where certain off-road vehicle trails cross streams, the vehicles should cross the streams on bridges rather than disrupting the stream beds, which causes silt pollution with its adverse effects on fisheries habitat.
On Page 16, the statement, "Certain animals will not be able to accommodate the opening of their habitat to off-road vehicle traffic and accompanying human activities" is quite true. In those instances where it is recognized that the use of off-road vehicles will have a significantly adverse effect upon certain wildlife resources, such use should be prohibited.

entries.summary_quote: The Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Department of Interior is to be congratulated for the work that has been done in the development of this Statement. However, we feel the Statement is of a general nature regarding the impact of off the road vehicles.
entries.summary: The Indiana Department of Natural Resources offers limited comments because their own ORV study is still ongoing. They commend BOR for the Statement but criticize it as too general, noting it leaves difficult management questions to individual bureaus rather than resolving them. They also call for clearer definitions of key terms, question allowing ORV use from dusk to dawn, and express doubt about permitting organized competitive events on public lands.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Watt:
We are writing in regard to Mr. Hofe's request for comments on the Draft Environmental Statement for the proposed implementation of executive order 11644 pertaining to the use of off the road vehicles on public lands. We wish to point out that the State of Indiana is currently involved in an off the road vehicle study through which we hope to assess demand for this activity, determine its environmental as well as human effects, and determine if there is compatibility between the use of this activity and the management philosophies that cover areas under our jurisdiction. Therefore, our comments at this time are of a limited nature since the results of our study have not been completed.
The Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Department of Interior is to be congratulated for the work that has been done in the development of this Statement. However, we feel the Statement is of a general nature regarding the impact of off the road vehicles. The very difficult areas with regard to this outdoor recreation activity have not been defined by this Statement, but have been left to the individual Bureaus of the Department of Interior to solve. The questions of how to effectively manage this activity and in which areas the activity is to take place must be answered if this activity is to be acceptable.
With regard to specific areas of the Statement, under operating criteria, a number of terms appear to need further definition such as defining "excessive damage or disturbance of the land, wildlife or vegetative resources" in Section D and "unusual or excessive noise" in Section V. Under Section IV, we question whether ORV's should be allowed to run from dusk to dawn because of the noise factor and also from a safety

Mr. James G. Watt . Washington, D. C.
Page 2 July 27, 1972
standpoint. We further question whether the scheduling of organized events such as rallies, meets, endurance contests, etc. should be permitted on public lands.
We would hope that further revision of the Statement will speak to these particular issues. We appreciate the opportunity to review this Draft Environmental Statement.
Sincerely,
S. Donald Durfee, Acting Director Department of Natural Resources

The Honorable Secretary of the Interior United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Sir:
The International Association of Geophysical Contractors is deeply concerned with the probable impact of your May 5, 1972 Memorandum to the Assistant Secretaries for Public Land Management, for Fish and Wildlife and for Parks and Water and Power Resources as concerns implementation of Executive Order 11644.
The Draft of the Environmental Statement by the Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation expended most of his wordage specifically at damages of all varieties which may and now are being consed by motocycles and snowmobiles. Finally on Page 25 he states
"The Department's proposed action makes provision for the demands of other rightful users of the public lands;"
Our culture is dynamic largely because of the technological advantages attained because of reasonably available energy. Approximately a third of the land and water surface of the United States is controlled by your Department. For years geological and geophysical investigations impart for education purposes but primarily for the economic discovery of hydrocarbons, uranium and other metals and waters both drinkable and superheated have been conducted on public lands and waters under your Department's regulations. These operations have been in harmony with other rightful users. The discoveries and development of our mineral resources is a National Necessity.

24

"any registered motorboat; any military, fire, emergency, or law enforcement vehicle; farm type tractors and other selfpropelled agricultural equipment when used exclusively for agricultural purposes; any self-propelled equipment for harvesting and transportation of forest products or for earth moving or construction while being used for these purposes;"
We now urge that you also exempt geological and geophysical equipment when used for their designed purposes so that there will not be misunderstandings in the future.

entries.role: Assistant Secretary for Environment and Urban Systems (Designate), Office of the Secretary of Transportation
entries.summary_quote: Our primary concern is with the sections covering regulation of noise emitted by these vehicles.
entries.summary: Hirten, writing on behalf of the Office of the Secretary of Transportation, reviewed the proposed regulations and draft EIS on off-road vehicle use on public lands. His primary concern was with the noise regulation sections, suggesting that the final regulations should include a statement on the need to develop appropriate noise standards since state regulations may be non-existent or inadequate. He also recommended that the final regulations address public hearings for area designations, preparation of environmental impact statements in advance of such hearings, and the establishment of a mechanism for handling complaints related to noise, pollution, or destruction caused by ORV operators.
entries.statement_text:
OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20590
JUL 26 1072
Honorable W. W. Lyons
Assistant Secretary
U.S. Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Lyons:
This office has reviewed the proposed regulations and the draft environmental impact statement concerning the use of off-road vehicles on public lands managed by bureaus of the Department of the Interior.
Our primary concern is with the sections covering regulation of noise emitted by these vehicles. It is stated that a vehicle which produces unusual or excessive noise or other pollutants shall not be permitted to operate on public lands. A statement on the need to develop appropriate noise standards would strengthen this section, as State regulations may be either non-existent or inadequate in some instances.
We suggest that the final regulations include discussion of the opportunity for public hearings with respect to designation of areas and trails for the use of off-road vehicles. If such hearings are anticipated, are environmental impact statements to be prepared in advance of these hearings in order to evaluate the environmental effects of off-road vehicles? Is there currently a mechanism set up for handling complaints because of noise, pollution, or other destruction to public lands or wildlife on the part of vehicles or their operators?

We hope these comments will be of some assistance to you, and we look forward to receiving the Department of the Interior's final regulations and the final environmental impact statement on the operation of off-road vehicles on public lands.
Sincerely yours,
John E. Hirten
Assistant Secretary for
XIATINE
Environment and Urban Systems
(Designate)

entries.summary_quote: We definitely support recent presidential action directing federal agencies to establish policies regarding ORV use on their public lands.
entries.summary: The Kentucky Program Development Office expresses conditional support for federal ORV regulation, endorsing the presidential directive to establish ORV policies on public lands while also supporting exclusion of ORV use from wilderness, primitive areas, national parks, and wildlife refuges. They suggest opening certain lands to ORV use on a demonstration basis under close supervision until more questions about environmental effects are resolved, and recommend parental guidance and manufacturer cooperation as complementary measures.
entries.statement_text:
Kentucky
Program Development Office
The Capitol
Frankfort, Kentucky 40601
Wendell H. Ford Governor
July 31, 1972
2.3 Y
Mr. James G. Matt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Reference: Implementation of Presidential
Executive Order 11644 (K14)
Dear Mr. Watt:
It is apparent that Kentuckians are contributing to the national popularity of comparison and subsequent use of off-road vehicles (ORV). For comparison, our state licensing records reveal a four-fold increase in ORV licensing for use on public roadways since 1960, from 6,944 to 29,451. To license an ORV for such use the owner-operator must be at least 16 years of age. We have no indication of the number of vehicles not licensed. There is no evidence that their popularity may be leveling off.
ORV use in Kentucky State Parks is generally permitted on park roads open to automobile and camper traffic, within established safety regulations. ORV use in Kentucky State Forests is generally discouraged. The City of Louisville, Kentucky Park Board recently rescinded an earlier decision permitting ORV use in certain designated park areas because of serious destruction of the natural environment. The State Attorney General's Office has ruled that public park roads are in effect public roads, and therefore, state licensing requirements for ORV operation must be enforced. The operator under 16 years of age is placed at a certain disadvantage.
We definitely support recent presidential action directing federal agencies to establish policies regarding ORV use on their public lands. The increased popularity of the ORV accompanied by apparent pressure for a place to ride certainly warrants this action. By definition, ORV use must legitimately be given a position among outdoor recreation activities and must be considered in terms of total demand.
We further support the policy that ORV use not be permitted on wilderness or primitive areas, and we encourage the federal agency heads to recommend a similar policy for the national parks and national wildlife refuges and game areas. Since our federal govern-

335
Letter to Mr. Watt Page Two July 31, 1972
ment already owns approximately 30 percent of all the land in the United States, and an even greater percentage in the Western United States, it would seem that sufficient land for ORV use could be located so as to not encroach upon parks and wildlife areas.
In the interim, until many of the questions can be resolved regarding the effects of ORV use on public lands, we suggest that consideration be given to opening certain lands to ORV use on a demonstration basis under close supervision and management. We also suggest that government leaders seek the cooperation of manufacturers concerning the operating features of the ORV. However, there is really no substitute for parental guidance and restraint in the teenager's selection of an ORV, with individual as well as the public interest in mind.
Thank you for the opportunity to review the subject environmental statement. We certainly want to be kept up-to-date on the policies established regarding ORV use on federal lands. If further state coordination is desired this office will be pleased to provide assistance.
Sincerely yours,
L. W. True
Administrator

mentions.stance_basis: Supports the presidential action but recommends demonstration areas, manufacturer cooperation, and exclusion of wilderness/wildlife areas

entries.summary: The Office of the Secretary of Transportation reviewed the proposed regulations and draft EIS concerning off-road vehicle use on public lands, focusing primarily on noise regulation. They noted that the current language prohibiting vehicles producing 'unusual or excessive noise' is insufficient and recommended developing specific noise standards, since state regulations may be non-existent or inadequate. They also raised questions about public hearings for area designations, whether environmental impact statements would precede such hearings, and whether a mechanism exists for handling complaints about noise, pollution, or destruction caused by ORV operators.
entries.statement_text:
OFFICE OF THE SECRETARY OF TRANSPORTATION
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20590
JUL 26 1072
Honorable W. W. Lyons
Assistant Secretary
U.S. Department of the Interior
Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Lyons:
This office has reviewed the proposed regulations and the draft environmental impact statement concerning the use of off-road vehicles on public lands managed by bureaus of the Department of the Interior.
Our primary concern is with the sections covering regulation of noise emitted by these vehicles. It is stated that a vehicle which produces unusual or excessive noise or other pollutants shall not be permitted to operate on public lands. A statement on the need to develop appropriate noise standards would strengthen this section, as State regulations may be either non-existent or inadequate in some instances.
We suggest that the final regulations include discussion of the opportunity for public hearings with respect to designation of areas and trails for the use of off-road vehicles. If such hearings are anticipated, are environmental impact statements to be prepared in advance of these hearings in order to evaluate the environmental effects of off-road vehicles? Is there currently a mechanism set up for handling complaints because of noise, pollution, or other destruction to public lands or wildlife on the part of vehicles or their operators?

We hope these comments will be of some assistance to you, and we look forward to receiving the Department of the Interior's final regulations and the final environmental impact statement on the operation of off-road vehicles on public lands.
Sincerely yours,
John E. Hirten

entries.summary: Robert Solles and co-signers oppose more restrictive federal regulations on off-road vehicles on federally owned land in Nevada. They consider access to these lands for outdoor recreation a sacred right.
entries.statement_text:
July 7, 1972
Bureau of Land Management Elko, Nevada
Gentlemen:
We wish to add our voice of protest to more restrictive regulations by the Federal Government of off road vehicles on federally owned land in the state of Nevada.
We have chosen to live in this large and sparsely populated area for the expressed purpose of being near free and open land areas and as you know we have less than one person per square mile in Nevada.
The terrain in northern and north eastern Nevada is so rugged it is almost an abstract to negotiate most of this area without four wheel drive vehicles.
The lakes and reserviors are in very remote areas, mostly without roads. Hunting and fishing is our most popular out door sport in Nevada. Deer and chuckar partridge country is located in the most rugged and remote sections of our state. Four wheel drive vehicles are virtually a must in the pursuit of this sport.
Flease consider these sports and our feelings that these are our sacred rights. We feel we do no harm to the terrain hunting in these rugged areas where we go for weeks without seeing another person.
Robert Solles
