entries.role: Chairman, Department of Physical Sciences; Associate Director, Joint Center for Environmental and Urban Problems, Florida International University
entries.summary_quote: Environmental preservation really ought to require elimination of ORV as recreational vehicles
entries.summary: Ruth F. Weiner argues that ORV use as recreation is fundamentally incompatible with environmental preservation and should ideally be eliminated, as there is no way to use ORVs without adversely affecting natural, aesthetic, scenic, or wildlife values. While acknowledging that BOR feels compelled to permit some ORV use, she calls for significantly stricter regulations, including mandatory federal registration, minimum operator age of 16, prohibition above timberline and in wildlife refuges, and fees for all ORV use. She also criticizes the draft statement for minimizing the certain increase in air and water pollution from ORVs and expresses hope that federal agencies will actively limit and discourage recreational ORV use.
entries.statement_text:
FLORIDA INTERNATIONAL UNIVERSITY
TAMIAMI TRAIL • MIAMI, FLORIDA 33144 • (305) 223-2300
27 July 1972
G. Douglas Hofe Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation U.S. Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
RE: K14 #72-1336
Dear Mr. Hofe:
I would like to make the following comments on the draft environmental impact statement for the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644:
First of all, it must be recognized that off-the-road vehicles (ORV), when used off of roads, cause damage to the terrain over which they travel. Environmental preservation really ought to require elimination of ORV as recreational vehicles (I am here excluding use of ORV in game patrolling, ski-patrol, or other non-recreational uses). There is no way to use an ORV that will not "adversely affect---natural, aesthetic, or scenic values" or wildlife in the area. The claim that ORV have positive values in the form of "strengthening family ties" (as stated on p. 12 of the impact statement) is spurious to the argument: families hike together, cross-country ski together, ride horses together, snowshoe together, and do any number of outdoor things which do not require, and are in fact disrupted by, ORV. BOR obviously feels some compulsion to permit ORV use, however. With this in mind, the criteria for their use should be made more stringent in several ways.
Distinctions must be made among various ORV. Jeeps and other four-wheel drive regular-pressure tire vehicles ought not to be considered ORV for recreational purposes: the damage they cause is much too extensive to sanction use except on roads and "jeep trails." Some additional blanket restrictions should also be made. No recreational use of ORV should be permitted above timberline, with the elevation of "timberline" determined by USGS or some other knowledgeable agency. (Even snowmobiles cause damage by packing snow in tundra regions, where the snow melts late in summer anyway.) Damage to tundra by trailbikes, etc., is generally permanent.

All ORV used on Federal lands should be registered, and have the registration number clearly displayed on the vehicle. State laws are frequently inadequate, and in many cases there is no state law requiring registration. If the vehicle is not registered how is one to apprehend violators? Similarly, state regulations on operators are not strict enough, as a rule. In Colorado a 10-year-old can legally operate a snowmobile. Such a child has not, in my opinion, sufficiently mature judgment to operate a vehicle capable of speeds up to 60 m.p.h., even if he may have the requisite mechanical skills. The Federal government should put a lower age limit of 16 years on operation of ORV on Federal lands. The motor vehicle license provision set out in the impact statement is good, and there should be no exception to it.
ORV rallies or other events should be limited to ungraded roads or areas where there is already considerable evidence of vehicular use. Such events are considerably more damaging to the environment than trail use. Fees for <u>all</u> ORV use should be established, in addition to fees for rallies or other events. Trail-bikes do infinitely more damage to trails than hikers, and considerably more than horses, and there is no reason they should not be charged for its repair.
The effect of ORV on wildlife is especially damaging; the effect of snowmobiles on wintering <u>cervidae</u> is disastrous. The Colorado Department of Game, Fish and Parks testified repeatedly to deer and elk deaths directly attributable to frightening or harassment by snowmobiles. Similarly, indiscriminate use of airboats in the Everglades during the dry season can drive amphibians far from watering places. Use of ORV in wildlife refuges should be prohibited, at least during those seasons when the animals in the refuge are weakest.
The impact of air and water pollutants produced by ORV is minimized in the draft impact statement. These are not "likely to increase with the number of vehicles involved" (p. 14), they are certain to increase with the number of vehicles involved, and in direct proportion to that number! When the impact of these of these pollutants becomes noticeable, it will be too late to do anything about their presence. We must take preventive action and severely limit the concentration of exhaust pollutants permitted. We must also remember that, in general, the flora and fauna exposed to ORV are exceedingly fragile.
My personal experience with ORV users is that they are almost uniformly rude, careless, and of dirty habits, especially when compared as a group with hikers. You can generally trace a snowmobile track or motorbike trail by the litter. They are disdainful of and discourteous to those who prefer non-mechanized forms of travel. My children have several times come close to severe injury from being run down by a snowmobile while cross-country skiing. Why should it be necessary for anyone to "experience an exhilarating feeling of freedom ...at high speeds..." if doing so means wrecking the surrounding environment and endangering the lives and safety of animals and walking humans? I would Sike to see some evidence that "family relationships are strengthened" (p.18) by this activity and then determine whether it is worth the price! I am happy to see BOR admit unequivocally that "land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use." Recreational ORV use may be with us to stay, but I hope that the Federal agencies involved will do what they can to limit and discourage it, since they seem to be quite aware of its detrimental impact.

I hope these comments will be of assistance to you.
Sincerely,
Ruth F. Weiner
Cha man, Department of Physical Sciences Associate Director, Joint Center for
Environmental and Urban Problems

entries.summary: Durfee offers conditional support for the Draft Environmental Statement, congratulating BOR for its work while noting the statement is too general and leaves difficult management questions unresolved for individual bureaus to solve. He calls for clearer definitions of vague terms like 'excessive damage' and 'unusual or excessive noise,' questions whether ORV use should be permitted from dusk to dawn, and expresses doubt about allowing organized competitive events on public lands. He hopes further revision will address these specific issues.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Watt:
We are writing in regard to Mr. Hofe's request for comments on the Draft Environmental Statement for the proposed implementation of executive order 11644 pertaining to the use of off the road vehicles on public lands. We wish to point out that the State of Indiana is currently involved in an off the road vehicle study through which we hope to assess demand for this activity, determine its environmental as well as human effects, and determine if there is compatibility between the use of this activity and the management philosophies that cover areas under our jurisdiction. Therefore, our comments at this time are of a limited nature since the results of our study have not been completed.
The Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Department of Interior is to be congratulated for the work that has been done in the development of this Statement. However, we feel the Statement is of a general nature regarding the impact of off the road vehicles. The very difficult areas with regard to this outdoor recreation activity have not been defined by this Statement, but have been left to the individual Bureaus of the Department of Interior to solve. The questions of how to effectively manage this activity and in which areas the activity is to take place must be answered if this activity is to be acceptable.
With regard to specific areas of the Statement, under operating criteria, a number of terms appear to need further definition such as defining "excessive damage or disturbance of the land, wildlife or vegetative resources" in Section D and "unusual or excessive noise" in Section V. Under Section IV, we question whether ORV's should be allowed to run from dusk to dawn because of the noise factor and also from a safety

Mr. James G. Watt . Washington, D. C.
Page 2 July 27, 1972
standpoint. We further question whether the scheduling of organized events such as rallies, meets, endurance contests, etc. should be permitted on public lands.
We would hope that further revision of the Statement will speak to these particular issues. We appreciate the opportunity to review this Draft Environmental Statement.
Sincerely,
S. Donald Durfee, Acting Director Department of Natural Resources

entries.role: Chairman, Environmental Impact Evaluation Committee, Utah Department of Natural Resources
entries.summary_quote: It would appear from experience that the best alternative to the proposed action would be that action, but with a much greater emphasis on management, supervision and planning than indicated in the Secretarial memorandum of May 5, 1972.
entries.summary: Stan Elmer, on behalf of Utah's Environmental Impact Evaluation Committee, supports ORV use on public lands but argues the draft environmental statement takes an overly negative tone and undervalues the role of management, design, and planning in mitigating environmental impacts. He contends that the best alternative to the proposed action is essentially the same action but with far greater emphasis on management and supervision than indicated in the Secretarial memorandum. He also objects to several specific provisions, including the age/licensing requirements for operators under 16, and urges an 'open unless closed' approach with dispersed, well-managed use rather than concentration in limited designated areas.
entries.statement_text:
MEMORANDUM
TO:
GORDON E. HARMSTON
FROM:
STAN ELMER, CHAIRMAN,
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT EVALUATION COMMITTEE
SUBJECT:
DRAFT ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT - USE OF OFF-ROAD VEHICLES
ON PUBLIC LANDS (IMPLEMENTATION OF EXECUTIVE ORDER 11644)
K 14
Utah is just completing its first year of implementation of a comprehensive Recreation Vehicle Act (attached) governing all off-road vehicle use on public land in Utah. The proposed program discussed in the ORV Environmental Statement is either identical or compatible with the Utah regulation in most respects.
1. Under "operating criteria," item (1). Since there is no evidence that operators under 16 years of age contribute disproportionately to accidents or other problems in the use of boats or ORV's, and they represent a significant portion of these family recreational pursuits, we can find no just reason to require a highway operators license or supervision by someone who is at least 21 years old. This is the kind of requirement which is designed more to stifle the use than to promote safety; and it would be contradictory if it recognized the responsibility of a 16 year old with a license but would not accept his ability to supervise those under 16. There should be general supervision of those under 16; but it could surely be by someone who is at least 16 who is experienced with the equipment.
2. In the section requiring permits for competitive events, the requirement for bonds and the provision for rehabilitating the use areas are good, but should not be used to discourage or prohibit activity by setting the costs unrealistically high.
90

3. The frequent use of the phrase "can" or "may have irreversible and irretrievable harmful effect on" throughout the report definitely encourages a negative frame of mind in the consideration of ORV programs. Much of the theory which is represented in the proposal was apparently developed by non-users and those without a great deal of expertise with ORV use. We, therefore, encourage an accelerated feeling of responsibility by all public land administering agencies to provide developed areas and trails in as many places as possible. In some of the areas with "excessive erosion or siltation characteristics," a properly developed and managed trail may be a better solution than closure.
4. The Utah Division of Parks and Recreation has enjoyed an excellent working relationship with BLM and other Federal agencies in implementation of our program, and the identification of legitimate use areas throughout Utah.
The following sections of the enclosed State Law (most of which encompass the Federal proposals) are now being enforced by Division officers and county sheriffs on public land in Utah:
Section 3 - Registration.
Section 10 - (3) (a) Mufflers, (b) lights, (c) brakes, (4) (a) reckless and negligent operation, (b) posted speeds, (c) buddy system (d) operator under 16.
Section 12 - (2) Operating in closed areas.
Section 13 - Vandalism, harrassment of animals, burglaries, damage to environment.
Section 14 - Operating under the influence.
Section 15 - Permission to hold competitive events.
Our Division of Water Resources has pointed out its reliance on ORV's in constructing and servicing many water transfer facilities, etc., which are generally inaccessible except by some type of ORV.
The State's need to construct, service and maintain these projects is echoed by the Utah Division of Oil and Gas Conservation which uses ORV's to reach isolated oil rigs. The needs of many other official government and private concerns to manage their resources and operations are dependent on some types of off-road vehicles.
It would appear from experience that the best alternative to the proposed action would be that action, but with a much greater emphasis on management, supervision and planning than indicated in the Secretarial memorandum of May 5, 1972.
90 Specific comments on the draft environmental statement follow:
Page 1: We question the use of the word "frequently" when disclosing ORV conflicts with wise resource management, etc.

Pages 2 and 3: We agree with the positive attitude expressed in most of these statements. We especially endorse the requirement for research and studies regarding the environmental impact of ORV's. We would add the need for research on management and design practices which can help reduce or eliminate detrimental environmental impacts of ORV use.
Page 7: We suspect that the wide range of resources available for ORV use, and the wide range of design and management practices available in the use of each different environmental form, gives the Department of the Interior the opportunity to provide for ORV use in a variety of ways as well as in a variety of areas.
Page 8: The "state-of-the-art" of eco-management is the real key to ORV use, as it is with traditional uses of the public lands.
Pages 9 and 10: While public use on the National Wildlife Refuge System is secondary to the primary responsibility of wildlife protection and perpetuation, it is safe to say there would be much less public use without the traditional pressures from the states for public use areas. These compromise practices have not been detrimental to wildlife, but have allowed greater use of the resource.
Page 10: We applaud the Bureau of Land Management's planning system and its management of land under multiple use principles. We urge that the approach taken to ORV use be one of "open unless closed" rather than "closed unless open." To confine ORV use as indicated may concentrate the use so greatly in too small an area as to destroy that area and thereby justify further closure.
Page 11: We agree that areas and trails should be selected on lands having vehicle use capability and having low erosion and siltation potentials. We do not think areas of low vegetative production are necessarily suitable, however. If an attitude prevailed based on management of the use, an area which could more quickly revegetate or recover from use might be a much better area than one which takes longer to respond. This entire impact statement seems to leave out the options created by intelligent planning, design, maintenance and management.
The consistent use of the word "control" rather than "manage" reflects an unfortunate negative attitude. Limiting use to areas too small to handle the growing demand will only concentrate the impact. A policy of dispursed, yet managed use will offer more recreation opportunity and create less environmental impact.
Page 12: We agree with all statements except the last paragraph. The word "some" reflects reality much better than "many."
Page 13: We agree that data is needed on both the use and environmental impact side of the question; but feel it is needed also on the design and management side. Additional monies are needed by all agencies involved to provide the opportunities for ORV use while managing that use and the resource itself.

We question again the negative attitude toward ORV use displayed in the writing of this environmental statement. The fact is that "no area of public lands is free from potential damage by . . ." almost any use. To suggest that all sand dune areas and all snow fields are "fragile and susceptible land forms" is to not understand that the next breeze or the next snowfall can completely mitigate the environmental impact of ORV tracks on sand or snow.
We agree with the use of soil erodibility appraisals in helping to identify areas for appropriate ORV use; but suggest that they are needed also in defining areas for many other traditional uses such as grazing, mining and timber. Again, the answer is not so much "open" or "close," but "manage."
Pages 15 and 16: The discussion of biological impacts sounds like all populations and species of wildlife have had a run-in with ORV's. We suspect that the discussion applies more realistically to isolated instances, as with other uses of the public lands. The writers and readers of such impact statements need to be reminded that even the revered backpackers can "disturb" wildlife.
Page 17: We see no reason to assume that properly managed use of ORV's would have a "minor adverse impact on the economic effects of outdoor recreation." To the contrary, safe and sane provision of ORV opportunities could increase the positive economic effect because of the increased interest and use which would be attracted by well-managed areas. As the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation should know, most ORV users are responsible individuals looking for protection of their "investment" as well.
Page 18: We question the use of the phrase "often at high speeds" when referring to exploring of areas. Anyone familiar with most ORV use would know that most exploring is at a leisurely pace and that the racing event, which is usually held at an appropriate site and under appropriate regulations, is at high speed; but is far from "exploring," and is not the kind of activity pursued by the average ORV user.
Page 19: We agree that the time when any user can use the public lands whenever and wherever he wishes is long gone. All must accept the idea that their use of public lands will of necessity be managed.
We wonder why trails, parking areas, rest stops and other developments are "unsightly" when associated with ORV use, but not an unmanageable problem when associated with camping, picnicking or backpacking use.
Page 20: We question the idea that concentrating vehicles and people in designated areas will help the situation. It could cause more environmental damage unless there are enough such areas, and they are large enough in terms of their capacity.
We think that ORV designated areas should be rated similar to ski runs: (1) beginning, (2) intermediate, (3) advanced, etc, so users can match their degree of skill with the terrain.

The public lands are also reservoirs of our recreation and leisure heritage, and, as they later state, the Department of the Interior also has a charge to provide outdoor recreation opportunities.
Page 21: We agree that implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memorandum will impose a substantial impact upon the Department of the Interior (and the Department of Agriculture) and that additional financial resources must be forthcoming if even the public's minimum needs are to be met.
Page 22: We agree that the needs of the users and the needs of the public lands themselves must be balanced. It is our impression, however, that the tone and attitude expressed in the Executive Order, the Secretarial memorandum and the environmental statement, are psychologically "heavy" on the side of resource protection; do not adequately consider the middle-ground options offered by good design and adequate management; and generally reflect a lack of appreciation for the recreation experience offered by ORV use.
As indicated above, we have attached a copy of Utah's ORV regulations which indicate operating criteria and registration requirements.
Page 23: Since Utah has actively attempted to regulate ORV use on public lands, and since more than 75% of Utah is either Federal or State land, we respectfully request State review of all proposed manual releases, regulations and administrative guidelines.
Page 24 and 26: The use of the word "will" instead of "may" in talking about detrimental effects of ORV use, again does not consider that management and design could prevent detrimental impact. Environmental impacts will occur. "Detrimental" environmental impacts may occur if ORV use areas are not properly located and managed. Good location and design could also prevent changes or destruction to historical and archaeological structures. To suggest, as is done, that these effects "cannot be avoided" is to admit that they do not rely on their professional landscape architects; that they do not intend to survey proposed ORV use areas for potential conflicts; and that they do not have the expertise to lay out an ORV use area or trail. We know that this is not the case, because we work with land management field personnel and they are capable of avoiding these kinds of impacts.
In addition to the Department of Interior responsibilities listed, we would add "... plus a responsibility to provide for man's needs through the wise use of these resources." This would cover such traditional uses as mining, timber harvesting, grazing, and pursuit of recreation activities.
Page 25: We agree that short term needs of the present should not preclude future management options; but we do not agree that backpacking and other wilderness or "natural" kinds of activities, as intimated, are the only compatible future uses.
To even suggest that "the current intensifying use of ORV may represent a temporary novelty . . ." is to clearly indicate a lack of

understanding and appreciation for this phenomena which does "represent the beginnings of a long-lasting mode of outdoor recreation."
Page 26: We recommend adding to the last sentence, "...in some areas which cannot withstand the pressure, or which are not being maintained during use and rehabilitated after use."
Page 27: We recommend adding to the last sentence " . . . and in providing for legitimate outdoor recreation use of those lands."
Page 28: To suggest that ORV use is the only one which can disturb animals and plants on public land areas is to ignore the impacts of other traditional uses.
We also recommend adding the following sentence to this discussion:
"It would also decrease the amount of enjoyment the ORV users could derive from using their vehicles, from appreciating the wonders of the public lands by ORV and from getting into otherwise distant areas in a relatively shorter amount of time."
Page 29: We agree that ORV use is a primary source of enjoyment to a significant number of recreationists. As an illustration, in Utah it is the 5th highest activity in terms of recreation days participated in, and 7th in terms of participant occasions.
Although we do not advocate opening <u>all</u> public lands to ORV use, a movement in that direction would certainly spread out the impact, and, if the use were managed, it could lessen the overall environmental impact.
The "widespread damage" discussed is exaggerated if Utah's experience is a just measurement. Much of this depends on management, which in turn depends on personnel, well-planned areas, and public (or user) education.
As you can tell, our main point is that proper planning, design, maintenance and regulation of ORV use can give many more options for management of the public lands to meet the legitimate needs of the public.

entries.summary_quote: We wish to add our voice of protest to more restrictive regulations by the Federal Government of off road vehicles on federally owned land in the state of Nevada.
entries.summary: Steven K. Burke, along with numerous co-signers, opposes more restrictive federal regulations on off-road vehicles on federally owned land in Nevada. They argue that the rugged terrain of northern and northeastern Nevada makes four-wheel drive vehicles virtually essential for hunting, fishing, and accessing remote lakes and reservoirs. They contend that their use of ORVs in these sparsely populated areas causes no harm to the terrain.
entries.statement_text:
July 7, 1972
Bureau of Land Management Elko, Nevada
Gentlemen:
We wish to add our voice of protest to more restrictive regulations by the Federal Government of off road vehicles on federally owned land in the state of Nevada.
We have chosen to live in this large and sparsely populated area for the expressed purpose of being near free and open land areas and as you know we have less than one person per square mile in Nevada.
The terrain in northern and north eastern Nevada is so rugged it is almost an abstract to negotiate most of this area without four wheel drive vehicles.
The lakes and reserviors are in very remote areas, mostly without roads. Hunting and fishing is our most popular out door sport in Nevada. Deer and chuckar partridge country is located in the most rugged and remote sections of our state. Four wheel drive vehicles are virtually a must in the pursuit of this sport.
Flease consider these sports and our feelings that these are our sacred rights. We feel we do no harm to the terrain hunting in these rugged areas where we go for weeks without seeing another person.

WILLIAM B. NYE DIRECTOR
DEPARTMENT OF MATURAL RESOURCES
OHIO DEPARTMENTS BUILDING COLUMEUS 43215
August 9, 1972
United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240 Attn: G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director
Draft Environmental Impact RE: Statement for Implementation of Executive Order 11644-Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public
Lands-Kl4
Dear Director Hofe:
In response to your letter of June 1, 1972 forwarding the draft environmental impact statement for the above referenced project, a review was coordinated by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources. Comments were solicited from other State agencies under the auspices of the Office of the Governor, State Clearinghouse.
This draft environmental impact statement is an excellent, well-thought product. It is thorough and easily understood. We have no comments on the five points.
The Department of Interior should proceed with finalization of the statement. We would, however, urge you to promote mechanisms for site selection for Off-Road Vehicles use which would allow for the least adverse impact and irretrievable loss in the area being considered. In addition, qualified personnel should periodically inspect areas in use to assess the deterioration of existing land forms.
In light of the fact that ORV site selections must take into account the preservation of unique natural areas, special soil and vegetative conditions, wildlife habitat areas, etc., perhaps the implementation of a public land use plan would aid and/or facilitate these selections.

Director G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. August 9, 1972 Page Two
Thank you for the opportunity to review and comment on the impact statement. We look forward to receiving the final form and to cooperation in any way with the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation personnel associated with the State of Ohio in implementing this Executive Order.
Sincerely,
WILLIAM B. NYE Director

entries.summary_quote: We would hope that the intent of the Executive Order and Environmental Statement is to regulate pleasure off-road vehicles, and not to impede the servicing of communications equipment.
entries.summary: William Friedman, representing Continental Telephone Corporation, expresses concern that the Executive Order and implementing regulations could inadvertently impede utility companies from accessing their authorized communications facilities on public lands. He hopes the regulations are intended to govern recreational ORV use only, and proposes that utility vehicles performing maintenance of authorized facilities be explicitly exempted from permit requirements. He also requests that any permit process clearly identify which federal land management agency holds transit authority over specific parcels.
entries.statement_text:
1800 K Street, N.W. Washington, D. C. 20006 (202) 466-2895
William Friedman
Vice President — Governmental Relations
August 3, 1972
, 31
Mr. James Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Re: Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644, Use of Off Road Vehicles (ORV) on Public Lands
Dear Mr. Watt:
Continental Telephone Corporation is the third largest independent telephone company in the United States. In our operations we have a number of installations which are located on public lands and require off road access.
We have followed with interest the subject Executive Order and the Draft Environmental Statement prepared by your office and published on May 26, 1972. We are obviously affected by any instructions which may be published on this matter. We are advised by your Mr. Stuart Davey and Mr. William Honore that an implementing order is soon to be published, but prior to its publication, they suggested we send you any comments that we may have.
As we can interpret, neither the Executive Order nor your draft memorandum specifically consider the problem of expressly permitting the use of vehicles off established roadways for the purpose of maintaining authorized communication (and other utilities) facilities without first requiring that a permit be obtained. We would hope that the intent of the Executive Order and Environmental Statement is to regulate pleasure off-road vehicles, and not to impede the servicing of communications equipment. Accordingly, you might wish to consider including a statement such as: "Vehicles belonging to utility companies performing maintenance of authorized facilities on public lands may transit those lands without permit."
Further, may we suggest that any regulation which does require permits establish the procedure of obtaining its permits and the mechanism for determining what federal land management agency will be exercising transit authority over a particular piece of federal land on which we may have to operate.
We trust that these comments may be of use to you. We would be pleased to discuss this further with you if you desire.
Very truly yours,
William Friedman

entries.role: Manager, Bruneau Dunes State Park, Idaho
entries.summary_quote: I strongly feel that some major guidelines, in addition to those stated in the draft, are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use.
entries.summary: Bryan W. Rowder, Manager of Bruneau Dunes State Park, supports the draft's goals but argues that stronger guidelines are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use. He recommends excluding ORVs from designated Wilderness, Primitive, National Park, Wildlife Refuge, and Game Range areas; capping total ORV-designated land at 0.5% of each state's public land; requiring organized groups with agency supervision for trail use outside designated tracts; and imposing a minimum 15% federal tax on ORV equipment to fund development, maintenance, and enforcement.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Sir:
I have reviewed your draft environmental statement on executive order 11644 pertaining to use of ORV on public lands. Along with other public land managers who have dealt closely with ORV users. I recognize that you have carefully defined the problems in regard to existing and potential ORV impacts. However, I strongly feel that some major guidelines, in addition to those stated in the draft, are necessary to prevent adverse effects of ORV use. I have four basic recommendations:
1. The statement on page 4, section iv, smould be changed to read, "treas and trails shall not be located in officially designated Wilderness areas, Primitive areas, National Parks and Monuments, National Wildlife Refuges, and Game Ranges."
2. The total public land area designated for ORV use should not exceed 0.5% of the total public land area of each state. Why? Here are three main reasons: 1) ORV sales are increasing at a fast rate. To delay making strong restrictions is to promote more sales and later cause an economic hardship to the expanded industry. 2) Irreversible land damage will occur. 3) The effects of CRV use negates the effects and raises the costs of tax-supported conservation programs.
3. The areas designated for intensive CRV use should be in tracts not less than ten square miles, with good natural or man-made boundaries. Trails outside of the tracts can be designated for CAV use. Such trails may be used only by organized groups of ten or more people who have registered with the land manager and who are accompanied by an agency representative on the trail who acts as guide, interpreter, and enforcer.
4. To finance the development, maintenance, and manpower necessary for these projects, a federal tax should be imposed on all DRV and related equipment. The minimum tax on retail value should be 15,00
Sincerely,
Bryan W. Rowder, henager Bruneau Dines State Fork

entries.summary: The Division of Wildlife (Denver, Colorado) conditionally supports ORV management but raises serious concerns about allowing any damage to land, wildlife, or vegetative resources, questioning whether ORVs should be permitted anywhere they cause such harm. They critique the draft statement's use of vague or permissive language (e.g., 'excessive' damage, 'minimized' impacts) and argue that bonding and fee mechanisms are inadequate substitutes for preventing irreplaceable resource loss. They recommend stronger coordination with state wildlife agencies, clearer definitions, and that the final statement include a controlled-use alternative.
entries.statement_text:
DIVISION OF WILDLIFE
Harry R. Woodward, Director 6060 Broadway
Denver, Colorado 80216 • 825-1192
August 10, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
We have reviewed the May 26, 1972 statement entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on the public lands" prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation. We have made some general observations and several specific comments.
The statement reiterates and possibly reinforces the policies and procedures established by Executive Order 11644, use of off-road vehicles on the public lands. Unfortunately, the Executive Order is directed to the Secretary of Interior alone; we believe the Order should be expanded to include the Secretary of Agriculture and possibly other appropriate land management agencies. We further feel that coordination could best be accomplished by the Department of Natural Resources. We also believe that comments from national conservation organizations should be solicited.
SPECIFIC COMMENTS
Page 3 - (2) I question whether all lands, both open and closed for use, should be designated. Why not just those open, this would lead to less signing, mapping and administration. Signing all lands could cause visual pollution.
The several states have laws which allow them to control the harassment of wildlife.
98

Mr. James G. Watt August 10, 1972 page 2.
Page 4  (iii) Determine the effect of the use of areas and trails of ORV on private lands adjacent to public lands.
Page 5  (Operating Criteria) A specific explanation of the meaning of "than conditions warrant" is needed.
We question whether ORV should be used at any time or place where they would cause damage and disturbance of land, wildlife or vegetative resources.
(d) Allows damage and qualifies the damage by inserting the word "excessive" which is purely judgemental.
Page 6  (2) We still question the wisdom of allowing even minimal damage. Assuming that minimum damage will be allowed we would like to see wildlife specifically mentioned.
Bonding a permittee so as to insure adequate moneys for restoration and rehabilitation of trails and areas used is an extremely questionable procedure: 1. There could be an irreplaceable loss to the resource,
2. The cost of restoration and rehabilitation would be measured monetarily with no consideration given to elapsed time for restoration,
3. No consideration for the destruction of a quality environment,
4. Estimate of costs would necessarily be judgemental, and 5. Administrative procedures would be cumbersome, i.e. how long would a permittees bond or deposit be held, would it be deposited and draw interest, would the interest be collected by the permittee or the federal government, etc.
We feel that it would be extremely difficult to assess an appropriate fee as authorized under the provisions of the Land and Water Conservation Fund Act. How much would be charged? Would the fee be charged before or after the rally or contest? Would the money collected be used for restoration in the area destroyed or would it go into a general fund and be spent in another area?
Continued citation of other executive orders, organic acts and laws without describing their purpose is not extremely enlightening. Perhaps attachment to the environmental statement of all the executive orders and rules and regulations cited would be beneficial.
The method proposed by the Bureau of Land Management for the administration of ORV use is incisive, comprehensive and appears to be a good solution.

Page 11  (U. S. Bureau of Reclamation) Who determines which regulations are appropriate?, the Bureau of Reclamation or the federal or non-federal agency, or a combination?
Page 12  "ORV do limited damage to the human environment, etc."
Possibly "limited" should be defined; preferably ORV should be limited to areas where no damage would be caused.
Page 13  (Physical Impact) Statement that damage could be "minimized" should read the damage could be "eliminated."
Page 16  We agree with the philosophy of prohibiting ORV in certain wildlife areas. Hopefully, this can be accomplished in close coordination with the state wildlife agencies.
There should be a definition of "established roadways."
Page 17 - (Human Impacts) Snowmobiling in the Great Lakes States probably cannot be compared with snowmobiling in the Western States.
We doubt whether there is a direct correlation between the use of ORV and economic enhancement.
Page 18 - We also doubt that in areas where ORV are prohibited, a negative impact will result.
The paragraph on ORV experience is purely conjecture. As you describe the exhilarating feeling you should also describe the feeling of sheer terror - in other words, feelings are highly individualized. Perhaps the incidence of snowmobile-auto accidents should be related. Crossing of highways is highly hazardous.
Page 19 - We agree noise levels must be reduced and standards rigidly enforced.
We agree that the proper procedure is to specify designated areas of use for ORV vehicles.
The Section on Human Impacts sounds like it was written by a PR man for ORV, not that we totally disagree with most of the statements; the thrust is one of promotion rather than attraction.

Page 23  Who will provide the technical assistance to all Interior Bureaus, and other federal agencies, etc.
Page 24  Land, water, air, wildlife, etc., need not always be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Page 28  We are not certain that the Department of Interior should be relied upon by private enterprise to support the economy of an area.
Page 30  More emphasis should be placed upon the interaction at the interface of the public lands with the non-public lands.
The draft environmental statement should contain the alternative of controlled use within the statement.
Sincerely,
Harry R. Woodward
Director

entries.summary_quote: We believe strong controls on off-road vehicles to be much needed and recommend that driving of any vehicles off established roads be prohibited, except on a few small tracts of land which may be determined suitable and designated for off-road vehicle use by the Department of Interior.
entries.summary: Don L. Spicer, writing on behalf of Florida's Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations, supports strong controls on off-road vehicles and recommends prohibiting driving off established roads except on a few small designated tracts deemed suitable by the Department of Interior. He notes that Florida does not require a driver's license for off-road vehicle operation, suggesting a federal permit system with fees for enforcement and land renovation would be more appropriate. His concern is grounded in the severe ecological damage ORVs have caused in South Florida, particularly in the Big Cypress Swamp and Everglades region.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Douglas:
Functioning as the state planning and development clearinghouse contemplated in U. S. Office of Management and Budget Circular A-95, we have reviewed the following draft environmental impact statement prepared by U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Ourdoor Recreation:
Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public Lands (K-14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
During the course of our reivew, we have referred the environmental impact statement to the following agencies, which we have identified as interested in the environmental effects of the project or in developing or enforcing standards relating to these effects: Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund; Department of Community Affairs; Game and Fresh Water Fish Commission; Department of Legal Affairs; Department of Natural Resources; Department of Pollution Control; Department of State - Division of Archives, History, and Records Management, Department of Transportation - Division of Transportation Planning and Programming; Central and Southern Florida Flood Control District and the Environmental Information Center.
Agencies were requested to review the statement and comment on the adequacy of treatment of environmental matters of their concern, additional alternatives which should be considered, and project modifications or special control measures to reduce or avoid adverse environmental effects. Agencies comments follow: The Department of Community Affairs suggests that alternate B in the statement be adopted and offers other comments which should be considered. See attached letter. The Department of Legal Affairs suggests that a test program to control off-road vehicles be instituted on a limited bas s; the Department offers comments on several other portions of the statement which should be considered. See attached letter. Letters endorsing the proposal or offering no adverse comments on the proposal and statement from the following agencies are attached: Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund; Game and Fresh Water Fish Commission; Department of Natural Resources; Department of State - Division of Archives History, and Records

Mr. Douglas Hofe, Jr. Page 2 August 14, 1972
Management; and Department of Transportation - Division of Transportation Planning and Programming. No response was received from the Central and Southern Florida Flood Control District. The final environmental impact statement should adequately consider each point of concern contained in the attached letters from the Department of Community Affairs and Department of Legal Affairs.
This statement was discussed at a conference held by the staff of the Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations on July 14. See attached conference agenda and attendance list. It was pointed out at the conference that, whereas item b(i) on page 5 of the statement states that a person must have a state driver's license or learner's permit to operate an off-road vehicle on Interior Lands, the State of Florida does not require a driver's license to operate a vehicle off public roads. Therefore, it may be more appropriate to require a federal permit to operate an off-road vehicle on federal lands. Further, the Department may wish to consider charging a fee for such a permit: revenues derived could be used for enforcement and land renovation. We believe strong controls on off-road vehicles to be much needed and recommend that driving of any vehicles off established roads be prohibited, except on a few small tracts of land which may be determined suitable and designated for off-road vehicle use by the Department of Interior. Our concern about off-road vehicles is due to the severe ecological damage caused by off-road vehicle in recent years in South Florida. Effects of off-road vehicles on our land is distinguishable on nearly any recent low altitude aerial photograph taken in the Big Cypress Swamp or Everglades region of the State.
Please append a copy of this letter, with attachments, to the final environmental impact statement submitted to the Council on Environmental Quality. This will assure the Council of our compliance with guidelines implementing the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (PL 91-190).
We request to be forwarded one copy of the final environmental statement submitted to the Council on Environmental Quality, and, in the letter of transmittal, refer to the SPDC number assigned this statement.
Sincerely,
Don L. Spicer
Chief
Bureau of Intergovernmental Relations

entries.summary: The Florida Department of Community Affairs conditionally supports the ORV regulations, suggesting that Alternative B be adopted while acknowledging the popularity of off-road vehicles and the challenges their increasing use presents. They recommend strong interagency cooperation in coordinating, planning, and developing areas for ORV use. They also raise questions about the proposed age requirements for supervisors and express concern about potential damage to historical and archaeological structures.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Mr. Still:
Thank you for your letter and the opportunity to review and comment on the U.S. Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public Lands (SPDC Project No. 72-1336).
While we might suggest that the Department of Interior choose "Alternative B)," we can appreciate the popularity of the vehicles and the problems that have arisen with their increasing use. We would recommend strong emphasis in the proposed cooperation between all agencies and levels of government in coordinating, planning and development of areas and facilities for the use of ORV.
Points of curiosity, with the voting age and, in some states, the age of majority being 18, why is it suggested that the supervisor be 21? Also, what number of persons under age can be supervise as conditions warrant? Finally, why do any historical or archeological structures have to be changed or destroyed by ORV use?
We feel the Department is to be commanded for their efforts in secking solutions to these very vexing problems.
Sincerely,
R. Charles Shepherd
Director
Division of Technical Assistance

entries.summary: The Florida Department of Legal Affairs (through Attorney General Robert L. Shevin) argues that the draft environmental impact statement inadequately evaluates the alternative of prohibiting off-road vehicle use on public lands, and that the policy choice to permit such use is questionable given acknowledged irreversible environmental harms. Rather than implementing a nationwide program of controlled ORV use, the Department recommends initiating a limited test program to allow for monitoring and data collection, with ORV use restricted to established roadways in the meantime. The letter also expresses concern that public lands should serve as a retreat from urban noise and annoyance, and that ORV use would undermine that purpose.
entries.statement_text:
TALLAHASSUE, PLOUIDA, 3290-1
August 7, 1972
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
State Planning and Development Clearinghouse
Department of Administration
725 South Bronough Street
Tallahassee, Florida 32304
Re: U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Outdoor Recreation: Draft Environmental Impact Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands (K14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
Dear Mr. Still:
The following are comments on the draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The general approach to the regulation of off-road vehicles on
public lands, as delineated in the proposed Impact Statement, appears
to be adequate and comprehensive, assuming that one agrees with the\nunderlying policy.
The President's Executive Order 11644 and the Memorandum from Interior Secretary Morton to various assistant secretaries appear to assume that off-road vehicles will be permitted to use public lands off established roadways. The entire draft statement addresses itself to minimizing the damage or conflict caused by the use of these vehicles off established roadways. It assumes that there should be allowed certain damage or conflict with the present activities that exist on these lands.
As a result of this policy choice, the draft statement attempts to make a case for the use of such vehicles, rather than fully evaluating the alternative of prohibiting such use. For example, on page 28 of the draft there is a statement that prohibiting

completely the use of these off-road vehicles on public lands would result in "effects on economic sectors which are presently influenced by current demand for and production of off-road vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near bepartment lands where off-road vehicle use takes place."

The would seem that the more important consideration here should be the tagnitude of impact on the economic sector as opposed to the rare presence of an effect. The amount of the economic effect is not ordinanted in the draft, and so one cannot evaluate the significance of any negative economic effect. On page 29 of the draft statement, there is a statement that
closing all Department of Interior lands to ORY use would constitute an action inconsistent with the Department's responsibility to maintain certain of its lands for the enjoyment and inspiration of the general public. It would, likewise, not be consistent with the Department's mandate to encourage the broadest possible mix of compatible multiple uses on certain of its lands— multiple uses which include recreation among the primary potentials and ORV use being a primary sounce of enjoyment to significant numbers of recreationists.
The draft does not discuss the bases for these conclusions. A policy or maintaining certain lands for the enjoyment and inspir tion of the general public hardly requires the use of areas off established roadways by off-road vehicles. Certainly, the Department does not allow all desired uses of its lands which may be sujoye le to certain members of the public. The necessity of evaluating competing uses of the land and determining acceptable uses must often come before the Department. The proposal to permit off-road vehicle use of public lands would seem to be one of those instances requiring an evaluation of competing and conflicting uses. The draft statement does not adequately treat this fundamental question.
In regard to the alternative of allowing off-road vehicle use of public lands, it seems highly questionable from comments in the draft statement that such use is a wise one. At page 12 of the draft, it is stated that whether operated properly or improperly, ORV can cause irreversible and irretrievable harm to man and the environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates that 0 W use will have an adverse effect on wildlife. The adverse effects of encessive noise from ORV on humans and wildlife are outlined at page 19.

Page 3
Part V of the draft statement, at page 24, states that
Even though the net effect of implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memoraneum would be a reduction in the adverse impact on human and natural values, there are certain continued unavoidable adverse effects.
* * *
Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Noise levels will be discomforting to some users of public lands.
Historical and archeological structures may be changed or destroyed by ORV use.
These conclusions are reiterated at page 26 in part VII, of the draft entitled "Tracversible and Irretrievable Commitments of Resources Which Would be Involved in the Proposel Action Should It be Implemented".
In addition to the above concerns and effects, the draft statement observes, at page 13, that there is less than satisfactory data available in regard to the impact of ORV on the lands in question. Therefore, I would suggest that instead of instituting a program of controlled ORV use throughout the Nation's public lands system, it would be more prudent to initiate a test program on a very limited basis. Such a program would facilitate monitoring and data collection, would not require the commitment and expenditure of large sums of money for additional policy and enforcement (see page 21 of draft statement), and would enhance the ability of the Department of Interior to fully evaluate ORV use on public lands. During the operation of such a test program, ORV use of public lands should be limited to established readways.
With the increase in the metropolitan style of living and all the attendant noise and pressure associated with that life, it seems that the public lands are playing an increasing role in providing

Page 4
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
the public with a retreat from the type of noise and annoyance associated with ORV. We should be reluctant to facilitate the intrusion onto those lands by urban sources of noise and annoyance, and so should scrutinize carefully any proposal for CRV use of public lands.
Sincerely
ROBERT L. SHEVIN Attorney General
RLS/DW

Dear Mr. Spicer:
The Floride Came and Fresh Water Fish Commission, through our biologist Mr. Jim McDaniels, has reviewed the above referenced environmental impact statement regarding the use of off-road vehicles and offers the following comments.
Our agency, whose prime responsibility is the management of game and fish, believes that most Department of Interior lands should be closed to off-road vehicle use. Damage to watersheds, plant and animal life, disruption of feeding and breeding grounds for wildlife are but a few of the problems caused by the use of such vehicles. entries.role: Director, Division of Wildlife, Denver, Colorado
entries.summary_quote: We question whether ORV should be used at any time or place where they would cause damage and disturbance of land, wildlife or vegetative resources.
entries.summary: Woodward conditionally supports ORV regulation but raises serious concerns about allowing any damage to land, wildlife, or vegetative resources, questioning whether ORVs should be permitted anywhere they cause such harm. He criticizes the draft statement for using subjective terms like 'excessive' damage and 'minimized' impact, arguing instead for elimination of damage and specific protection of wildlife. He also questions the practicality of bonding and fee mechanisms for restoration, and urges that the statement include a controlled-use alternative.
entries.statement_text:
DIVISION OF WILDLIFE
Harry R. Woodward, Director 6060 Broadway
Denver, Colorado 80216 • 825-1192
August 10, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
We have reviewed the May 26, 1972 statement entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to the use of off-road vehicles on the public lands" prepared by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation. We have made some general observations and several specific comments.
The statement reiterates and possibly reinforces the policies and procedures established by Executive Order 11644, use of off-road vehicles on the public lands. Unfortunately, the Executive Order is directed to the Secretary of Interior alone; we believe the Order should be expanded to include the Secretary of Agriculture and possibly other appropriate land management agencies. We further feel that coordination could best be accomplished by the Department of Natural Resources. We also believe that comments from national conservation organizations should be solicited.
SPECIFIC COMMENTS
Page 3 - (2) I question whether all lands, both open and closed for use, should be designated. Why not just those open, this would lead to less signing, mapping and administration. Signing all lands could cause visual pollution.
The several states have laws which allow them to control the harassment of wildlife.
98

Mr. James G. Watt August 10, 1972 page 2.
Page 4  (iii) Determine the effect of the use of areas and trails of ORV on private lands adjacent to public lands.
Page 5  (Operating Criteria) A specific explanation of the meaning of "than conditions warrant" is needed.
We question whether ORV should be used at any time or place where they would cause damage and disturbance of land, wildlife or vegetative resources.
(d) Allows damage and qualifies the damage by inserting the word "excessive" which is purely judgemental.
Page 6  (2) We still question the wisdom of allowing even minimal damage. Assuming that minimum damage will be allowed we would like to see wildlife specifically mentioned.
Bonding a permittee so as to insure adequate moneys for restoration and rehabilitation of trails and areas used is an extremely questionable procedure: 1. There could be an irreplaceable loss to the resource,
2. The cost of restoration and rehabilitation would be measured monetarily with no consideration given to elapsed time for restoration,
3. No consideration for the destruction of a quality environment,
4. Estimate of costs would necessarily be judgemental, and 5. Administrative procedures would be cumbersome, i.e. how long would a permittees bond or deposit be held, would it be deposited and draw interest, would the interest be collected by the permittee or the federal government, etc.
We feel that it would be extremely difficult to assess an appropriate fee as authorized under the provisions of the Land and Water Conservation Fund Act. How much would be charged? Would the fee be charged before or after the rally or contest? Would the money collected be used for restoration in the area destroyed or would it go into a general fund and be spent in another area?
Continued citation of other executive orders, organic acts and laws without describing their purpose is not extremely enlightening. Perhaps attachment to the environmental statement of all the executive orders and rules and regulations cited would be beneficial.
The method proposed by the Bureau of Land Management for the administration of ORV use is incisive, comprehensive and appears to be a good solution.

Page 11  (U. S. Bureau of Reclamation) Who determines which regulations are appropriate?, the Bureau of Reclamation or the federal or non-federal agency, or a combination?
Page 12  "ORV do limited damage to the human environment, etc."
Possibly "limited" should be defined; preferably ORV should be limited to areas where no damage would be caused.
Page 13  (Physical Impact) Statement that damage could be "minimized" should read the damage could be "eliminated."
Page 16  We agree with the philosophy of prohibiting ORV in certain wildlife areas. Hopefully, this can be accomplished in close coordination with the state wildlife agencies.
There should be a definition of "established roadways."
Page 17 - (Human Impacts) Snowmobiling in the Great Lakes States probably cannot be compared with snowmobiling in the Western States.
We doubt whether there is a direct correlation between the use of ORV and economic enhancement.
Page 18 - We also doubt that in areas where ORV are prohibited, a negative impact will result.
The paragraph on ORV experience is purely conjecture. As you describe the exhilarating feeling you should also describe the feeling of sheer terror - in other words, feelings are highly individualized. Perhaps the incidence of snowmobile-auto accidents should be related. Crossing of highways is highly hazardous.
Page 19 - We agree noise levels must be reduced and standards rigidly enforced.
We agree that the proper procedure is to specify designated areas of use for ORV vehicles.
The Section on Human Impacts sounds like it was written by a PR man for ORV, not that we totally disagree with most of the statements; the thrust is one of promotion rather than attraction.

Page 23  Who will provide the technical assistance to all Interior Bureaus, and other federal agencies, etc.
Page 24  Land, water, air, wildlife, etc., need not always be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Page 28  We are not certain that the Department of Interior should be relied upon by private enterprise to support the economy of an area.
Page 30  More emphasis should be placed upon the interaction at the interface of the public lands with the non-public lands.
The draft environmental statement should contain the alternative of controlled use within the statement.
Sincerely,
Harry R. Woodward
Director

entries.summary_quote: In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
entries.summary: Henry N. Barkhausen, Director of the Illinois Department of Conservation, commends the Department of the Interior for the comprehensive Environmental Statement and ORRV Task Force Study, but expresses serious concerns about ORV use on public lands. He argues that ORV use has been imposed by default rather than design, that the statement is overly promotional of ORV use at the expense of environmental stewardship, and that enforcement and resource degradation problems are severe. He calls for strict limitations on ORV area expansion, controlled access, and careful consideration of how federal guidelines will pressure smaller state properties with denser populations.
entries.statement_text:
State of Illinois
DEPARTMENT OF CONSERVATION
Springfield 62706
RICHARD B OGILVIE
HENRY N. BARKHAUSEN DIRECTOR
August 8, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Director Watt:
It is with pleasure the Illinois Department of Conservation responds to your invitation to review the draft "Environmental Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-the-Road Recreation Vehicles".
In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
We do, however, have several comments regarding the Statement which I am attaching to this letter.
Sincerely,
Henry N. Barkhausen Director
.0

The Illinois Department of Conservation in general has felt that recreational opportunities which are not particularly dependent on natural resources should more appropriately be provided by local government rather than state or federal government. Our feelings have been based more with consideration to state owned lands of this Department than in the context of the federal properties. We feel that, in general, the types of recreational experiences provided to the public should proceed from a strong natural resource orientation to a less strong natural resource orientation as one proceeds from the federal to local levels of government.
Our feelings are that the imposition of off-the-road vehicles on public lands has been more by default than by design. The tremendous increase, however, in production and use of off-the-road vehicles has brought us to a point in time where it will be very difficult to step back and prohibit use of these vehicles in all cases even though there are many instances where they seem to exhibit a disharmonious factor with major objectives and uses of lands involved, particularly those uses which are more traditional. We may be exhibiting the polarization in viewpoints here, representing the more resource-oriented opinions, as discussed in the Task Force Study; however, it is difficult for us, with 11 million people to serve in Illinois, to adequately view the extent of the problem in the much less populated states of the west. At the same time we have a 250,000 acre federal forest within our state, and we are aware of the tremendous pressure placed by the motorcycle industry for utilization of the federal lands in Indiana and their desire to move into Illinois.
In spite of this, we have a feeling that use of off-the-road recreational vehicles on some public lands is an accepted recreational activity. We view very apprehensively, however, the likelihood that pressure for use, and expansion of 'territory' will cause a legal or illegal use to be imposed upon state lands which may be adjacent to these larger federal properties in our midwestern states.
Implied in these comments is our feeling that the intensity of pressure will be applied more toward states like Illinois than toward the federal government because our properties are so much smaller, relatively, and because we have such dense concentrations of people.
TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROPOSED
In light of the above general comments and as a result of the proposal to provide technical assistance to a variety of agencies including state governments, it is desired that these demographic factors be considered in order, that promotion for the development of areas and facilities does not overburden state and local resources. The recent task force study promulgated by the Conservation Foundation proposed a recreation extension service, which if operated at the state level, would serve to bring unique factors such as those mentioned, into proper focus.

Comments from the Illinois Department of Conservation
on
Draft Environmental Statement
Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles
on the Public Lands
Submitted to: Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
August 8, 1972

The use criteria proposed appear to be very adequate. It is recommended, however, that whenever trails or areas are proposed that, wherever possible, controlled access be a prerequisite to the establishment of these areas. Because it is anticipated that guidelines for use of ORV's on federal properties will serve as guidelines to the states, it seems important that ramifications be considered because of expected greater intensity of use with greater numbers of people on smaller properties.
DESCRIPTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT & ENRIVONMENTAL IMPACTS
Much like the more restrictive conditions proposed to prevail on National Park Service lands, this is also desired when considering state lands and the smaller units of federal properties such as many of the Corps of Engineers reservoirs. Low pool stages of many federal reservoirs provide an additional possibility for minimum environmental damage except when concentrations of wildlife are present.
The fact that determination has not been made on what peak use will be, nor the extent to which the demand will continue to increase, and because of the lack of adequate research data on environmental degradation, it is our desire that limits be placed upon the extension of facilities available for use by ORV's. In the words of the Draft Environmental Statement, "No areas are really inaccessible anymore". It is anticipated that as we allow new areas and new types of uses to be allowed that even more severely harmful uses may be requested and/or experienced in the future.
Perhaps our most critical comment regarding the Draft Environmental Statement is that because we feel we are in the ORV business by default, that the Statement is designed to reduce adverse public relations effects by providing an abundance of positive reactions to CRV use. It is our feeling that ORV use in almost every situation is going to cause a deleterious effect on the environment. In our own activities in Illinois regarding use of state properties by snowmobiles, all terrain vehicles, metercycles, etc., we question seriously whether we are adequately exhibiting the responsibility we have in the proper stewardship of public lands. We question this as well in the federal context.
Again, quoting from your Statement, "Growth of public interest in ORV use has outstripped easy control of controversial impacts". You follow this statement saying, "The current thrust will be to alleviate this controversy by providing space for users and space for non-users and protection of the natural legacies several Interior bureaus are charged with". We feel this is a very dangerous practice which will result in naive public interest (pressure) or economic interests at the expense of the environment, causing an expansion of the system which will only serve to further damage existing natural resources. Limitations must be imposed. It is anticipated that funds derived from registration fees, etc. will be insufficient to provide adequate repairs for environmental damage, capital expenditures necessary to provide desired facilities,

and monies needed for administration and management: Our own experience has shown that enforcement necessary to control of ORV usage is the most serious of the problems, this in spite of the fact that our Department has even purchased snowmobiles for enforcement and maintenance purposes.
It is our feeling that enforcement problems would be reduced if areas rather than trails were provided.
ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED ACTION
Alternatives to the Draft Environmental Statement are perhaps the key to the necessity for the Environmental Statement. We agree the proposed alternatives are absolutely unsatisfactory. Therefore, the best thing expected to happen is that environmental concerns be studied with resultant action which will have the least environmental damage.
The State of Illinois, as the result of the initiative by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, anticipates the application of the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement to a review of our own properties as they may be affected by ORV use. We commend the Department of Interior for again setting the tone for proper management of public lands.
