entries.summary: The Illinois Department of Conservation conditionally supports the ORV framework but expresses serious concern that the Draft Environmental Statement downplays environmental harm and that expansion of ORV use will damage natural resources, particularly on smaller state properties near federal lands. They insist that firm limitations must be imposed, warning that registration fees and other funds will be inadequate to cover environmental repairs, facility costs, and administration, and that enforcement is the most serious practical problem. They commend Interior for taking initiative but urge that demographic pressures on Midwestern states be factored into any technical assistance or promotion of ORV facilities.
entries.statement_text:
State of Illinois
DEPARTMENT OF CONSERVATION
Springfield 62706
RICHARD B OGILVIE
HENRY N. BARKHAUSEN DIRECTOR
August 8, 1972
Mr. James G. Watt, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Director Watt:
It is with pleasure the Illinois Department of Conservation responds to your invitation to review the draft "Environmental Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-the-Road Recreation Vehicles".
In general, we feel the Statement and the associated ORRV Task Force Study is very comprehensive and we wish to commend the Department of the Interior for taking the initiative regarding this work.
We do, however, have several comments regarding the Statement which I am attaching to this letter.
Sincerely,
Henry N. Barkhausen Director
.0

The Illinois Department of Conservation in general has felt that recreational opportunities which are not particularly dependent on natural resources should more appropriately be provided by local government rather than state or federal government. Our feelings have been based more with consideration to state owned lands of this Department than in the context of the federal properties. We feel that, in general, the types of recreational experiences provided to the public should proceed from a strong natural resource orientation to a less strong natural resource orientation as one proceeds from the federal to local levels of government.
Our feelings are that the imposition of off-the-road vehicles on public lands has been more by default than by design. The tremendous increase, however, in production and use of off-the-road vehicles has brought us to a point in time where it will be very difficult to step back and prohibit use of these vehicles in all cases even though there are many instances where they seem to exhibit a disharmonious factor with major objectives and uses of lands involved, particularly those uses which are more traditional. We may be exhibiting the polarization in viewpoints here, representing the more resource-oriented opinions, as discussed in the Task Force Study; however, it is difficult for us, with 11 million people to serve in Illinois, to adequately view the extent of the problem in the much less populated states of the west. At the same time we have a 250,000 acre federal forest within our state, and we are aware of the tremendous pressure placed by the motorcycle industry for utilization of the federal lands in Indiana and their desire to move into Illinois.
In spite of this, we have a feeling that use of off-the-road recreational vehicles on some public lands is an accepted recreational activity. We view very apprehensively, however, the likelihood that pressure for use, and expansion of 'territory' will cause a legal or illegal use to be imposed upon state lands which may be adjacent to these larger federal properties in our midwestern states.
Implied in these comments is our feeling that the intensity of pressure will be applied more toward states like Illinois than toward the federal government because our properties are so much smaller, relatively, and because we have such dense concentrations of people.
TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROPOSED
In light of the above general comments and as a result of the proposal to provide technical assistance to a variety of agencies including state governments, it is desired that these demographic factors be considered in order, that promotion for the development of areas and facilities does not overburden state and local resources. The recent task force study promulgated by the Conservation Foundation proposed a recreation extension service, which if operated at the state level, would serve to bring unique factors such as those mentioned, into proper focus.

Comments from the Illinois Department of Conservation
on
Draft Environmental Statement
Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles
on the Public Lands
Submitted to: Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
August 8, 1972

The use criteria proposed appear to be very adequate. It is recommended, however, that whenever trails or areas are proposed that, wherever possible, controlled access be a prerequisite to the establishment of these areas. Because it is anticipated that guidelines for use of ORV's on federal properties will serve as guidelines to the states, it seems important that ramifications be considered because of expected greater intensity of use with greater numbers of people on smaller properties.
DESCRIPTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT & ENRIVONMENTAL IMPACTS
Much like the more restrictive conditions proposed to prevail on National Park Service lands, this is also desired when considering state lands and the smaller units of federal properties such as many of the Corps of Engineers reservoirs. Low pool stages of many federal reservoirs provide an additional possibility for minimum environmental damage except when concentrations of wildlife are present.
The fact that determination has not been made on what peak use will be, nor the extent to which the demand will continue to increase, and because of the lack of adequate research data on environmental degradation, it is our desire that limits be placed upon the extension of facilities available for use by ORV's. In the words of the Draft Environmental Statement, "No areas are really inaccessible anymore". It is anticipated that as we allow new areas and new types of uses to be allowed that even more severely harmful uses may be requested and/or experienced in the future.
Perhaps our most critical comment regarding the Draft Environmental Statement is that because we feel we are in the ORV business by default, that the Statement is designed to reduce adverse public relations effects by providing an abundance of positive reactions to CRV use. It is our feeling that ORV use in almost every situation is going to cause a deleterious effect on the environment. In our own activities in Illinois regarding use of state properties by snowmobiles, all terrain vehicles, metercycles, etc., we question seriously whether we are adequately exhibiting the responsibility we have in the proper stewardship of public lands. We question this as well in the federal context.
Again, quoting from your Statement, "Growth of public interest in ORV use has outstripped easy control of controversial impacts". You follow this statement saying, "The current thrust will be to alleviate this controversy by providing space for users and space for non-users and protection of the natural legacies several Interior bureaus are charged with". We feel this is a very dangerous practice which will result in naive public interest (pressure) or economic interests at the expense of the environment, causing an expansion of the system which will only serve to further damage existing natural resources. Limitations must be imposed. It is anticipated that funds derived from registration fees, etc. will be insufficient to provide adequate repairs for environmental damage, capital expenditures necessary to provide desired facilities,

and monies needed for administration and management: Our own experience has shown that enforcement necessary to control of ORV usage is the most serious of the problems, this in spite of the fact that our Department has even purchased snowmobiles for enforcement and maintenance purposes.
It is our feeling that enforcement problems would be reduced if areas rather than trails were provided.
ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED ACTION
Alternatives to the Draft Environmental Statement are perhaps the key to the necessity for the Environmental Statement. We agree the proposed alternatives are absolutely unsatisfactory. Therefore, the best thing expected to happen is that environmental concerns be studied with resultant action which will have the least environmental damage.
The State of Illinois, as the result of the initiative by the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, anticipates the application of the Task Force Study and the Draft Environmental Statement to a review of our own properties as they may be affected by ORV use. We commend the Department of Interior for again setting the tone for proper management of public lands.

entries.role: Director, Recreation Vehicle Division, Trailer Coach Association
entries.summary_quote: Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government.
entries.summary: Lee W. Moses, on behalf of the Trailer Coach Association, strongly supports a multi-use concept for all public lands, arguing that restricting access to preserve natural resources denies the public—particularly families and working people—the recreational opportunities they need. He criticizes the Draft Environmental Statement as overly influenced by 'hard core preservationists' and contends that off-road vehicle users are responsible conservationists, not destroyers of the environment. He offers numerous constructive suggestions for expanding and better managing public recreational lands while keeping them open to all users with minimal regulation.
entries.statement_text:
3855 EAST LA PALMA AVENUE + ANAHEIM, CALIFORNIA 92806 (714) 630-1440 August 4, 1972
RE: INT DES 72-62
The Honorable Rogers C. Morton Secretary U. S. Department of the Interior Washington, D. C.
Dear Sir:
Trailer Coach Association wishes to thank the Department for this opportunity to express our views on federal land use and recreational policies.
Trailer Coach Association was formed in 1936 and is the oldest association in the United States which represents the manufacturers of recreation vehicles. Recognizing the difference in marketing areas between those states east and west of the Rocky Mountains, Trailer Coach Association has endeavored to curtail its major sphere of operation to the 11 westernmost states and is extremely active in the promotion and protection of the industry in those states.
Additionally to deal with matters of national concern to the industry, Trailer Coach Association maintains a staffed office in the Washington, D. C. area. This office enables the industry to carry out expeditious liason with various departments of the federal government.
The term 'recreation vehicle' has been applied to many varied types of vehicles currently being used in the pursuit of outdoor recreation. However, the types of vehicles which are of direct concern to TCA are the recreational housing type vehicles which include Motor Homes, Travel Trailers, Camping Trailers, Truck Campers and Converted Vans (see Attachment #1 - Illustrated Definitions). There are currently in excess of four and a half million (4,500,000) of these types of vehicles in use in the United States which are used for varying periods of time during the year by over thirteen million (13,000,000) Americans for recreation, vacation and travel use. The industry is currently producing nearly one-half million (500,000) of these vehicles annually with a value which exceeds one and a half billion dollars ($1,500,000,000). If current trends continue, these figures will double within ten (10) years. These impressive figures are but a small part of the estimated one-hundred and five billion
. BOR [13"Codod"[11"]
100
#5-45860

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 2 August 4, 1972
dollars ($105,000,000,000) pumped into the national economy each year by the current leisure time/recreation boom which we are experiencing. The money spent in this country in spare time pursuits is in excess of the cost of national defense; it is more than we spend on the construction of new homes; it is greater than the aggregate income of all the country's farmers and exceeds the over-all value of this country's exports.
The current boom in outdoor recreation shows no signs of slowing down. Since there are currently in excess of 2,000 firms working on a four-day week, the establishment of five three-day holiday weekends each year and the fact that over forty million (40,000,000) workers enjoy a three week vacation each year, one can only anticipate continued increases. Early retirements too will contribute heavily to increased leisure time spending. It is currently estimated that over seventy-five percent (75%) of the people who are nine years of age or above indulge in some form of outdoor recreation. Unfortunately, due to a lack of urban recreation facilities and restrictive uses on rural land use, Americans continue to be faced with more and more time to do less and less.
Recreation vehicles are currently the only means by which families with small children and retired people may enjoy the pleasures of camping. Recreational camping vehicles offer the user sanitation facilities which are totally self-contained and provide a convenient way to carry their litter back home for proper disposal unlike the hiker who must find ways to dispose of waste materials in the out-of-doors without proper facilities.
Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government. The desire to preserve our "natural resources" by denying the use of land to the people who own and wish to make use of it is certainly not in the best interest of providing the needed opportunities for man to seek recreation and preserve their "human resources."
Over-use and conflict of interest have created a need for regulation of the use of federally-controlled public lands, as has become only too obvious by the preponderance of somewhat ill-conceived actions by extremest preservation groups. If regulation is to be fair, then certainly the prime objectives must be coordinated between various bureaus and departments charged with administrating the lands, equal consideration given to all recreational uses currently being pursued on those lands and an area by area determination must be made of the necessary regulation of individual sites.
The prime consideration must be to keep all lands open for all uses with minimum regulation unless there is a specific well-documented reason for establishing more restrictive regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 3 August 4, 1972
The need for an input from groups other than those interested in total preservation of our natural resources has recently given birth to several new organizations devoted to assisting the federal government in planning for the administration of land use and recreational policies. Among the most prominent of these new organizations is the "Outdoor Nation" (see Attachment #2). We are hopeful that this organization will provide your department with a realistic viewpoint and approach to solving some of the problems to which this statement is addressed.
Trailer Coach Association cannot help but feel that the definition of recreation vehicle as found in Presidential Order No. 11644 was never intended to include the vehicles as described above and in Attachment #1. However, the true off-road vehicles -- motorcycles, dune buggies, snow-mobiles, four-wheel drive, etc. are also of importance to the industry we represent. A recent study of the users of recreational camping vehicles in the State of California indicated that 40% of the vehicles surveyed were carrying or towing some type of off-road vehicle. We can only conclude that restrictions on the operation of these off-road vehicles will definitely effect the use and marketing of recreational camping vehicles and we, therefore, have a common interest in maintaining areas for their use.
We would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Department of Interior Task Force which developed the November 1971 study on Off-Road Recreation Vehicles. We feel that this is a true and objective look at the pros and cons of this legitimate form of outdoor recreation. On the other hand, we fail to understand the thinking of the Department as expressed in their Draft - Environmental Statement of May 26, 1972, which differs greatly from the ORRV Study. It would appear that the hard core preservationists must have had a hand in the drafting of the environmental statement.
Many unfortunate assertions have been made concerning the use and users of off-road vehicles by over-reactionary preservationist groups. Most of these extremists would have the nation believe that anyone who entered into the public domain on or in a mechanized vehicle was there for the sole purpose of damaging or destroying any or all things which came into his view. This most certainly is not the case. The users of recreation vehicles of all types are family people participating in family activities. They are conservationists interested in a clean, healthful environment and are concerned for the safety of themselves, their families and others while pursuing their preferred type of recreation. Through the use of public lands, people from all walks of life are brought together in a common interest, and healthy communication is often fostered between child and parent through their participation in activities which interest them mutually.

. The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 4
August 4, 1972
In the past year or so, many proposals have been made to not only restrict the use of public lands but to prohibit recreation vehicle use by classifying these areas as wilderness or primitive thereby denying use to some 98% of the national population. Since less than 2% of the nation's people are active hikers and backpackers, areas which restrict vehicle use become inaccessible to a very large majority. We have no quarrel with back-packing; however, the time required and the physical demands account for the relatively small number of people who are able to enjoy this type of activity. Surveys conclude that the majority of back-packers in the United States understandably are school teachers and students who have long summer vacations and are able to spend the long periods of time necessary to pursue this type of recreation. The average working man with two weeks annual vacation plus a few holiday weekends must restrict his recreational activities to those which may be reasonably pursued within a relatively short period of time.
It is interesting to note that the same groups who advocate increasing our country's wilderness areas and totally preserving our natural resources actively solicit and spend tax free funds to impair American commerce. These self-appointed guardians of the American public devote full time to lobbying and have filed lawsuits against nearly every large scale economically beneficial project which has been pursued by American industry during the past three to five years. Shocking examples of this unwarranted use of the country's judicial system are the halting of the Trans-Alaskan pipeline and the Florida Barge Canal. From where industry sits, it looks as if the government is "running scared" from a very vocal minority of the people.
Evidence of the preservationist impact on the United States economy is evidenced by the U. S. Chamber of Commerce's decision to take a stand against such groups, and to assume a more aggressive roll in shaping decisions being made not only by the courts, but by government agencies responsible for implementing environmental protection laws.
Areas which we feel worthy of exploration as a means of solving some of the problems created by the public's demand for outdoor recreation follow:
1. There are many tracts of government-owned land which at one time served as military reservations that are no longer in use which could be turned into recreation facilities to serve a portion of the close-in urban recreational needs.
2. The availability of low interest loans to recreational area development firms would stimulate development from the private sector.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 5 August 4, 1972
3. A problem currently being created by land closures is a higher concentration of use is being experienced by those areas which remain open which in turn auguments any problems that might be created by over-use. Therefore, very thorough consideration must be given to any closure of the public domain.
4. A reevaluation is in order of the types of recreation which are in one way or another subsidized by the government in relation to the numbers of people involved in various recreational pursuits.
5. The Bureau of Land Management should reevaluate their leasing practices of public lands for sheep and cattle grazing and mining operations. To prevent such unfair practices as "checkerboard leasing", current practices allow a lessee to lease sections of land which are diagonally adjacent to one another in a "checkerboard" pattern without paying for the lease rights on those sections of land which become entrapped by surrounding leaseholds. This practice allows leaseholders to monopolize 100% more land than they actually pay rental on and gives them the right to deny tresspass privileges to the general public.
6. An immediate and inexpensive solution to the problem of over-crowded existing recreation areas might be a rescheduling of vacation periods in the schools of our country. By requiring approximately 25% of the student bodies to vacation during each of four quarters annually, we would not only eliminate the summer vacation conjection but would make better use of our educational facilities as well.
7. A very effective program which was instituted by the government during the late 1930s under the banner of 'CCC' might be revitalized to assist in building new and rehabilitating our existing recreation facilities across the country while making use of the very large unemployed labor force which is currently available. Since through various welfare and unemployment compensation plans we, the taxpayers, support the unemployed while they are idle, it would make economical sense to accomplish some worthwhile end while supporting these people.
8. When conflicts occur between various groups interested in the use of a specific tract of land, we feel that the best solution is to call together the representatives from those interested groups and allow them to work out their differences in a democratic manner. The government body responsible for the operation and administration of the area in question should be called upon to moderate any arbitration of this type. Trailer Coach Association strongly believes in the theory of self-government and therefore feels that the people who are directly involved in the results of regulation are entitled to a say in the writing and implementation of those regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton
U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 6
August 4, 1972
9. Conflicts between user groups could be avoided to a large degree through proper education of the individuals involved and by encouraging users to understand the needs and motivations of other users. Through proper education by both government and organized user groups, policies of self-policing should be encouraged.
10. Under the present restrictions placed on wilderness and primitive areas, any "man-made" structures are prohibited. We suggest a reevaluation of these policies in view of the fact that the very people who demand expansion of our existing wilderness systems have a need for sanitary facilities, trash disposal and some degree of fire control in the existing areas.
11. A clean environment and balanced Ecosystem are among the top priorities involved in conservation and preservation of natural resources. We would suggest that the Department of the Interior take a close look at the sewage disposal facilities of any of the major cities in our country. It is appalling in this day of advanced technology that cities the size of San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago, New York, etc., etc., dump raw, untreated sewage into our rivers and oceans daily. It is naive indeed to think that we can solve our problems by continuing to pollute the areas in which we live while expending our financial resources to seek refuge away from those areas which we have polluted.
Again, we appreciate this opportunity to make our views known to your Department and trust that your consideration will be given to these remarks. We stand ready to assist in whatever manner which might be appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
Lee W. Moses, Director
Recreation Vehicle Division

entries.summary: The National Park Service offered detailed comments on the draft EIS, raising concerns about specific wording, the need to segregate positive and negative consequences, and the lack of attention to protection of historic, archeological, and paleontological resources. They emphasized that compliance with Executive Order 11593 and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act must be assured when implementing ORV regulations on federal lands. They also noted that National Park System lands are already protected from uncontrolled ORV use by existing legislation and regulations.
entries.statement_text:
United States Department of the Interior
NATIONAL PARK SERVICE . WASHINGTON, D.C. 20240
マ8年
L7427-0CC
AUG 2 1 1972
Memorandum
To:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
Through: Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Notes &
From:
Assistant Director, Cooperative Activities
Subject: Draft environmental statement for the proposed implementation
of Executive Order 11644
We are pleased to send you our comments on the subject draft environmental statement in accordance with former Director Douglas Hofe Jr.'s memorandum of June 1.
However, before commenting on the draft statement, we offer the following comments on the Secretary of the Interior's memorandum of May 5 containing guidelines for use by Interior bureaus in preparing regulations to implement Executive Order 11644.
1. Page 3, b.(1), lines 6, 7 and 8: Thirty-six CFR 2.34[e] provides that a person under licensing age may operate an off-road vehicle (ORV) within a unit of the National Park System if he is supervised by a licensed operator of 21 years of age or more. A licensed operator may supervise only one unlicensed operator.
2. Page 3, b.(1)(a): The meaning of "reckless and careless manner" should be made as clear as possible in any proposed regulations. The National Park Service has attempted to do this in 36 CFR 4.14.
The following comments pertain to the draft environmental statement:
1. We suggest that comments or the draft statement also be solicited from the Advisory Council for Historic Preservation.
2. Page 9, line 9: Add "The Service is currently enforcing regulations pertaining to ORVs which appear in CFR Title 36."

3. Page 11: The section entitled <u>The Environmental Impact of the Proposed Action</u> would be more effective if the positive and negative consequences were segregated.
4. Page 12, 2nd paragraph, 2nd and 3rd sentences: We believe that these two sentences should be modified to read "Many areas are accessible and available to public use every season of the year and all hours of the day."
5. Page 12, 3rd paragraph: We suggest evidence be submitted to support the claim that ORVs "can strengthen family ties."
6. Page 13, line 1: We suggest that "ORV" be inserted between "by" and "user" for further clarification.
7. Page 16, last paragraph: This paragraph lists beneficial effects of ORV use by recreationists and by land managers. We question the value of ORV use for protection of forests from fire. Where wild land fire from natural causes is recognized as a natural ecological process, there is no advantage in allowing ORV use under the guise of fire protection. Back country fires may be approached more rapidly and effectively with helicopters.
8. Page 24: The section entitled Any Adverse Effects Which Cannot Be Avoided Should The Proposal Be Implemented is so general that it lacks substance. It should be strengthened by listing and discussing specific negative effects.
9. Page 26, VIII, A): The text should recognize that National Park System lands are protected from uncontrolled ORV use by existing legislation, policies and regulations, and therefore, would be affected little or not at all by the proposed action. Also, for the sake of balance and completeness, positive economics and social benefits, as well as negative effects, should be identified and discussed.
10. Page 29, VIII C): This section also should identify and discuss possible economic and social benefits.
In addition to offering the above specific comments, we wish to express our concern about lack of attention to protection of historic (including archeological and paleontological) resources. We believe that Section 2(b) of Executive Order 11593 of May 13, 1971, must be observed in contemplating use of ORVs on federally-owned lands. Section 2(b) requires that certain cautionary steps be taken to assure that no historic resources worthy of preservation and nomination to the National Register of Historic

Places will be inadvertently damaged or destroyed. We believe that the subject statement should indicate whether compliance with E. O. 11593 will be assured during implementation of E. O. 11644.
Also, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 (P.L. 89-665) requires certain procedures prior to any Federal action that might affect a property listed in the National Register of Historic Places. We believe that the subject statement should indicate whether compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act will be assured during implementation of E. O. 11644.
We appreciate having an opportunity to review the subject draft environmental statement, and we offer you our comments in a spirit of assisting you in complying with requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
Thereor Q. Swern

Motorcycles are limited to improved main roads and must be properly muffled, while dune buggies and ATVs are confined to designated areas only, with recreational use areas and beaches off-limits. All such vehicles are prohibited during nighttime hours.
entries.statement_text:
STATE PARK
AND RECREATION COMMISSION
REGULATION NO. 18 STATE PARK REGULATIONS
18. Motorcycles, Dune Buggies and All-Terrain Vehicles.
The operations of motorcycles within the State Park system shall be permitted on improved, main roads only and shall be properly muffled.
The operations of dune buggies and all-terrain vehicles within the State Park system shall be permitted in designated areas only. All recreational use areas and beaches are off limits. Check with park personnel in each respective park prior to operations.
The use of motorcycles, dune buggies and all-terrain vehicles is prohibited between the hours of 9:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. during daylight savings time and 7:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. during standard time.
Adopted by the New Mexico State Park and Recreation Commission the 18th day of July, 1972.

WILLIAM B. NYE DIRECTOR
DEPARTMENT OF MATURAL RESOURCES
OHIO DEPARTMENTS BUILDING COLUMEUS 43215
August 9, 1972
United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240 Attn: G. Douglas Hofe, Jr., Director
Draft Environmental Impact RE: Statement for Implementation of Executive Order 11644-Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public
Lands-Kl4
Dear Director Hofe:
In response to your letter of June 1, 1972 forwarding the draft environmental impact statement for the above referenced project, a review was coordinated by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources. Comments were solicited from other State agencies under the auspices of the Office of the Governor, State Clearinghouse.
This draft environmental impact statement is an excellent, well-thought product. It is thorough and easily understood. We have no comments on the five points.
The Department of Interior should proceed with finalization of the statement. We would, however, urge you to promote mechanisms for site selection for Off-Road Vehicles use which would allow for the least adverse impact and irretrievable loss in the area being considered. In addition, qualified personnel should periodically inspect areas in use to assess the deterioration of existing land forms.
In light of the fact that ORV site selections must take into account the preservation of unique natural areas, special soil and vegetative conditions, wildlife habitat areas, etc., perhaps the implementation of a public land use plan would aid and/or facilitate these selections.

Director G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. August 9, 1972 Page Two
Thank you for the opportunity to review and comment on the impact statement. We look forward to receiving the final form and to cooperation in any way with the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation personnel associated with the State of Ohio in implementing this Executive Order.
Sincerely,
WILLIAM B. NYE Director

He recommends strong interagency cooperation in coordinating, planning, and developing areas for ORV use. He also raises specific questions about the proposed age requirements for supervisors and expresses concern about potential damage to historical and archaeological structures from ORV use.

Dear Mr. Still:
Thank you for your letter and the opportunity to review and comment on the U.S. Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Public Lands (SPDC Project No. 72-1336).
While we might suggest that the Department of Interior choose "Alternative B)," we can appreciate the popularity of the vehicles and the problems that have arisen with their increasing use. We would recommend strong emphasis in the proposed cooperation between all agencies and levels of government in coordinating, planning and development of areas and facilities for the use of ORV.
Points of curiosity, with the voting age and, in some states, the age of majority being 18, why is it suggested that the supervisor be 21? Also, what number of persons under age can be supervise as conditions warrant? Finally, why do any historical or archeological structures have to be changed or destroyed by ORV use?
We feel the Department is to be commanded for their efforts in secking solutions to these very vexing problems.
Sincerely,
R. Charles Shepherd
Director
Division of Technical Assistance

entries.summary: Robert L. Shevin, as Florida's Attorney General, argues that the draft EIS inadequately evaluates the alternative of prohibiting ORV use entirely and fails to quantify the economic effects of such a prohibition. He contends that given the acknowledged irreversible environmental damage and insufficient data on ORV impacts, it would be more prudent to initiate a limited test program rather than implement controlled ORV use across all public lands. During any such test program, ORV use should be restricted to established roadways, and the public lands' role as a retreat from urban noise and annoyance should be carefully protected.
entries.statement_text:
TALLAHASSUE, PLOUIDA, 3290-1
August 7, 1972
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
State Planning and Development Clearinghouse
Department of Administration
725 South Bronough Street
Tallahassee, Florida 32304
Re: U. S. Department of Interior - Bureau of Outdoor Recreation: Draft Environmental Impact Statement Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands (K14) SPDC Project No. 72-1336.
Dear Mr. Still:
The following are comments on the draft Environmental Impact Statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the public lands.
The general approach to the regulation of off-road vehicles on
public lands, as delineated in the proposed Impact Statement, appears
to be adequate and comprehensive, assuming that one agrees with the\nunderlying policy.
The President's Executive Order 11644 and the Memorandum from Interior Secretary Morton to various assistant secretaries appear to assume that off-road vehicles will be permitted to use public lands off established roadways. The entire draft statement addresses itself to minimizing the damage or conflict caused by the use of these vehicles off established roadways. It assumes that there should be allowed certain damage or conflict with the present activities that exist on these lands.
As a result of this policy choice, the draft statement attempts to make a case for the use of such vehicles, rather than fully evaluating the alternative of prohibiting such use. For example, on page 28 of the draft there is a statement that prohibiting

completely the use of these off-road vehicles on public lands would result in "effects on economic sectors which are presently influenced by current demand for and production of off-road vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near vehicles. The closing would also affect the economics near bepartment lands where off-road vehicle use takes place."

The would seem that the more important consideration here should be the tagnitude of impact on the economic sector as opposed to the rare presence of an effect. The amount of the economic effect is not ordinanted in the draft, and so one cannot evaluate the significance of any negative economic effect. On page 29 of the draft statement, there is a statement that
closing all Department of Interior lands to ORY use would constitute an action inconsistent with the Department's responsibility to maintain certain of its lands for the enjoyment and inspiration of the general public. It would, likewise, not be consistent with the Department's mandate to encourage the broadest possible mix of compatible multiple uses on certain of its lands— multiple uses which include recreation among the primary potentials and ORV use being a primary sounce of enjoyment to significant numbers of recreationists.
The draft does not discuss the bases for these conclusions. A policy or maintaining certain lands for the enjoyment and inspir tion of the general public hardly requires the use of areas off established roadways by off-road vehicles. Certainly, the Department does not allow all desired uses of its lands which may be sujoye le to certain members of the public. The necessity of evaluating competing uses of the land and determining acceptable uses must often come before the Department. The proposal to permit off-road vehicle use of public lands would seem to be one of those instances requiring an evaluation of competing and conflicting uses. The draft statement does not adequately treat this fundamental question.
In regard to the alternative of allowing off-road vehicle use of public lands, it seems highly questionable from comments in the draft statement that such use is a wise one. At page 12 of the draft, it is stated that whether operated properly or improperly, ORV can cause irreversible and irretrievable harm to man and the environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates environment. The draft_statement, at pages 15 and 16, indicates that 0 W use will have an adverse effect on wildlife. The adverse effects of encessive noise from ORV on humans and wildlife are outlined at page 19.

Page 3
Part V of the draft statement, at page 24, states that
Even though the net effect of implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memoraneum would be a reduction in the adverse impact on human and natural values, there are certain continued unavoidable adverse effects.
* * *
Land, water, air, wildlife, and vegetation resources will be detrimentally affected in areas of ORV use.
Noise levels will be discomforting to some users of public lands.
Historical and archeological structures may be changed or destroyed by ORV use.
These conclusions are reiterated at page 26 in part VII, of the draft entitled "Tracversible and Irretrievable Commitments of Resources Which Would be Involved in the Proposel Action Should It be Implemented".
In addition to the above concerns and effects, the draft statement observes, at page 13, that there is less than satisfactory data available in regard to the impact of ORV on the lands in question. Therefore, I would suggest that instead of instituting a program of controlled ORV use throughout the Nation's public lands system, it would be more prudent to initiate a test program on a very limited basis. Such a program would facilitate monitoring and data collection, would not require the commitment and expenditure of large sums of money for additional policy and enforcement (see page 21 of draft statement), and would enhance the ability of the Department of Interior to fully evaluate ORV use on public lands. During the operation of such a test program, ORV use of public lands should be limited to established readways.
With the increase in the metropolitan style of living and all the attendant noise and pressure associated with that life, it seems that the public lands are playing an increasing role in providing

Page 4
Mr. Homer E. Still, Jr.
the public with a retreat from the type of noise and annoyance associated with ORV. We should be reluctant to facilitate the intrusion onto those lands by urban sources of noise and annoyance, and so should scrutinize carefully any proposal for CRV use of public lands.
Sincerely
ROBERT L. SHEVIN Attorney General

entries.summary: The New Mexico State Planning Office, having coordinated review with multiple state agencies, found the draft environmental statement well-prepared and adequate in presenting ORV impacts. They strongly support implementing restrictions on off-road vehicles and believe those restrictions should apply not only to federal lands but to state lands as well. entries.statement_text:
STATE PLANNING OFFICE
SANTA FE
OFFICE OF DIRECTOR
August 9, 1972
Mr. Thomas Watts, Director Bureau of Outdoor Recreation United States Department of the Interior Washington, D. C. 20204
Dear Mr. Watts:
In reference to your draft environmental statement of off-road vehicles, I have coordinated a careful study of this document with the Department of Game and Fish, the State Park and Recreation Commission, the State Land Office, and the Division of Recreation and Historic Preservation of the State Planning Office, and have the following comment to offer.
It is felt that your statement is well prepared and adequately presents the impact of off-road vehicles on recreation, wildlife, and preservation. It is further felt that certain restrictions must be implemented on all off-road vehicles, as well as the various terrains involved, to minimize the indiscriminate abuse of public lands; and moreover, that these regulations be strictly enforced.
The State Planning Office strongly feels that off-road vehicle restrictions should not only apply to federal lands, but certainly to State lands as well. For your additional information, actions that the State of New Mexico has taken concerning off-road vehicle travel is enclosed.
Thank you for allowing us to review your draft statement. If I may be of additional service on this or any other matter please feel free to contact me anytime.
Sincerely,
David W. King
State Planning Office

entries.summary_quote: Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government.
entries.summary: The Trailer Coach Association strongly supports a true multi-use concept for all public lands, particularly those administered by the federal government, arguing that restricting access denies the public their right to enjoy lands they own. They contend that ORV users and recreation vehicle users are responsible family people and conservationists, not the destructive actors portrayed by 'extremist preservation groups.' They offer numerous constructive suggestions for managing public lands and urge that all lands remain open for all uses with minimum regulation unless specific, well-documented reasons exist for more restrictive rules.
entries.statement_text:
Trailer Coach Association wishes to thank the Department for this opportunity to express our views on federal land use and recreational policies.
Trailer Coach Association was formed in 1936 and is the oldest association in the United States which represents the manufacturers of recreation vehicles. Recognizing the difference in marketing areas between those states east and west of the Rocky Mountains, Trailer Coach Association has endeavored to curtail its major sphere of operation to the 11 westernmost states and is extremely active in the promotion and protection of the industry in those states.
Additionally to deal with matters of national concern to the industry, Trailer Coach Association maintains a staffed office in the Washington, D. C. area. This office enables the industry to carry out expeditious liason with various departments of the federal government.
The term 'recreation vehicle' has been applied to many varied types of vehicles currently being used in the pursuit of outdoor recreation. However, the types of vehicles which are of direct concern to TCA are the recreational housing type vehicles which include Motor Homes, Travel Trailers, Camping Trailers, Truck Campers and Converted Vans (see Attachment #1 - Illustrated Definitions). There are currently in excess of four and a half million (4,500,000) of these types of vehicles in use in the United States which are used for varying periods of time during the year by over thirteen million (13,000,000) Americans for recreation, vacation and travel use. The industry is currently producing nearly one-half million (500,000) of these vehicles annually with a value which exceeds one and a half billion dollars ($1,500,000,000). If current trends continue, these figures will double within ten (10) years. These impressive figures are but a small part of the estimated one-hundred and five billion
. BOR [13"Codod"[11"]
100
#5-45860

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 2 August 4, 1972
dollars ($105,000,000,000) pumped into the national economy each year by the current leisure time/recreation boom which we are experiencing. The money spent in this country in spare time pursuits is in excess of the cost of national defense; it is more than we spend on the construction of new homes; it is greater than the aggregate income of all the country's farmers and exceeds the over-all value of this country's exports.
The current boom in outdoor recreation shows no signs of slowing down. Since there are currently in excess of 2,000 firms working on a four-day week, the establishment of five three-day holiday weekends each year and the fact that over forty million (40,000,000) workers enjoy a three week vacation each year, one can only anticipate continued increases. Early retirements too will contribute heavily to increased leisure time spending. It is currently estimated that over seventy-five percent (75%) of the people who are nine years of age or above indulge in some form of outdoor recreation. Unfortunately, due to a lack of urban recreation facilities and restrictive uses on rural land use, Americans continue to be faced with more and more time to do less and less.
Recreation vehicles are currently the only means by which families with small children and retired people may enjoy the pleasures of camping. Recreational camping vehicles offer the user sanitation facilities which are totally self-contained and provide a convenient way to carry their litter back home for proper disposal unlike the hiker who must find ways to dispose of waste materials in the out-of-doors without proper facilities.
Trailer Coach Association is in favor of a true multi-use concept of all public lands and particularly those administered by the federal government. The desire to preserve our "natural resources" by denying the use of land to the people who own and wish to make use of it is certainly not in the best interest of providing the needed opportunities for man to seek recreation and preserve their "human resources."
Over-use and conflict of interest have created a need for regulation of the use of federally-controlled public lands, as has become only too obvious by the preponderance of somewhat ill-conceived actions by extremest preservation groups. If regulation is to be fair, then certainly the prime objectives must be coordinated between various bureaus and departments charged with administrating the lands, equal consideration given to all recreational uses currently being pursued on those lands and an area by area determination must be made of the necessary regulation of individual sites.
The prime consideration must be to keep all lands open for all uses with minimum regulation unless there is a specific well-documented reason for establishing more restrictive regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 3 August 4, 1972
The need for an input from groups other than those interested in total preservation of our natural resources has recently given birth to several new organizations devoted to assisting the federal government in planning for the administration of land use and recreational policies. Among the most prominent of these new organizations is the "Outdoor Nation" (see Attachment #2). We are hopeful that this organization will provide your department with a realistic viewpoint and approach to solving some of the problems to which this statement is addressed.
Trailer Coach Association cannot help but feel that the definition of recreation vehicle as found in Presidential Order No. 11644 was never intended to include the vehicles as described above and in Attachment #1. However, the true off-road vehicles -- motorcycles, dune buggies, snow-mobiles, four-wheel drive, etc. are also of importance to the industry we represent. A recent study of the users of recreational camping vehicles in the State of California indicated that 40% of the vehicles surveyed were carrying or towing some type of off-road vehicle. We can only conclude that restrictions on the operation of these off-road vehicles will definitely effect the use and marketing of recreational camping vehicles and we, therefore, have a common interest in maintaining areas for their use.
We would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Department of Interior Task Force which developed the November 1971 study on Off-Road Recreation Vehicles. We feel that this is a true and objective look at the pros and cons of this legitimate form of outdoor recreation. On the other hand, we fail to understand the thinking of the Department as expressed in their Draft - Environmental Statement of May 26, 1972, which differs greatly from the ORRV Study. It would appear that the hard core preservationists must have had a hand in the drafting of the environmental statement.
Many unfortunate assertions have been made concerning the use and users of off-road vehicles by over-reactionary preservationist groups. Most of these extremists would have the nation believe that anyone who entered into the public domain on or in a mechanized vehicle was there for the sole purpose of damaging or destroying any or all things which came into his view. This most certainly is not the case. The users of recreation vehicles of all types are family people participating in family activities. They are conservationists interested in a clean, healthful environment and are concerned for the safety of themselves, their families and others while pursuing their preferred type of recreation. Through the use of public lands, people from all walks of life are brought together in a common interest, and healthy communication is often fostered between child and parent through their participation in activities which interest them mutually.

. The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 4
August 4, 1972
In the past year or so, many proposals have been made to not only restrict the use of public lands but to prohibit recreation vehicle use by classifying these areas as wilderness or primitive thereby denying use to some 98% of the national population. Since less than 2% of the nation's people are active hikers and backpackers, areas which restrict vehicle use become inaccessible to a very large majority. We have no quarrel with back-packing; however, the time required and the physical demands account for the relatively small number of people who are able to enjoy this type of activity. Surveys conclude that the majority of back-packers in the United States understandably are school teachers and students who have long summer vacations and are able to spend the long periods of time necessary to pursue this type of recreation. The average working man with two weeks annual vacation plus a few holiday weekends must restrict his recreational activities to those which may be reasonably pursued within a relatively short period of time.
It is interesting to note that the same groups who advocate increasing our country's wilderness areas and totally preserving our natural resources actively solicit and spend tax free funds to impair American commerce. These self-appointed guardians of the American public devote full time to lobbying and have filed lawsuits against nearly every large scale economically beneficial project which has been pursued by American industry during the past three to five years. Shocking examples of this unwarranted use of the country's judicial system are the halting of the Trans-Alaskan pipeline and the Florida Barge Canal. From where industry sits, it looks as if the government is "running scared" from a very vocal minority of the people.
Evidence of the preservationist impact on the United States economy is evidenced by the U. S. Chamber of Commerce's decision to take a stand against such groups, and to assume a more aggressive roll in shaping decisions being made not only by the courts, but by government agencies responsible for implementing environmental protection laws.
Areas which we feel worthy of exploration as a means of solving some of the problems created by the public's demand for outdoor recreation follow:
1. There are many tracts of government-owned land which at one time served as military reservations that are no longer in use which could be turned into recreation facilities to serve a portion of the close-in urban recreational needs.
2. The availability of low interest loans to recreational area development firms would stimulate development from the private sector.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 5 August 4, 1972
3. A problem currently being created by land closures is a higher concentration of use is being experienced by those areas which remain open which in turn auguments any problems that might be created by over-use. Therefore, very thorough consideration must be given to any closure of the public domain.
4. A reevaluation is in order of the types of recreation which are in one way or another subsidized by the government in relation to the numbers of people involved in various recreational pursuits.
5. The Bureau of Land Management should reevaluate their leasing practices of public lands for sheep and cattle grazing and mining operations. To prevent such unfair practices as "checkerboard leasing", current practices allow a lessee to lease sections of land which are diagonally adjacent to one another in a "checkerboard" pattern without paying for the lease rights on those sections of land which become entrapped by surrounding leaseholds. This practice allows leaseholders to monopolize 100% more land than they actually pay rental on and gives them the right to deny tresspass privileges to the general public.
6. An immediate and inexpensive solution to the problem of over-crowded existing recreation areas might be a rescheduling of vacation periods in the schools of our country. By requiring approximately 25% of the student bodies to vacation during each of four quarters annually, we would not only eliminate the summer vacation conjection but would make better use of our educational facilities as well.
7. A very effective program which was instituted by the government during the late 1930s under the banner of 'CCC' might be revitalized to assist in building new and rehabilitating our existing recreation facilities across the country while making use of the very large unemployed labor force which is currently available. Since through various welfare and unemployment compensation plans we, the taxpayers, support the unemployed while they are idle, it would make economical sense to accomplish some worthwhile end while supporting these people.
8. When conflicts occur between various groups interested in the use of a specific tract of land, we feel that the best solution is to call together the representatives from those interested groups and allow them to work out their differences in a democratic manner. The government body responsible for the operation and administration of the area in question should be called upon to moderate any arbitration of this type. Trailer Coach Association strongly believes in the theory of self-government and therefore feels that the people who are directly involved in the results of regulation are entitled to a say in the writing and implementation of those regulations.

The Honorable Rogers C. Morton
U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 6
August 4, 1972
9. Conflicts between user groups could be avoided to a large degree through proper education of the individuals involved and by encouraging users to understand the needs and motivations of other users. Through proper education by both government and organized user groups, policies of self-policing should be encouraged.
10. Under the present restrictions placed on wilderness and primitive areas, any "man-made" structures are prohibited. We suggest a reevaluation of these policies in view of the fact that the very people who demand expansion of our existing wilderness systems have a need for sanitary facilities, trash disposal and some degree of fire control in the existing areas.
11. A clean environment and balanced Ecosystem are among the top priorities involved in conservation and preservation of natural resources. We would suggest that the Department of the Interior take a close look at the sewage disposal facilities of any of the major cities in our country. It is appalling in this day of advanced technology that cities the size of San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago, New York, etc., etc., dump raw, untreated sewage into our rivers and oceans daily. It is naive indeed to think that we can solve our problems by continuing to pollute the areas in which we live while expending our financial resources to seek refuge away from those areas which we have polluted.
Again, we appreciate this opportunity to make our views known to your Department and trust that your consideration will be given to these remarks. We stand ready to assist in whatever manner which might be appropriate.
Respectfully submitted,
Lee W. Moses, Director
Recreation Vehicle Division

entries.summary: Antje B. Weaver generally supports the Draft Environmental Statement as sound and in the interest of all public lands users, while acknowledging that some environmental damage is unavoidable. She takes issue with specific claims in the draft, such as the assertion that ORVs strengthen family ties, and questions why rallies and races should be permitted on public lands when existing facilities could be used instead. She also expresses doubt that the proposal will be effectively implemented given budget cuts to federal agencies.
entries.statement_text:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior C Street between 18th and 19th, N. W. Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
I read with great interest the Draft Enviornmental Statement of the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the Public lands prepared by your Bureau on May 26, 1972.
On the whole, the proposal is sound and in the interest of all users of public lands. It is evident that, given our society and our standards, some long term damage to the environment cannot be avoided. But we should try to minimize the damage.
I have the following comments:
1. On page 12 of the Draft Enviornmental Statement I take issue with the statement that "ORV's can strengthen family ties." That may be so, but I don't think the use of these vehicles should be promoted on that basis, since there are numerous ways of strengthening family ties which do not pollute the air with fumes and noise and damage the enviornment physically.
2. In part b, Operating Criteria, page 6, it is stated that permits may granted for rallies, contests and organized races on land approved for such purposes. Why should there be such activities at all on public lands? Why can't these be held at facilities already existing for drag racing, stock-car racing and demolition derbies? Many communities have these facilities already--by using them the ORV users would not cause any damage at all, probably save a great deal of money and be close to help in case of accident.
3. Any program, to be effectively executed, must have sufficient manpower and funds. In view of the fact that President Nixon has made significant cuts in the budgets of many Federal agencies, I am doubtful that your proposal will be very effective, unless you are able to obtain trained manpower and funds for the implementation of your Draft Enviornmental Statement. After all, a program is only as good as the people who execute it, and in this case you need many and good people to do a good job.
Thank you for the opportunity to make these comments.
Very truly yours,
111
Antje B. Weaver

entries.statement_text:
14 Mar 1973
Mr. Nathaniel Reed US Department of Interior Washington, D.C. 20340
Dear Mr. Reed,
Attached is a position paper of the Milwaukee Audubon Society dealing with the subject of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land.
It is our understanding that public reaction was invited to a draft statement on ORV use issued by one of Interior's subagencies - the Eureau of Outdoor Recreation.
We trust that you will see that our position on the ORV matter gets to the proper agency in time for the hearing on this matter.
Sincerely
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society
12259 Underwood Fkwy
Wauwatosa, Wis 53226
CC: Cynthia Wilson (Natl Audubon)
CC: Ed Brigham (Natl Midwest Audubon Rep)
114
3/27/1

Position Paper
Milwaukee Audubon Society
regarding
The Use of Off The Road Recreational Vehicles on Public Land
prepared by
David Tillotson
President
Milwaukee Audubon Society
12 March 1973
In our assessment of the Draft Impact Statement on Off The Road Recreational Vehicles (prepared by the Department of Interior to implement Presidential Executive Order #11644) we believe that one serious weakness immediately presents itself. This is the fact that the Department of Interior Draft Statement helps institutionalize motorized recreational vehicles on the public lands and waters. It appears to make proper and acceptable what we in the Audubon Society believe is improper and un-acceptable. Before we as a Nation decide on THERE to use the ORV's schould we not decide THETHER to use them?
We seriously challenge and question the environmental wisdom in conceding to the thought that ORV's really belong, in almost any setting, on Federal Lands.

In a time of fast diminishing recreational space, is it wise to give any Governmental help (by an ORV policy statement) to ORV's, that simply by their existance and normal method of operation shrink recreational space at a disproportionately rapid rate. One can hear the motors for miles. The outdoor atmosphere is spoiled and diluted. ORV's swallow up land in minutes that would take a hiker hours to traverse. The new recreational vehicles are simply sophisticated ways for exploiting untouched nature more rapidly. Their growing use and popularity fits neatly, we will admit, into our current environmental milieu which is quite frankly hedonistic and materialistic.
The draft statement by implying that since the vehicles are here and are now using Public Lands, that it is proper for such use to continue without challenge.
Our second objection is that the statement as it stands is conciliatory and even not neutral in that it more or less takes the position of the ORV manufacturer and user by saying that this or that use MAY harm the soil, MIGHT damage lakes, etc, etc. In point of fact there are numerous documented instances where lakes, forests, waters, lands and wildlife are actually being harmed.
To mention just a few:
1. Trout spawning area spoiled by motorcycles in Sequoia Natl Forest (Calif) Documented Audubon Mag Jan '72
114. Coyotes run over by snowmobilers in Grand Teton Park (Wyo) Documented Audubon Mag Jan 172 
3. Snow compaction (in Canada) injures microenvironment of small mammals shrinking food chains Aud Mag Jan '72

4. Motorized outdoorsman can cause 200 times more damage to landscapes than the walker Audubon Mag Jan 172
5. Elk & Deer harassment by snowmobiles in S.E. Idaho "drains these animals of as much energy as a week's normal winter existance."

Aud Mag Jan '72
6. A Federal Game manager says that "snowmobiles can harm wild animals by driving them from protective cover & food supplies".

documented Milwaukee Journal Feb 6 '72
7. In Humbolt Natl Forest (Nev) jeeps and ORV's caused $50,000 damage to soil and vegetation. Aud Mag Jan 172
8. In one BLM study area in the west, trail bikers stripped away 60% of the vegetation in a 1500 acre area Aud Mag Jan 172
We question the unsubstantiated statement in the draft that a snowmobile or other ORV's are a boost to family ties. Considering what the car is generally known to have done to the American home and family life - 
_{\rm We}
 challenge the idea that ORV's are going to "Cement family relationships".
It will be argued that tens of thousands of individuals already own ORV's, that it is too late to outlaw on public lands; we can only regulate. We do not concele this point. On private lands, where motors are operated in such fashion that they do not infringe on the legitimate rights of contiguous property owners, we have no argument.
But we do question whether the larger, long term interests of today's and tomorrow's citizens (and ecosystems?) are best served by opening government lands to general use by ORV's.
We believe that the multiple use concept is deformed and abused 114 by asking that it stretch far enough to blanket, simultaneously, wilderness values and values pursued by ORV users.

We question the wisdom of permitting the great wilderness and wildlife sanctuaries (whether "official" or unofficial) to be overwhelmed by ORV activity. We believe the chief value of much undesignated federal land is that it furnishes a valuable staging area, a resting area, a cosmic mood, a wilderness retreat (incidentally for man and primarily for wildlife) and that non-use is healthful and recharges the intricate (not totally known) mechanisms of the various ecosystems. "Unused" wilderness, for example, is responsible for clean water coming out of mountain country as clean as it is.
Stricter controls, stricter enforcement is needed, with the focus on THE SPECIAL KIND OF HARM done to nature by ORV activity. Beyond the obvious damage to plants, lands, and animals and waterways, there is a loss of mood, a loss of authentic outdoor atmosphere which may be far more significant than all other kinds of damage combined.
The "differentness" of the land - the land undominated by ORV's is why we believe a vast majority of outdoor oriented citizens like the out of doors. These are the citizens, many now deceased, who have helped see to it that one third of the land of the United States has remained in public hands and in one sense, still "whole".
We of Audubon feel about all landscapes as Theodore Roosevenlt felt about one landscape, the Grand Canyon of the Colorado. The ages have been at work upon it - let it be.
114 Historian Will Lurant has written that Mations are born stoic and die epicurian. Are the CRV's an example of a mechanized epicurianism? A squandering of all the untouched land in America? Land that has not thus far been defiled by the joyous fact that it is remote?

ORV
ORV's don't give citizens who want to escape into nature the opportunity to do just that. The ORV catches the eye, it dominates the scene with motion, it kills solitude and stunts the growth and development of outdoor aesthetics. Its root is commercial, not esthetic; hedonistic and pagan, not frugal, disciplined, and sacrificial. In other words, the kinds of philosophies that are pre-requisites to the conservation movement are really not yet understood to the ORV user and manufacturer.
Because of the nature of the ORV itself, we must put restraints on it we will not put on other kinds of recreational devices; sail boats, kayaks, canoes, rowboats, bicycles, skis, snowshoes, ice boats. We believe that ORV's (land, water, air) pose very serious threats to several of our endangered species. By means of the ORV we visualize an ever growing number of ill-informed hunters having access to timber wolves, condors, eagles, antelope, prairie dogs, mountain lions. The consequences, for wildlife, of access by way of ORV use, is ominous for the future of many species.
People are coming into nature hopeful of finding enough quality in the way of the environment to save them the extra expense and time of driving a thousand miles more to a place—like a National Fark where severe restrictions have curtailed ORV activity. Much public land, all over the nation, should be free of the blight of the machine.

114 Vast, intact acreages, not subdued by ORV activity, ought to be available to those who are gentler users of the land.

To sum up, we do not believe that certain conflicting uses on ' public lands can be reconciled and no amount of cosmetic rhetoric should be allowed to conceal this fact.
The draft statement, as written, is, in a sense, a commentary on the permissive temper of our times. Rather than ever say NO to anybody, be it the Army Corps of Engineers, the Highways builders, the stream channelizers, the rioters on the campus, or group X,Y, or Z that has siezed a park or a building or a National Forest and then demands that we negotiate. We can't seem to consider the social and environmental imperative of using the simple word, NO!
Merely because Federal managers have thus far (apparently in lieu of directives from anyone) failed to halt the mushrooming encroachments by ORV's on Federal lands, is no reason to assume that the presence of these vehicles is proper or that it should be allowed to continue.
In the absence of a directive, we believe managers should have held the Line and not accommodated the ORV user.
The assumption by Federal land managers that ORV's do BELONG is far more pernicious than one would think. For it leads to institutionalization of the idea that the ORV on Federal land is here to stay.
The land managers are put in a position of accomodating themselves to the CRV and being on the defensive from the beginning.
114 We are convinced that the long suffering but concerned silent majority of the American public gets a great feeling of solace from merely contemplating the fact that vast chunks of Federal land are as yet unspoiled by the Users and producers of ORV's.

And further, that these lands are going to be protected by Federal managers for all time to come, regardless of the talk (and money) of the advocates of motorized exploitation.
In World War II when gas rationing and the war effort cut the visits to the National Forests, there was a 50% drop in the losses due to forest fire. Natural (lightning) fires tend to start high on the mountain while man caused fires (9 out of 10 forest fires are still man caused) start at a lower level and can do much more damage. Thy does the draft statement emphasize the potential of the ORV in preventing fire, when there is historical evidence from World War II and the National Forests, that human access to the forest, especially the remote forests, will increase the number of fires. Come studies that have delved into the psychological make-up of the ORV user indicates that they have a significantly higher accident rate that the non-user. The ORV buff turns out to be a "risk taker" and thus has a higher accident rate. This risk taker is going to pose amever greater threat by fire in the forest and on the grasslands - and game law violators are going to be next to impossible to stop because the ORV will provide opportunity to go anywhere.
114 On most public lands, in such places as the National Parks and monuments, in State Parks, in nearly all the Mational and State Forests, and on the vast tracts controlled by the Bureau of Land Management, we believe motors are a mistake. The evidence of ecological damage and impairment of the natural mood is going to increase, not decrease.

Therefore we believe that a phasing out of the motors from various "established" places should begin at once. We believe that conservation authorities should not develop or promote trails as these trails lead to "locking in" a kind of outdoor use that must eventually be phased out. Also trails are merely "way stations" on the road to ever greater development.
When Congress created the Park System in 1916 it stated that "Above all, the mood of naturalness should prevail."
Except for emergency rescue work, law enforcement activity, and necessary patrols of one kind or another, we believe that concept should eventually govern ORV activity on all public land. Private holdings, private lands, vasts tracts furnished by the manufacturers of the ORV's themselves (two thirds of this Nation's land mass is private) - this is where ORV activity can legitimately be expanded.
Respectfully submitted
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society 12259 Underwood Pkwy Wauwatosa, Wis 53226

entries.summary_quote: We concur with the general approach outlined by the Department for regulating ORV use, and urge that the specific regulations developed by Interior's land managing agencies to designate lands for ORV use contain stringent provisions for: (1) analyzing the environmental impact of the specific types of ORV use contemplated on an area-by-area basis prior to opening any lands; (2) controlling the type and intensity of ORV use in lands opened; (3) monitoring the effects of such use; and, (4) if significant damage to environmental values is occurring, taking prompt corrective measures, including restrictions or prohibition of further ORV use.
entries.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency concurred with the Department of Interior's general approach to regulating ORV use but urged that specific regulations include stringent provisions for environmental impact analysis, use controls, monitoring, and prompt corrective measures including restrictions or prohibition if significant damage occurs. EPA deferred its detailed comments pending review of proposed regulations from the land managing bureaus and the National Park Service. Overall, EPA's stance was conditionally supportive, endorsing the framework while pressing for robust environmental safeguards in implementation.
entries.statement_text:
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY WASHINGTON, D.C. 20460
1 5 SEP 1972
Mr. James G. Watt
Director
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
U.S. Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
The Environmental Protection Agency has reviewed the draft environmental impact statement for the Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands prepared by the Department of Interior and dated May 26, 1972. We concur with the general approach outlined by the Department for regulating ORV use, and urge that the specific regulations developed by Interior's land managing agencies to designate lands for ORV use contain stringent provisions for: (1) analyzing the environmental impact of the specific types of ORV use contemplated on an area-by-area basis prior to opening any lands; (2) controlling the type and intensity of ORV use in lands opened; (3) monitoring the effects of such use; and, (4) if significant damage to environmental values is occurring, taking prompt corrective measures, including restrictions or prohibition of further ORV use.
We are advised that the official comment period for this environmental impact statement has been extended to cover the period allowed for review of the regulations proposed by the Bureaus of Land Management, Reclamation and Sport Fisheries and Wildlife and the National Park Service. Therefore, we are deferring transmittal of our detailed comments on this draft impact statement until after we have had an opportunity to review the proposed regulations.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this statement. We look forward to reviewing the pending regulations on ORV use on public lands and the subsequent operating regulations.
Sincerely yours,
Sheldon Meizers
Sheldon Meyers
Director
Office of Federal Activities

entries.summary: The Federated Conservationists of Westchester County argues that the Draft EIS fails to adequately address the growing energy crisis and the increasing reliance on petroleum imports. On the basis of national policy, the organization recommends adopting the alternative of closing all Interior lands to ORV use (except for emergencies), contending that encouraging recreational ORV use exacerbates demand on scarce petroleum resources. They urge the Department of the Interior to factor energy conservation into its land use policy.

FEDERATED CONSERVATIONISTS OF WESTCHESTER COUNTY, INC.
Dedicated to environmental planning and education for the preservation of our natural resources.

Box 1306, Marymount College, Tarrytown, New York 10591 (914) 631-8336
March 9, 1973

OFFICERS

MRS. DAVID DONALDSON
President

GEORGE M. RAYMOND
1st Vice President

2nd Vice President

Secretary
JOHN THIES
Treasurer
Directors At Large

Altred Forsyth

William Hoppen
Dr. Jay Jacobson
