Dr. John J. McMahon
Mrs. Robert L. Reed
Pieter H. Vree
Director, Eureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior Washington, D.C. 20240
SUBJECT: Relation of Energy Crisis to Encouragement of Off-Road Vehicle Use
Dear Sir:
These comments are submitted in response to the Draft Environmental Impact Statement of the Department of the Interior, dated May 27, 1972, published June 2, 1972, with regard to Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands.
Apart from the normal environmental considerations, not enough attention has been paid in the draft statement to the growing energy crisis, as it has been termed, and the effect upon the domestic economy and transit generally of increasing reliance on imports to meet our growing fuel and energy needs.
In light of this, FCWC questions, as a matter of national policy, the encouragement of recreational use, through the opening of public lands to snowmobiles and off-road vehicles, with the consequent increasing demand upon ever-shrinking petroleum and energy supplies.
This would indicate, on the basis of national policy, the wisdom of adoption of the alternative as referred to in Item "4" of the Draft Statement, to close all Interior lands to ORV use (except for emergency purposes, of course). Eventually, we may simply find that priorities in use of scarce petroleum resources require further limitations on use thereof by recreational vehicles.
The Department of the Interior, as a matter of environmental responsibility, must take this into consideration in establishing its current land use policy on land administered by the Department.
Sincerely,
600
Mrs. David C. Lonaldson
anne Donaldson
Fresident

The assumption by Federal land managers that ORV's do BELONG is far more pernicious than one would think. For it leads to institutionalization of the idea that the ORV on Federal land is here to stay.
The land managers are put in a position of accomodating themselves to the CRV and being on the defensive from the beginning.
114 We are convinced that the long suffering but concerned silent majority of the American public gets a great feeling of solace from merely contemplating the fact that vast chunks of Federal land are as yet unspoiled by the Users and producers of ORV's.

And further, that these lands are going to be protected by Federal managers for all time to come, regardless of the talk (and money) of the advocates of motorized exploitation.
In World War II when gas rationing and the war effort cut the visits to the National Forests, there was a 50% drop in the losses due to forest fire. Natural (lightning) fires tend to start high on the mountain while man caused fires (9 out of 10 forest fires are still man caused) start at a lower level and can do much more damage. Thy does the draft statement emphasize the potential of the ORV in preventing fire, when there is historical evidence from World War II and the National Forests, that human access to the forest, especially the remote forests, will increase the number of fires. Come studies that have delved into the psychological make-up of the ORV user indicates that they have a significantly higher accident rate that the non-user. The ORV buff turns out to be a "risk taker" and thus has a higher accident rate. This risk taker is going to pose amever greater threat by fire in the forest and on the grasslands - and game law violators are going to be next to impossible to stop because the ORV will provide opportunity to go anywhere.
114 On most public lands, in such places as the National Parks and monuments, in State Parks, in nearly all the Mational and State Forests, and on the vast tracts controlled by the Bureau of Land Management, we believe motors are a mistake. The evidence of ecological damage and impairment of the natural mood is going to increase, not decrease.

Therefore we believe that a phasing out of the motors from various "established" places should begin at once. We believe that conservation authorities should not develop or promote trails as these trails lead to "locking in" a kind of outdoor use that must eventually be phased out. Also trails are merely "way stations" on the road to ever greater development.
When Congress created the Park System in 1916 it stated that "Above all, the mood of naturalness should prevail."
Except for emergency rescue work, law enforcement activity, and necessary patrols of one kind or another, we believe that concept should eventually govern ORV activity on all public land. Private holdings, private lands, vasts tracts furnished by the manufacturers of the ORV's themselves (two thirds of this Nation's land mass is private) - this is where ORV activity can legitimately be expanded.
Respectfully submitted
David Tillotson
President - Milwaukee
Audubon Society 12259 Underwood Pkwy Wauwatosa, Wis 53226

entries.summary: Mrs. David C. Donaldson, as President of the Federated Conservationists of Westchester County, argues that the Draft EIS fails to adequately address the growing energy crisis and the impact of increased ORV use on dwindling petroleum supplies. She contends that encouraging recreational ORV use on public lands is contrary to sound national policy, and therefore recommends adopting the alternative of closing all Interior lands to ORV use (except for emergencies). She urges the Department of the Interior to factor energy resource constraints into its land use policy.

SUBJECT: Relation of Energy Crisis to Encouragement of Off-Road Vehicle Use
Dear Sir:
These comments are submitted in response to the Draft Environmental Impact Statement of the Department of the Interior, dated May 27, 1972, published June 2, 1972, with regard to Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands.
Apart from the normal environmental considerations, not enough attention has been paid in the draft statement to the growing energy crisis, as it has been termed, and the effect upon the domestic economy and transit generally of increasing reliance on imports to meet our growing fuel and energy needs.
In light of this, FCWC questions, as a matter of national policy, the encouragement of recreational use, through the opening of public lands to snowmobiles and off-road vehicles, with the consequent increasing demand upon ever-shrinking petroleum and energy supplies.
This would indicate, on the basis of national policy, the wisdom of adoption of the alternative as referred to in Item "4" of the Draft Statement, to close all Interior lands to ORV use (except for emergency purposes, of course). Eventually, we may simply find that priorities in use of scarce petroleum resources require further limitations on use thereof by recreational vehicles.
The Department of the Interior, as a matter of environmental responsibility, must take this into consideration in establishing its current land use policy on land administered by the Department.
Sincerely,

entries.summary_quote: This correspondence is for the purpose of registering my indignation and opposition concerning the implementation of Executive Order 11644.
entries.summary: R. H. Schif strongly opposes Executive Order 11644, viewing it as an unconstitutional infringement on personal freedoms and an act of recreational discrimination against the roughly 15 million four-wheel-drive vehicle users compared to skiers. He argues that the claimed ecological damage from off-road vehicles in Colorado is exaggerated and overstated, and that the order creates undue hardship for hunters, mineral developers, the aged and infirm, and disabled veterans. He demands the order be rescinded and that such decisions be returned to Congress.
entries.statement_text:
Dear Sir:
This correspondence is for the purpose of registering my indignation and opposition concerning the implementation of Executive Order 11644. This order is apparently the result of pressures from various hysterical groups such as the Sierra Club and the hippies, if there's a difference.
Following are a few reasons which I feel justify my attitude toward the subject.
Contrary to the opening wording of the order, I feel that indirectly it says that, "By virtue of the power vested in me as President of the United States, I hereby revoke your constitutional right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."
The immediate result of this order has been to create a profusion of puppet dictators in the guise of land administrators.
Here in Colorado West, the authoritative agencies have installed large signs advising one to restrict travel to constructed roads only, under threat of monetary and penal consequences. They then post many constructed roads "off limits."
It can be assumed that this regulation has been imposed as a result of erroneous reports of excessive terrain or ecological damage. In my opinion, the majority of the complainants probably can't even define the word "ecology." Regrettably, you are probably not in a position to see and establish the truth in fact for yourself.
I have no quarrel with skiers or skiing and cannot speak for the rest of the country; however, I sincerely believe that the claimed vehicular damage in Colorado West, if laid end to end, would not equal the 27 miles by 60 feet of timber and vegetation eliminated for ski trails on public lands involved in just one small complex near here.
Statistically, there are roughly We to 5 million skiers and approximately 5 million four-wheel drive vehicles averaging three occupants each. This obviously affects 15 million public land users in contrast and indicates recreational group discrimination.

Colorado derives income each year of 5 to 7 million dollars from the sale of hunting and fishing licenses alone. I predict that this income will be effectively reduced by 85 percent within two years as a result of this order.
Location and development of much needed new mineral and petroleum resources are severely handicapped accordingly.
There are many all-terrain vehicles available which, because of their construction, virtually eliminate the possibility of terrain damage. The ground contact P.S.I. being 1/350 that of a horse. These apparently were not taken into consideration with the issuance of this order.
This literally forces off-road enthusiasts to streets and high-ways and probably will be reflected by a proportionate percentage increase in accident and fatality statistics.
The aged and infirm are pretty much left out of public land participation as a result.
There are many of us who, because of damages sustained in the battle against dictatorial oppression during World War II, do not go along with the aura surrounding this subject.
I personally believe that decisions such as these should be returned to the authority where they rightfully belong: The United States Congress.
Last year, Gordon Allott sent tapes to the regional radio stations proclaiming the Flat Tops area as a natural for inclusion into the wilderness because it was devoid of human development. In reality, the area has many rouds, etc., constructed under the authority of the Forest Service for the purpose of harvesting beetle-killed timber resulting from excessive predator control. This could have been a contributing factor in Allott's defeat because we are really not that stupid.
In no way do I feel that consideration should be extended for further land addition to the wilderness concept until Executive Order 11644 is rescinded.
Very truly yours,
R. H. Schif

entries.summary: Roger A. Dean supports the Draft Environmental Statement as a sound approach to managing off-road vehicle use on public lands, but conditions his approval on effective enforcement of the usage guidelines. He endorses responsible ORV use and expresses concern that the Executive Order's intent to balance ORV access with environmental protection not be undermined by those who would ban all off-road vehicle traffic.
entries.statement_text:
1428 Tomasita St. NE Albuquerque, New Mexico 87112
12 Oct 72
Mr. James W. Monroe United States Department of Interior Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Mr. Monroe:
I have recently received the copy of the department's Draft Environmental Statement along with a copy of the letter you sent to my congressman, the Honorable Manuel Lujan, Jr. Thank you for such a comprehensive reply to my inquiries concerning off-raod vehicle use of public lands.
It is apparrent from the documents sent me that the President and the Department of Interior are concerned with providing public lands that are available for all sorts of recreation, both for use by off-road vehicles and others. I feel that the Draft Environmental Statement represents a sound approach to the problem of off-road vehicle use of public lands, however the dev to the problem will be the efficacy with which the usage guidelines for these areas are enforced. I wholeheartedly support the responsible use of public lands, and do not wish to have my usage of these areas curtailed by irresponsible use by others.
I hope that the intent of the Executive Order, to provide suitable areas for off-road vehicles as well as protecting the environment, is not compromised by excessive pressure from those individuals who would ban all off-road vehicle traffic.
I am looking forward to seeing the results of this study in ensuing months.
Respectfully yours,
ROGER A. DEAN

entries.summary: Sheldon Meyers, on behalf of the EPA, concurs with the Department of Interior's general approach to regulating ORV use but urges that specific regulations include stringent provisions for area-by-area environmental impact analysis, controlling the type and intensity of use, monitoring effects, and taking prompt corrective measures if significant damage occurs. The EPA deferred its detailed comments pending review of proposed regulations from the land managing agencies. Overall, the EPA's stance is conditionally supportive, contingent on robust environmental safeguards being incorporated into the final regulations.
entries.statement_text:
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY WASHINGTON, D.C. 20460
1 5 SEP 1972
Mr. James G. Watt
Director
Director
Bureau of Outdoor Recreation
U.S. Department of Interior
Washington, D.C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
The Environmental Protection Agency has reviewed the draft environmental impact statement for the Proposed Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11644 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands prepared by the Department of Interior and dated May 26, 1972. We concur with the general approach outlined by the Department for regulating ORV use, and urge that the specific regulations developed by Interior's land managing agencies to designate lands for ORV use contain stringent provisions for: (1) analyzing the environmental impact of the specific types of ORV use contemplated on an area-by-area basis prior to opening any lands; (2) controlling the type and intensity of ORV use in lands opened; (3) monitoring the effects of such use; and, (4) if significant damage to environmental values is occurring, taking prompt corrective measures, including restrictions or prohibition of further ORV use.
We are advised that the official comment period for this environmental impact statement has been extended to cover the period allowed for review of the regulations proposed by the Bureaus of Land Management, Reclamation and Sport Fisheries and Wildlife and the National Park Service. Therefore, we are deferring transmittal of our detailed comments on this draft impact statement until after we have had an opportunity to review the proposed regulations.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this statement. We look forward to reviewing the pending regulations on ORV use on public lands and the subsequent operating regulations.
Sincerely yours,
Sheldon Meizers
Sheldon Meyers
Director
Office of Federal Activities
